sweeps.topic: Dual-system architectures where a slow language model steers a fast controller and the robot talks while acting — precedents for Parcel's Model B (steering/narration) on top of Model A (duplex trainable controller)

findings.claim: Hi Robot is the closest precedent for Model B over Model A: a PaliGemma-3B high-level VLM re-runs inference 'either when one second has elapsed, or when a new interaction with the user takes place', emits an atomic language command for the pi0 low-level policy, grounds interjections like 'that's not trash' in the current image, and can include a verbal utterance played through TTS; the high level trains in ~2 h on 8xH100 from VLM-synthesised interjections (negative task / situated correction / specific constraint).
findings.source_title: Hi Robot: Open-Ended Instruction Following with Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Models (Physical Intelligence; ICML 2025)
findings.kind: primary paper (arXiv full text) + project page https://www.pi.website/research/hirobot
findings.numbers: HL tick 1 s or on user event; LL 73 ms/step on-board, 50 Hz with chunking; avg instruction accuracy 76% vs flat VLA 36% vs GPT-4o HL 30%; avg task progress 81/44/64%; per task IA/TP: bussing 74/77, sandwich 83/80, grocery 72/85; HL training ~2 h on 8xH100, AdamW lr 1e-5, batch 512; inference 1-2 RTX 4090; STT Whisper large-v2; robots UR5e, bimanual ARX, mobile ARX (16-D action); no weights released
findings.relevance: Defines the event-driven prompt-refresh injection, the language-subtask interface, the optional-utterance talk-back, and the synthetic interjection data recipe Parcel's Model B can copy; stated limitation 'lacks memory' is what Parcel's last-minute + global-history streams address.

findings.claim: ELLSA is the first single-model full-duplex listen/look/speak/act system: speech, image, text and action tokens are interleaved in fixed 1 s time blocks, the model itself decides barge-in and turn-taking, and it can answer progress questions while acting — but speaking while acting costs 11 points of manipulation success and it is simulation-only.
findings.source_title: End-to-end Listen, Look, Speak and Act (ELLSA)
findings.kind: primary paper (arXiv full text) + HF model card https://huggingface.co/tsinghua-ee/ELLSA
findings.numbers: SA-MoE: LLaMA-3.1-8B speech expert + Emu3 action expert, 18B params total, Apache-2.0 weights on HF; 1 s blocks: speech in 5 Hz, 1 image/s, 8 text tokens out, 1 s speech+action out; per-block latency 854 ms (speech-to-speech) / 786 ms (speech-to-action) on A100; LIBERO avg 89.4% vs pi0-FAST 85.5%, CoT-VLA 81.1%; action barge-in 94.3%; dialogue/action turn-taking 100%; defective-instruction rejection 100%; speaking-while-acting 73.2% vs 84.4% acting alone (LIBERO-LONG); context-grounded progress VQA ~80%; data: LIBERO 3,386 + 1,693 rejection samples, 729k QA, LibriSpeech 281k + GigaSpeech 200k; limitations: no backchannel, 'yet to be validated in real-world settings'
findings.relevance: Gives the only measured cost of tight speech-action coupling in one network and a six-behaviour duplex benchmark (turn-taking, action turn-taking, rejection, barge-in, speaking-while-acting, progress VQA) Parcel can adopt; argues for keeping narration off Model A's control path.

findings.claim: DuplexSLA shows a native duplex model can carry a rate-limited 'action channel' (planning text, interrupt/backchannel labels, JSON tool calls) alongside continuous assistant speech on a 160 ms chunk clock, deciding interrupt/pause/backchannel from internal semantic state with sub-second delay — the closest published shape to a 'representation stream' the voice narrates from, though its actions are tool calls, not robot motion.
findings.source_title: DuplexSLA: A Full-Duplex Spoken Language Model with Synchronized Speech, Language, and Action
findings.kind: primary paper (arXiv full text) + GitHub README https://github.com/hyzhang24/DuplexSLA
findings.numbers: 160 ms chunks; assistant TA4 = 1 text anchor + 4 audio tokens at 40 ms stride; user channel 2 features per chunk at 80 ms stride; action channel capped at 10 text tokens/chunk (overflow spills to next chunks); backbone Step-Audio-2-mini ~7B (README; HTML extractor read '77B' — conflict noted); CPT ~500k h audio (duplex dialogue ~320k h) + 1.92M text; post-training ~50k h; DuplexSLA-Bench 2,100 cases: interrupt 99.33% @ 0.40 s, backchannel 98.33% @ 0.32 s, pause 93.33% @ 0.27 s, normal 96.00% @ 0.27 s; without prefill 94.34% @ 0.30 s vs GPT-4 Realtime 96.50% @ 1.57 s; tool-call 85.56% @ 0.64 s vs ASR+LLM cascade 91.33% @ 2.77 s; 50-function cabin/smart-home schema; MIT license; checkpoints 'not yet released'
findings.relevance: Concrete design for emitting plan/status text without halting speech, and a benchmark (pause/interrupt/backchannel + in-conversation tool call) for Parcel's conversational-amendment evals; also warns that per-chunk decoding budget leaves only a few action tokens per chunk.

findings.claim: Yell At Your Robot demonstrates the simplest injection mechanism: a spoken correction (Whisper) temporarily overrides the high-level policy's language output and goes straight to the low-level language-conditioned policy, and fine-tuning the high level on those corrections (4-11% of base data) lifts success by 15-45 points.
findings.source_title: Yell At Your Robot: Improving On-the-Fly from Language Corrections
findings.numbers: HL (ViT/CLIP) queried every 4 s; LL = ACT with EfficientNet-b3 + DistilBERT; pi_deploy uses l_user if intervention else l_H; 'stop' to intervene; 2 s pre-intervention context saved; base data bag packing 1,170 traj / 41,517 segments / 1,054 commands, trail mix 317 / 7,008 / 104, plate cleaning 265 / 3,236 / 33; correction data 4.2-10.8% of base; gains after finetune +20-45 (bag), +15-20 (trail mix), +15-25 (plate) pts over 20 trials; ALOHA, 14-D action, 4 cameras
findings.relevance: The override-switch rule maps directly onto Parcel's task executive (suspend/amend/resume) and gives a data-efficiency benchmark for learning Model B from owner corrections in sim.

findings.claim: TIC-VLA is the only published dual-system navigation stack measured on a Unitree Go2 with a Jetson Orin: a 0.5 Hz VLM writes KV-cache features + waypoints that a 10 Hz action policy consumes asynchronously, and RL fine-tuning keeps success high despite multi-second reasoning latency.
findings.source_title: TIC-VLA: A Think-in-Control Vision-Language-Action Model for Robot Navigation in Dynamic Environments
findings.numbers: VLM = InternViT-300M + Qwen2.5-0.5B at 0.5 Hz; action policy 10 Hz; reasoning features 256->512 dims + waypoints; data SCAND 8.7 h + GND 11 h + DynaNav 5.1 h; sim SR 55.29% vs OmniVLA 31.76% / MobileVLA 32.94%, collision 28.24%; real Go2: 0.85 SR on RTX 4060 Laptop (50 W), 0.75 on Jetson Orin NX (25 W); 85 test cases, 4 environments
findings.relevance: Sets the realistic on-device slow/fast rates (0.5-1 Hz / 10 Hz) and model size (~0.5B VLM) for Parcel's Model A on the AGX Orin, matching the existing 10 Hz frame clock.

findings.claim: pi0.5 folds the hierarchy into one network — it first predicts the semantic subtask in language, then the 50 Hz action chunk — and shows that 'verbal instruction' data (a person coaching the robot step by step) is a training source whose removal causes significant degradation.
findings.source_title: pi0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization
findings.kind: primary paper (arXiv full text) + blog https://www.pi.website/blog/pi05
findings.numbers: ~400 h mobile-manipulation data in ~100 homes; 97.6% of phase-1 data from other sources (ME, CE+OXE, HL labels, web CapsFusion/COCO/Cambrian-7M/PixMo/VQAv2, VI); 50 Hz with chunking, 10 denoising steps; evaluated in 3 unseen real homes; ~100 training environments approaches in-domain baseline; 'no VI' -> significant degradation; implicit-HL ablation second best; pi0 base (https://arxiv.org/html/2410.24164): PaliGemma 3B + 300M action expert = 3.3B, H=50, 10,000+ h, 7 embodiments, 73 ms on RTX 4090; no weights stated
findings.relevance: Precedent for Model A emitting a language subtask as its narratable representation from inside the controller, and for using owner coaching transcripts as training data.

findings.claim: Figure Helix couples a 7B VLM at 7-9 Hz to an 80M-parameter 200 Hz controller through a single continuous latent vector — fast, but with no language in the fast loop and no speech, so nothing is narratable without an extra head.
findings.source_title: Helix: A Vision-Language-Action Model for Generalist Humanoid Control (Figure AI)
findings.numbers: S2 7B open-weight VLM at 7-9 Hz; S1 80M cross-attention encoder-decoder at 200 Hz; interface = single continuous latent vector, S1 uses most recent; ~500 h teleop (<5% of prior VLA datasets); hindsight instructions from auto-labelling VLM; each system on a dedicated low-power embedded GPU; no success %; no speech
findings.relevance: Counter-example for the Model A representation: a latent interface is uninformative to the hosted voice; also the highest fast-loop rate in the field.

findings.claim: NVIDIA GR00T N1 is the open dual-system reference: a 1.34B Eagle-2 VLM at 10 Hz feeding a flow-matching diffusion transformer at 120 Hz via cross-attention, trained on a real/synthetic/human-video data pyramid and released under CC BY 4.0.
findings.source_title: GR00T N1: An Open Foundation Model for Generalist Humanoid Robots
findings.numbers: VLM 1.34B (2.2B total) at 10 Hz on L40; DiT 4 inference steps, chunk H=16, 120 Hz, 63.9 ms/chunk bf16 on L40; data 88 h humanoid teleop + 827 h neural trajectories + 780,000 sim trajectories (6,500 h); ~50,000 H100 GPU-h pretrain, up to 1024 GPUs; RoboCasa 32.1% vs DP 25.6%, DexMimicGen 66.5% vs 56.1%, GR-1 50.0% vs 32.7%; real robot avg 76.8% vs 46.4%, 10%-data 42.6% vs 10.2%; CC BY 4.0 weights/data/benchmarks
findings.relevance: Open weights and the 10 Hz / 120 Hz split are a template for Model A's controller side; its System 1 is what VITA-E reuses under a speaking VLM.

findings.claim: VITA-E makes the VLM itself the controller via special tokens ([RES]/[ACT]/[HALT]/[END]/[INST]) and runs two VLA instances (Active/Standby) so a new user utterance preempts ongoing speech or action; the [INST] token separates the spoken part of a response from the internal action instruction.
findings.source_title: VITA-E: Natural Embodied Interaction with Concurrent Seeing, Hearing, Speaking, and Acting
findings.numbers: VLM VITA-1.5 (frozen) + GR00T diffusion action expert; output S_t=(control token, spoken text, action instruction); speech interruption 100%, emergency stop 100%, task switching 93.3% (30 trials); voice response latency 2.26 s avg (10 tests); 300 teleop demos/task at 20 Hz; bs 64, lr 1e-4, 20k steps; Fourier GR2 humanoid (26 DoF), RealSense D455; below GR00T on LIBERO; no code release stated
findings.relevance: A concrete output format for Model B (spoken part vs action instruction, explicit completion token = the 'Done!' trigger) and a preemption pattern for mid-task interruptions.

findings.claim: RoboEgo (FLM-Ego) is a 7B omnimodal backbone with native full duplexity and an 80 ms theoretical duplex latency that watches, listens, speaks and drives a humanoid's locomotion/gestures from a shared hidden state, but discloses no data sizes and releases nothing.
findings.source_title: RoboEgo System Card: An Omnimodal Model with Native Full Duplexity
findings.numbers: 7B autoregressive backbone; 80 ms theoretical duplex latency; text-first monologue placed at t - spk_delay; lightweight audio/language/action decoders off shared hidden state; LEJU Kuavo: locomotion 96.5%, telepathy 97.2%; vs Qwen2.5-Omni helpfulness 7.2/7.4, naturalness 8.2/7.9, responsiveness 8.8/8.1, robustness 8.0/7.7 (5 annotators); data sizes and inference hardware not disclosed; no release
findings.relevance: Existence proof that one duplex model can speak while commanding locomotion; the text-first monologue trick is a way to expose narratable text before audio.

findings.claim: RT-H makes language the interface inside one 55B model: it predicts a 'language motion' then the action, lets a human overwrite the language motion in a correction mode re-queried at a fixed frequency, and only the language-motion query needs retraining on corrections.
findings.source_title: RT-H: Action Hierarchies Using Language
findings.numbers: PaLI-X 55B; >2,500 language motions; 100K demos (70K kitchen + 30K diverse), 30+ task categories, 8 eval tasks; +15% over RT-2 (6/8 tasks); ~20% lower MSE than RT-2, 40% with ground-truth motions; interventions raise avg success 40% -> 63% with 30 correction episodes/task; novel objects 65% vs 55%; async querying predicts the skill one step ahead
findings.relevance: Shows the override of a language intermediate is enough to steer without touching the action head — the same decoupling Parcel wants between Model B and Model A.

findings.claim: Inner Monologue is the canonical language-feedback replanning loop: success detection, scene descriptions and human answers are appended to the LLM prompt after each skill, and the planner switches goals when a human changes the plan mid-task, roughly doubling real-world success under disturbances.
findings.source_title: Inner Monologue: Embodied Reasoning through Planning with Language Models
findings.kind: primary paper (ar5iv full text; abs https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05608)
findings.numbers: InstructGPT + CLIP-Transporter (tabletop), PaLM 540B + SayCan skills (kitchen); sim tabletop 80% -> 90% (+success) -> 94% (+scene); real tabletop 45% -> 90%; real kitchen with disturbances SayCan 30.8% -> 60.4%; LLM re-queried after each skill
findings.relevance: Establishes that a language success/scene digest fed back to the planner is the key signal — Parcel's StateDigest is that digest; Code as Policies (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.07753, 39.8% HumanEval) by contrast has no interruption handling.

findings.claim: Gemini Robotics 1.5 splits an embodied-reasoning orchestrator (GR-ER 1.5) that calls the VLA as a tool and performs success detection at 5 Hz from a VLA that 'thinks' in natural language before each action, with thinking traces visualisable to the user; the agent roughly doubles long-horizon progress but the report does not address user interruption.
findings.source_title: Gemini Robotics 1.5: Pushing the Frontier of Generalist Robots with Advanced Embodied Reasoning, Thinking, and Motion Transfer
findings.kind: primary technical report (arXiv full text) + blog https://deepmind.google/blog/gemini-robotics-15-brings-ai-agents-into-the-physical-world/
findings.numbers: Thinking traces appended to context before each action; orchestrator success detection evaluated at 5 Hz; agent 'near 80%' progress vs thinking-VLA alone 'up to 44 percent'; failure 22% vs 44.5% (planning 9 vs 25.5, success-detection 4 vs 6, action 9 vs 13); GR-ER 1.5 best on 15 embodied-reasoning benchmarks; ER 1.5 in Gemini API / AI Studio, VLA to select partners; Gemini Robotics 1.0 (https://arxiv.org/html/2503.20020): cloud backbone <160 ms, e2e ~250 ms, 50 Hz, no speech, thousands of hours over 12 months
findings.relevance: The orchestrator-as-tool-caller + language thinking traces is the hosted-model-friendly variant of Model B; 5 Hz success detection is a reference rate for progress reporting.

findings.claim: Embodied Chain-of-Thought shows reasoning text emitted before actions is both a narration source and a steering handle (a human edits the chain and it is held for 5 steps), at a 50x token cost per step mitigated by freezing or asynchronous dual instances.
findings.source_title: Robotic Control via Embodied Chain-of-Thought Reasoning (ECoT)
findings.numbers: OpenVLA-7B; TASK/PLAN/SUBTASK/MOVE/GRIPPER/OBJECTS; ~350 tokens/step vs 7; 5-step freeze +24% speed at 72% success; async execution +40% speed; Bridge V2 2.5M transitions; +45/+22/+19/+18 abs over Octo/OpenVLA/RT-2-X/naive CoT (in-dist), +48/+34/+16/+16 OOD views; human intervention +48% on hardest tasks
findings.relevance: Quantifies the latency price of language-level representations in the control loop and the benefit of holding an injected correction for a fixed number of steps.

findings.claim: Moshi is the reference full-duplex speech backbone: user and model audio streams are modelled jointly with an inner-monologue text stream at 12.5 Hz / 80 ms frames, so overlaps, interruptions and backchannels need no explicit turn model, at ~200 ms practical latency.
findings.source_title: Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue
findings.numbers: 7B temporal transformer + 6-layer depth transformer; Mimi codec 12.5 fps, 80 ms frames, 1.1 kbps, 8 codebooks x 2048; theoretical 160 ms, practical 200 ms vs 230 ms human turn gap; 7M h audio, Fisher 2,000 h, 170 h conversations, >20k h synthetic; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
findings.relevance: Sets the token-stream clock (80 ms) that RoboEgo/DuplexSLA inherit and a latency floor against which Parcel's hosted Realtime lane plus Model B translation must be judged.

findings.claim: DualVLN / InternVLA-N1 is the open dual-system VLN model deployed on a Go2: a 7B Qwen2.5-VL at 2 Hz emits pixel goals + latent queries to a 30 Hz diffusion policy, achieving state-of-the-art VLN-CE scores but requiring a remote RTX 4090 and taking one instruction per episode.
findings.source_title: Ground Slow, Move Fast: A Dual-System Foundation Model for Generalizable Vision-and-Language Navigation (DualVLN / InternVLA-N1)
findings.numbers: System 2 Qwen2.5-VL-7B at 2 Hz; System 1 DiT (384 hidden, 12 layers, 6 heads) at 30 Hz, 32 trajectories in 0.03 s; latent goal fixed between S2 ticks; 763K social-nav episodes over 60 MP3D scenes; R2R val-unseen SR 64.3 / SPL 58.5 / NE 4.05 m (StreamVLN 56.9 / 51.9 / 4.98); RxR 61.4 / 51.8; VLN-PE 51.60 / 42.49; real Turtlebot4 / Go2 / G1, 20 trials x 3 scenarios, remote RTX 4090 using 20 GB; code/model/data released (InternNav)
findings.relevance: Shows the 2 Hz / 30 Hz split for navigation and the compute cost of a 7B slow level, which does not fit beside the hosted voice + SigLIP-2 on an AGX Orin.

findings.claim: On a Unitree Go2 guide-dog prototype, an LLM dialog thread running concurrently with the navigation thread that verbalises scene + plan ('We are approaching an office door', 'will take about three minutes') was rated most useful by blind users; spatial planning was delegated to a symbolic planner because 'LLMs often struggle with spatial reasoning'.
findings.source_title: From Woofs to Words: Towards Intelligent Robotic Guide Dogs with Verbal Communication
findings.numbers: Unitree Go2; GPT-4 + Answer Set Programming planner; Vosk STT; safeguard post-processing; <= 6 dialog turns for task specification; 7 legally blind participants: Scene+Plan utility 4.83/5, communication ease 4.50/5; sim task identification 94.8%, -5.2% under 0.3 speech-noise probability; project site sites.google.com/view/woofs-words
findings.relevance: Same platform as Parcel and a user-validated narration register for progress reporting during navigation; supports keeping planning deterministic and letting the language model narrate.

findings.claim: The canonical 'Verbalization' work defines a three-axis space (abstraction, locality, specificity) for narrating a mobile robot's route experience from its plan and execution log, and users prefer intermediate abstraction and locality.
findings.source_title: Verbalization: Narration of Autonomous Robot Experience (Rosenthal, Selvaraj, Veloso, IJCAI 2016)
findings.numbers: CoBot; verbalisation space axes abstraction / locality / specificity; 20-participant study; preference for intermediate abstraction and locality
findings.relevance: Gives Model B a principled set of knobs for how much of Model A's stream to surface ('Sure, I'll check the sofa' vs step-level), grounded in a user study.

findings.claim: Hierarchical episodic-memory verbalisation lets an LLM answer questions about weeks of robot experience by expanding a summary tree (raw -> scene graphs -> events -> goals -> summaries) at a fraction of the token cost of stuffing the log into context.
findings.source_title: Episodic Memory Verbalization using Hierarchical Representations of Life-Long Robot Experience (H-EMV)
findings.numbers: TEACh histories up to 100 episodes (6.2 +/- 5.3 min each) over ~2 months: 34% correct / 62% partial @ 10.4K tokens vs 1-pass 21% / 52% @ 249K; Armar-7 3.3 h over 2 months, 30 QA: 43% / 70% @ 12.8K tokens vs Gemini 1-pass 43% / 53% @ 227K; LLMs Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3-8B; code hierarchical-emv.github.io
findings.relevance: A structure for Parcel's 'global history' stream and the historical plan queue Model B narrates from.

findings.claim: Interactive Task Planning shows the simplest robust rule for mid-task amendments: on a new user request the high-level LLM replans from completed steps + task guidelines + the new request + chat history, beating Code as Policies on varied requests despite multi-second GPT-4 latency.
findings.source_title: Interactive Task Planning with Language Models
findings.numbers: GPT-4 HL planner + LL executor (function calling); 10/10 vs Code as Policies 5/10 on varied drink requests; VirtualHome 0.84 +/- 0.10 vs ProgPrompt 0.61 +/- 0.29; 'latency of several seconds'; code release only hoped
findings.relevance: Directly encodes the owner's revise/keep/queue semantics as a replan-from-history operation on Parcel's task executive.

findings.claim: Additional speaking-while-acting HRI precedents: HSAC-LLM lets a DRL navigator emit discrete 'interaction codes' that GPT-4 verbalises to pedestrians and parses replies back into actions; CLIO synchronises per-sentence co-speech gestures and waypoints on a Jetson AGX Orin + Mid-360 platform; ZIPON/ORION issues a 'Talk' action to confirm with the user and scores success weighted by interaction turns; Hey Robot lets an LLM reconfigure an MPC cost on the fly; QUART-Online syncs an 8B MLLM to a 50 Hz quadruped controller via action-chunk discretisation.
findings.source_title: Socially-Aware Robot Navigation Enhanced by Bidirectional Natural Language Conversations Using LLMs (HSAC-LLM); plus CLIO https://arxiv.org/html/2512.05389, ZIPON https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2310.07968, Hey Robot https://arxiv.org/html/2409.13393, QUART-Online https://arxiv.org/html/2412.15576
findings.numbers: HSAC-LLM SR 0.91/0.93/0.91 vs TD3 0.85/0.77/0.85, JetAuto Pro on Jetson Nano; CLIO: o3-pro script parsing, Jetson AGX Orin 64GB + Livox Mid-360, 28 participants, all metrics p<0.001, time-to-first-fixation 6.92 s -> 2.02 s; ZIPON: GPT-4 sim SR 83.8 / SPL 56.6 / SIT 53.5, real TIAGo SR 72.5, procedural feedback +21-26% SR; Hey Robot: GPT-4o-mini, assistants 1.16-4.02 s, ~3 s param update / ~7 s new cost fn, 0/10 collisions; QUART-Online: Fuyu-8b, 2 Hz -> 50 Hz, avg SR 0.52 -> 0.79
findings.relevance: Shows talk-back channels for navigation (interaction codes, co-speech scheduling, confirm-on-arrival), the SIT metric for conversational-nav evals, and two ways a slow LLM steers a fast controller without a language interface.

design_implications: Model A's narratable representation should be a language-level subtask + status string on a slow tick (~1 Hz, refreshed on user events), not a latent: every system that talks (Hi Robot, pi0.5, ELLSA, VITA-E, DuplexSLA, GR 1.5) does so from text, while latent interfaces (Helix, GR00T, DualVLN, TIC-VLA) are uninformative to a hosted voice.

Model B's injection should be YAY's override switch plus ITP's replan-from-history (completed steps + guidelines + new request + chat history), mapped onto the existing task executive (submit/suspend/resume, transactional amendment) with Hi Robot's 'switch back to the previous command' as the keep/queue case; native duplex token merging (ELLSA/DuplexSLA/RoboEgo) buys 0.3-0.4 s barge-in but needs a 7-18B model and 10^5-hour audio corpora that are out of Parcel's sim training budget.

Keep narration off the control path: ELLSA measured an 84.4 -> 73.2 success drop when the same network speaks while acting; Parcel's split (hosted Realtime voice + local controller coupled through the representation stream and StateDigest) is the right shape, with VITA-E's [INST] split (spoken part vs internal action instruction) and [END] completion token as Model B's output format.

Rates and sizes for the Orin: slow level 0.5-2 Hz with a 0.5B-3B VLM (TIC-VLA 0.5B at 0.5 Hz on Orin NX = 0.75 SR on a Go2; Hi Robot PaliGemma-3B at 1 Hz), fast level at Parcel's existing 10 Hz frame clock (TIC-VLA) up to 50 Hz (pi0/QUART-Online); a 7B slow level (DualVLN) needs a remote 4090 with 20 GB and will not fit beside the hosted voice and SigLIP-2.

Trainable Model B recipe: generate synthetic mid-task interjections from sim traces the way Hi Robot does (VLM imagines negative-task / situated-correction / specific-constraint prompts conditioned on the skill label and prior labels; HL trains in ~2 h on 8xH100; ablating synthetic data makes the model ignore clarifications), then fine-tune on owner corrections at YAY's 4-11%-of-base scale (+15-45 pts); use pi0.5's finding that verbal-coaching transcripts are a valuable co-training source.

Progress/completion reporting: use a language success/scene digest fed back to the planner (Inner Monologue 30.8 -> 60.4% under disturbances; GR-ER 1.5 success detection at 5 Hz), narrate at intermediate abstraction/locality (Verbalization 2016; Woofs-to-Words scene+plan 4.83/5 on a Go2 with blind users), and keep global history as an H-EMV-style summary tree so the historical plan queue is queryable at ~10K tokens instead of ~250K.

Benchmark blueprint for the study's evals: ELLSA's six duplex behaviours (dialogue turn-taking, action turn-taking, defective-instruction rejection, action barge-in, speaking-while-acting, context-grounded progress VQA), DuplexSLA-Bench's pause/interrupt/backchannel accuracy + delay, ZIPON's SIT (success weighted by interaction turns), and Hi Robot's instruction accuracy / task progress; literature targets: barge-in >= 94%, halt 100%, interrupt decision ~0.4 s, progress-question accuracy ~80%, instruction accuracy ~76%.

Design around the documented failure modes: Hi Robot's high level 'lacks memory' (Parcel's last-minute + global-history streams fix this) and its HL/LL are 'not aware of one another's capabilities' (StateDigest capability grounding is the mitigation); GR 1.5 does not address user interruption; ELLSA has no backchannel and is sim-only; expect a fixed hold (ECoT: 5 steps; RT-H: fixed re-query frequency) after an injected correction so the fast loop does not thrash.
open_questions: Can a language representation be emitted on Parcel's 10 Hz frame clock on an AGX Orin? DuplexSLA notes per-chunk decoding 'leaves room for only a small number of action-channel tokens per chunk' and ELLSA needs 786-854 ms per 1 s block on an A100; the evidence supports a 1 Hz slow tick over a 10 Hz fast loop, not a 10 Hz language stream.

No paper compares a latent interface (Helix/GR00T) against a language interface (Hi Robot/pi0.5) on the same task for control quality or narratability; the choice for Model A is currently argued from narration needs, not measured.

No published system trains the interjection channel end-to-end for navigation with mid-task amendments plus speech: ELLSA and VITA-E are tabletop manipulation, DualVLN and TIC-VLA take one instruction per episode, DuplexSLA's 'actions' are tool calls; Parcel's instruction-following-with-amendment eval would be a first.

Sim-to-real transfer of speech-conditioned behaviours is unmeasured (ELLSA is sim-only; RoboEgo discloses no data); the Go2-on-Orin numbers (TIC-VLA 0.75 SR) are for single-instruction navigation without speech.

DuplexSLA's backbone size is reported as ~7B in the README but the HTML extractor read '77B-scale'; and pi0.5's blog language-following percentages (86/83 in-dist, 94/94 OOD) are figure-read values — both should be verified against the PDFs before being cited as load-bearing.

How much of the 11-point speaking-while-acting penalty (ELLSA) is due to sharing weights versus sharing the token budget is unknown; a split design with a separate narration model has not been ablated against the unified one.

results.claim: Hi Robot is the closest precedent for Model B over Model A: a PaliGemma-3B high-level VLM re-runs inference 'either when one second has elapsed, or when a new interaction with the user takes place', emits an atomic language command for the pi0 low-level policy, grounds interjections like 'that's not trash' in the current image, and can include a verbal utterance played through TTS; the high level trains in ~2 h on 8xH100 from VLM-synthesised interjections (negative task / situated correction / specific constraint).
results.evidence_quote: "we rerun high-level inference and recompute ℓ̂t either when one second has elapsed, or when a new interaction with the user takes place." | "user feedback is incorporated via a high-level policy that provides atomic commands to a learned low-level policy." | "The low-level policy is the π0 VLA, which is trained by finetuning PaliGemma-3B with an additional flow matching 'action expert'" | "The high-level policy has the option to include a verbal utterance ut in the command ℓ̂t ... When ut is included, we use a text to speech system to play the utterance to the user, and remove it from ℓ̂t before passing it into the low-level policy." | "we classify interactions into different scenario types, such as negative task (where the user instructs the robot what not to do), situated correction (where the user adjusts an earlier command based on the evolving task state), and specific constraint (where the user specifies particular constraints, such as dietary preferences)." | "Training the high-level policy is highly efficient, requiring approximately 2 hours on 8×H100 GPUs." | Project page: "If it is cleaning a table and the user says 'that's not trash,' the model understands what this means, grounding the object ('that') to the thing the robot is manipulating in the image" | "Difficulty with instructions requiring long-context reasoning, since the current system lacks memory"
results.correction: Claim text fully supported (verified in arXiv HTML, the PDF text, and pi.website/research/hirobot). Caveat on the metadata numbers: the headline instruction-accuracy / task-progress percentages (76/36/30, 81/44/64, per-task rows) appear only as Figure 5 bar charts; the only numeric statement in text is 'Hi Robot averages over 40% higher instruction accuracy than GPT-4o', so those exact figures could not be verified from the paper text. Latency table confirmed: 'Total (on-board) 73 [ms]', '∼10 Hz control rates. With action chunking ... 50 Hz'; Whisper large-v2, lr 1e-5, batch 512, 1-2 RTX 4090, 16-D mobile ARX action all confirmed. No weights/code release statement found.

results.claim: ELLSA is the first single-model full-duplex listen/look/speak/act system: speech, image, text and action tokens are interleaved in fixed 1 s time blocks, the model itself decides barge-in and turn-taking, and it can answer progress questions while acting — but speaking while acting costs 11 points of manipulation success and it is simulation-only.
results.evidence_quote: "ELLSA ... is the first full-duplex, end-to-end model that simultaneously perceives and generates across vision, text, speech, and action within a single architecture" | "ELLSA operates on a one-second time block, within which it processes one second of speech input and a single video frame, generates eight tokens of text output (or a single <silence> token when no verbal response is required), and produces one second of speech and action output." | Table 4(b) 'Robot manipulation performance when speaking while acting': SPATIAL 93.3%, OBJECT 96.6%, GOAL 86.1%, LONG 73.2% vs acting alone (Table 2/14) 90.8%, 95.8%, 86.4%, 84.4% — Table 14 annotates: "93.3% (+2.8%) 96.6% (+0.8%) 86.1% (-0.3%) 73.2% (-13.3%)" | "its performance exhibits a noticeable decline since ELLSA may be distracted when doing two things at once. This drop is particularly visible on more difficult benchmarks, such as LIBERO LONG and TriviaQA." | "ELLSA has yet to be validated in real-world settings. Future work will focus on real-world deployment" | Table 3(c): Interruptive command 94.3%; context-grounded VQA "average accuracy of approximately 80%" | HF card: "18B params", "apache-2.0"
results.correction: Corrected statement: speaking while acting costs ~11 points ONLY on LIBERO-LONG (84.4% -> 73.2%, which the paper reports as -13.3% relative); on SPATIAL/OBJECT/GOAL the change is +2.5/+0.8/-0.3 points, so the four-suite average cost is ~2 points (89.4% -> 87.3%). Everything else in the claim is verbatim-supported (first single-model full-duplex; fixed 1 s blocks; self-determined turn-taking/barge-in; ~80% progress VQA while acting; LIBERO-only with 'yet to be validated in real-world settings'). Note: the 18B parameter count and Apache-2.0 license come from the HF model card, not the paper; the paper text gives no total parameter count. Metadata numbers 854/786 ms per block, 89.4 vs 85.5 vs 81.1, 94.3% barge-in, 100% turn-taking, 96.4-100% rejection, 5 Hz speech input, 'backchanneling remain unaddressed' all confirmed.

results.claim: DuplexSLA shows a native duplex model can carry a rate-limited 'action channel' (planning text, interrupt/backchannel labels, JSON tool calls) alongside continuous assistant speech on a 160 ms chunk clock, deciding interrupt/pause/backchannel from internal semantic state with sub-second delay — the closest published shape to a 'representation stream' the voice narrates from, though its actions are tool calls, not robot motion.
results.evidence_quote: "DuplexSLA models a spoken interaction as a sequence of fixed-size chunks. Let ∆ = 160 ms be the chunk size on the conversational clock" | "Action Channel: a textual stream that may contain delayed transcript text, planning text, interaction-control labels, or structured tool calls" | "We therefore cap the action channel at 10 text tokens per chunk, with a safe margin against the per-chunk wall-clock budget; tokens that do not fit spill into the action segments of the following chunks." | "Crucially, all three decisions are made based on the model's internal semantic state, rather than on a separate VAD module" | "DuplexSLA achieves sub-second latency in all four turn-taking scenarios on the proposed DuplexSLA-Bench" | "the multi-action tool calls in Figure 3b are emitted in the order of the user's request without delaying the spoken response" | "structured tool calls ... JSON body wrapped in <|toolcall_begin|> … <|toolcall_end|>" over "50 cabin and smart-home function schemas"
results.correction: Claim text fully supported. Corrections to the metadata numbers: (1) the backbone is 7B, not 77B — the paper says "autoregressive decoding throughput of a 7B-scale backbone" and "DuplexSLA is initialized from Step-Audio 2 mini [20], a 7B-scale audio language model"; README: "initialised from Step-Audio-2-mini (~7B parameters)" — the '77B' was an HTML-extractor misread, resolve the noted conflict to 7B. (2) The realtime baseline is 'gpt-realtime-1.5 (semantic-vad-high)', not 'GPT-4 Realtime': Table 7 (no prefill) gpt-realtime-1.5 96.50% @ 1.57 s vs DuplexSLA 94.34% @ 0.30 s. Confirmed: Table 6 (prefill) DuplexSLA normal 96.00/0.27, pause 93.33/0.27, interrupt 99.33/0.40, backchannel 98.33/0.32; tool-call DuplexSLA 85.56% @ 0.64 s vs 'ASR + LLM sys' 91.33% @ 2.77 s; 2,100-case bench; ~500k h CPT audio, ~320k h duplex, ~1.92M text, ~50k h post-training. Checkpoint status is from the README only ('Inference code, deployment recipes, and model checkpoints are not yet released'; MIT license); the paper itself does not state it. Note the HTML now serves v2 (11 Jun 2026).

results.claim: Yell At Your Robot demonstrates the simplest injection mechanism: a spoken correction (Whisper) temporarily overrides the high-level policy's language output and goes straight to the low-level language-conditioned policy, and fine-tuning the high level on those corrections (4-11% of base data) lifts success by 15-45 points.
results.evidence_quote: "The recorded audio is then transcribed into text using the Whisper model and synchronized with the robot's trajectory." | "The user's verbal interventions temporarily override the high-level policy's output, directly influencing the low-level policy to enable on-the-fly adaptation" | "π_deploy(a_t|o_{t-k:t}) = {π_L(a_t|o_t,l^user) if intervention; π_L(a_t|o_t,l^H) otherwise}" | "We finetune the high-level policy on the correction dataset...along with the base dataset." / "The low-level policy is kept frozen." | "The post-training dataset is significantly smaller than the base dataset – the number of skill segments is 4%-11% of those in the base dataset." | "finetuning with our approach improves success rates at each stage by 20%-45% in Bag Packing, 15%-20% in Trail Mix Preparation, and 15%-25% in Plate Cleaning." | "We conduct 20 trials for each evaluation."
results.correction: No correction needed. Minor nuances: the gains are per-stage success-rate improvements (Figure 5), reported as ranges per task, not a single end-to-end number; the high level is fine-tuned on the corrections mixed with the base data (low level frozen); the 'every 4 seconds' high-level query cadence is stated in the post-training data-collection section. Dataset sizes (1,170/41,517/1,054; 317/7,008/104; 265/3,236/33), per-task correction ratios 4.8/4.2/10.8%, ALOHA 14-D action, four cameras, EfficientNet-b3 + DistilBERT + FiLM in ACT, frozen CLIP ViT high level all confirmed.

results.claim: TIC-VLA is the only published dual-system navigation stack measured on a Unitree Go2 with a Jetson Orin: a 0.5 Hz VLM writes KV-cache features + waypoints that a 10 Hz action policy consumes asynchronously, and RL fine-tuning keeps success high despite multi-second reasoning latency.
results.evidence_quote: "TIC-VLA adopts a dual-system execution paradigm in which high-level semantic reasoning and low-level control operate asynchronously." | "We evaluate all methods on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot. The primary computing setup consists of a laptop equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU and an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX mounted onboard." | Table 3: "TIC-VLA 4060 0.85 85.73 / 3430.73; TIC-VLA Orin NX 0.75 120.27 / 4831.73; TIC-VLA (no RL) 4060 0.70; Dual-VLN (7B) A6000 0.50; NaVILA (7B) A6000 0.35" | "TIC-VLA maintains a 0.75 success rate on the Jetson Orin NX despite multi-second VLM reasoning latency" | "All experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, with the action policy running at 10 Hz and asynchronous VLM reasoning running at 0.5 Hz." | "the action policy conditions on the most recent cached hidden state ... (i.e., the last-layer key-value cache)" | "The VLM guidance is provided either in the form of abstract waypoint predictions or as key-value (KV) cache features from the final Transformer layer of the VLM." | "The waypoint-based interface leads to inferior performance due to its sparsity" | "the RL-fine-tuned policy maintains consistently higher success rates across all latency settings, demonstrating improved robustness to inference latency."
results.correction: Corrected statement: TIC-VLA is a published dual-system navigation stack measured on a Unitree Go2 with an onboard Jetson Orin NX (0.75 SR at 25 W vs 0.85 on an RTX 4060 laptop; RL fine-tuning lifts 0.70 -> 0.85), where an asynchronous InternVL3-1B VLM (InternViT-300M + Qwen2.5-0.5B) hands the 10 Hz action policy its last-layer KV-cache features plus latency metadata. Three details are off: (1) 'the only published' is not asserted anywhere in the paper and could not be independently verified (search budget exhausted); the paper's own Go2 comparison includes two other dual-system stacks (DualVLN 7B, NaVILA 7B) that had to run on a remote A6000, so 'only one run on the Orin' is an inference, not a source claim. (2) The final policy consumes KV-cache features, not waypoints — the VLM does emit waypoint tokens, but the waypoint interface is the inferior ablation in Table 2 (SR 22.35 vs 47.06 without RL). (3) 0.5 Hz / 10 Hz are the simulation (L40S) rates; on the Orin NX measured runtimes were 120.27 ms policy (~8 Hz) and 4,831.73 ms VLM (~0.2 Hz). Sim numbers confirmed: TIC-VLA SR 55.29 vs OmniVLA 31.76 / MobileVLA 32.94; 85 test cases; four scenes; SCAND 8.7 h, GND >11 h, DynaNav 5.1 h; KV features projected 256 -> 512.

sweeps.topic: Streaming / online vision-language navigation and embodied models that act on continuous input (StreamVLN, Uni-NaVid/NaVid, NaVILA, DualVLN/InternVLA-N1, LiveVLN, TIC-VLA, VLN-CE/R2R-CE/RxR-CE, VLN-PE, LOVON, MapGPT/NavGPT/DiscussNav, VLMnav, Mobility VLA, QUART/QUART-Online, LocoVLM, UrbanVLA, TartanGround)

findings.claim: StreamVLN is the reference streaming VLN design: a LLaVA-Video (Qwen2-7B) video-LLM run as an online multi-turn dialogue over the camera stream, with a sliding-window KV cache of the last 8 dialogue turns, a slow-updating memory of 8 frames x 196 tokens, and depth-voxel token pruning; it emits 4 discrete actions per turn and was deployed on a Unitree Go2 (RealSense D455) from a remote RTX 4090.
findings.source_title: StreamVLN: Streaming Vision-and-Language Navigation via SlowFast Context Modeling (ICRA 2026)
findings.numbers: R2R-CE val-unseen SR 56.4 / SPL 50.2 / NE 4.90 / OS 63.6 (prune+mem: 57.4 / 51.1 / 4.73); RxR-CE (README) SR 54.4 / SPL 45.4 / nDTW 63.7; window = 8 turns; memory 8x196 tokens; token reduction 28% R2R / 22% RxR; training 450K MP3D + 300K ScaleVLN + 240K DAgger + 248K video VQA + 230K MMC4, ~1500 A100 GPU-h; inference 0.27 s per 4 actions on RTX 4090, comm 0.2 s indoor / 1.0 s outdoor; 20 real trials per scenario; weights CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (HF card: 8B params BF16)
findings.relevance: Closest existing architecture to Model A's continuous-input, action-plus-context output; its KV-window + compressed-memory recipe is the 'last 1 minute' mechanism, and its Go2 deployment numbers set the latency baseline.

findings.claim: DualVLN / InternVLA-N1 splits navigation into a 2 Hz Qwen2.5-VL planner (System 2) that emits a pixel goal plus 4 latent query tokens, and a 30 Hz Diffusion-Transformer policy (System 1) that outputs 32-waypoint trajectories; the two run asynchronously so the fast lane handles dynamic obstacles while the slow lane reasons, and it is deployed on Turtlebot4, Unitree Go2 and Unitree G1.
findings.source_title: Ground Slow, Move Fast: A Dual-System Foundation Model for Generalizable Vision-and-Language Navigation (DualVLN / InternVLA-N1)
findings.numbers: S2 Qwen2.5-VL 7B at 2 Hz (HF card: 8B BF16); S1 DiT hidden 384, 12 layers, 6 heads, 30 Hz, 0.03 s with TensorRT; R2R-CE val-unseen SR 64.3 / SPL 58.5 / NE 4.05 / OS 70.7; RxR-CE SR 61.4 / NE 4.58 / nDTW 70.0; VLN-PE zero-shot SR 51.60 / SPL 42.49; S1 competitive with 1% of trajectories; Social-VLN 763K episodes / 60 MP3D scenes; 20 GB GPU memory on remote RTX 4090; S2 latency 1.1 s -> 0.7 s with KV cache; 20 real trials per scenario; weights CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
findings.relevance: Direct template for the Model A (slow, narratable latent/goal) + 10 Hz act-token loop coupling; the pixel-goal + latent interface is a concrete candidate for the 'representation the hosted voice narrates from'.

findings.claim: Even 'streaming' navigators stall on real robots: LiveVLN measured StreamVLN/NaVILA-class models on a Unitree G1 at 30.5% idle time with 94.9% of rounds stop-and-go, and fixed it without retraining by a guarded handoff (committed guard buffer sized from measured sense+inference latency, plus a revisable tail), cutting waiting time 73-78% while preserving success.
findings.source_title: LiveVLN: Breaking the Stop-and-Go Loop in Vision-Language Navigation
findings.numbers: Baseline: 10.64 s waiting per episode (30.5% waiting ratio), 94.9% stop-and-go rounds, 1.09 s visible gap; StreamVLN+LiveVLN R2R SR 57.2 (vs 56.4), SPL 50.0, RxR SR 53.7; NaVILA+LiveVLN R2R 59.9 (vs 61.4); real G1: StreamVLN waiting 7.32 -> 1.63 s (-77.7%), pauses 6.75 -> 0.80, episode 41.98 -> 36.71 s, gap 0.96 -> 0.11 s; NaVILA waiting 10.64 -> 2.89 s (-72.8%); RTX 5090 server, D455f camera, Wi-Fi <50 ms jitter; metrics: waiting ratio, visible gap, N_pause (>0.5 s)
findings.relevance: Defines the runtime contract Parcel's act-token codec needs (committed prefix vs revisable tail) and the continuity metrics the eval suite should add beside SR/SPL.

findings.claim: NaVILA (legged, Go2/H1/G1) shows language itself can be the action interface: an 8B VILA model outputs mid-level text actions ('move forward 75cm', 'turn right 30 degrees') that are cast to fixed velocity commands for a 50 Hz Isaac-Lab RL locomotion policy, reaching 88% on 25 real instructions at about 1 s per action.
findings.source_title: NaVILA: Legged Robot Vision-Language-Action Model for Navigation (RSS 2025)
findings.numbers: R2R-CE val-unseen SR 54.0 / SPL 49.0 / NE 5.22; RxR-CE zero-shot SR 34.3 / SPL 28.2; VLN-CE-Isaac (1,077 of 1,839 trajectories): Go2 vision 50.2 SR vs blind 36.2, H1 45.3 vs 24.4; real 25 instructions x 3 trials: 88% overall, 75% complex; ~1 s wait per action, VLA 0.6 s/sample, W4A16 594.58 -> 367.80 ms; velocities {0.5 m/s, pi/6 rad/s}; policy 50 Hz from proprioception + LiDAR heightmap; 8 frames in real world (8-64 tested); data: R2R/RxR/EnvDrop/ScanQA + 2K YouTube touring videos -> 20K trajectories; checkpoints a8cheng/navila-llama3-8b-8f (no license on card)
findings.relevance: Text mid-level actions are exactly a narratable representation for the hosted voice; the VLA-over-RL-policy stack matches Parcel's Go2 plus existing sport-mode gateway.

findings.claim: The Go2 sim-to-real gap is dominated by camera height, lighting and locomotion-controller mismatch rather than data scale: on the physics-realistic VLN-PE platform NaVid's zero-shot success collapses from 22.4% (humanoid) to 4.7% on a 0.5 m quadruped, RGB-only models lose ~12 points in low light while RGB-D lose ~2-3, and 14 real Go2 episodes went from 7.1% to 28.6% SR after fine-tuning on physics-sim data.
findings.source_title: Rethinking the Embodied Gap in Vision-and-Language Navigation: A Holistic Study of Physical and Visual Disparities (VLN-PE, ICCV 2025)
findings.numbers: VLN-CE -> VLN-PE zero-shot (H1): Seq2Seq 25.99 -> 15.00, CMA 32.08 -> 16.04, NaVid 40.67 -> 22.42; NaVid by embodiment: H1 22.42, Aliengo 4.73, Jetbot 11.02; lighting: NaVid 22.42 -> 9.95 (DL300) / 11.17 (camera light); controller consistency: CMA SR 18.78 with controller both phases, fall rate 18.63%, stuck 3.12%; cross-embodiment training SR 18.78 -> 26.87, SPL 14.56 -> 23.54; real Go2 + D455, 14 episodes: CMA 7.14 -> 28.57 SR, OS 14.29 -> 57.14; 441 synthetic episodes fine-tune CMA-CLIP 15.31 -> 22.46
findings.relevance: Tells Parcel to render the MuJoCo city at Go2 camera height with gait oscillation and lighting variation, to feed depth/LiDAR to Model A, and to collect training traces with the same motion gateway used at deployment.

findings.claim: Uni-NaVid unifies VLN, ObjectNav, EQA and human-following in one 7B video-LLM with an online token-merge memory (64 tokens current frame / 4 per short-term frame / 1 per long-term frame) and 4 discrete actions per step at ~5 Hz on an A100; code and weights are MIT-licensed.
findings.source_title: Uni-NaVid: A Video-based Vision-Language-Action Model for Unifying Embodied Navigation Tasks (RSS 2025)
findings.numbers: Vicuna-7B + EVA-CLIP, 1 FPS video; tokens 64/4/1 (alpha 2/8/16), merge threshold 0.95; actions FORWARD 25 cm / TURN 30 deg / STOP, 4 per step, ~0.2 s per 4 actions on remote A100, ~5 Hz; data 3.6M nav samples (VLN 2.4M, ObjectNav 483k, EQA 250k, following 544k) + 2.3M VQA, 40 H800 x 35 h = 1400 GPU-h; R2R-CE SR 47.0 / SPL 42.7 (paper), README 51.8 / 47.7; RxR-CE 48.7 / 40.9 (paper), README 56.1 / 44.5; HM3D ObjectNav SR 73.7 / SPL 37.1; EQA 54.4%; human following SR 61.21, following rate 71.93
findings.relevance: Proves one video-LLM can serve the companion-dog task set (follow me / go check X / answer what you see) with a shared action vocabulary; MIT license makes it the most permissive base to fine-tune.

findings.claim: NaVid (the ancestor of Uni-NaVid/StreamVLN) established the video-LLM-to-discrete-action recipe with 510k sim navigation samples, but needs 1.2-1.5 s per action and reached only 37-42% SR on R2R-CE and ~42-66% on 200 real Turtlebot instructions.
findings.source_title: NaVid: Video-based VLM Plans the Next Step for Vision-and-Language Navigation (RSS 2024)
findings.numbers: Vicuna-7B + EVA-CLIP + Q-Former; 64+1 tokens current frame, 4+1 per history frame; 320k oracle + 180k DAgger + 10k reasoning + 763k web video; 672 A100 GPU-h; 1.2-1.5 s per action; R2R-CE SR 37.4 / SPL 35.9 / NE 5.47 / OS 49.1 (repo: 41.9 / 36.5); RxR-CE cross-dataset 23.8 / 21.2; real Turtlebot4 + Kinect, 200 instructions: ~66% simple, ~42% complex; 1,839 R2R val-unseen episodes take 2.5 h on 8 A100
findings.relevance: Baseline for what per-frame video-LLM inference costs without KV caching; shows why streaming/memory mechanisms were needed.

findings.claim: TIC-VLA runs a 1B VLM on a Unitree Go2 with a 10 Hz action policy and 0.5 Hz asynchronous reasoning, trains explicitly under randomized reasoning latency (0-10 s), and is the only fetched Go2 result on Jetson-class compute (0.75 SR on an Orin NX), beating DualVLN (0.50) and NaVILA (0.35) on the same real tasks.
findings.source_title: TIC-VLA: A Think-in-Control Vision-Language-Action Model for Robot Navigation in Dynamic Environments
findings.numbers: InternVL3-1B (InternViT-300M + Qwen2.5-0.5B) + 6-layer cross-attn action expert; policy 10 Hz, reasoning 0.5 Hz; 30 chunks of (dx,dy,dtheta) over 3 s; data ~25 h (SCAND 8.7 h, GND 11 h, DynaNav 5.1 h); latency-IL delays U[0,10] s; PPO stage; DynaNav SR 55.29 / CR 28.24 (no RL 47.06 / 34.12; NavDP 54.12 / 30.59); real Go2: 0.85 SR on RTX 4060 laptop (85.73 / 3430.73 ms action/reasoning), 0.75 on Jetson Orin NX (120.27 / 4831.73 ms)
findings.relevance: Only datapoint for on-robot Orin inference of a navigation VLA; its latency-conditioned training is the method to make Model A robust to its own slow lane.

findings.claim: VLN-CE (R2R-CE) is the standard continuous benchmark: 4475 Matterport3D trajectories in Habitat with a low-level action space (forward 0.25 m, turn 15 deg in the paper / 30 deg in the challenge config, stop) averaging ~56 actions per episode; the original baselines reached only 20-32% SR and the paper showed nav-graph results were ~2x inflated.
findings.source_title: Beyond the Nav-Graph: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (ECCV 2020) + jacobkrantz/VLN-CE repo
findings.numbers: 4475 trajectories; average action length 55.88 vs 5 in R2R; Seq2Seq val-unseen SR 20% / SPL 0.18 / NE 8.94; CMA+aug SR 32% / SPL 0.30 / NE 7.37; continuous 0.21 SPL vs nav-graph ~0.47; 90 MP3D scenes, Habitat-Sim 0.1.7, 480x640 RGBD; challenge config 30 deg turns, 0.25 m step; R2R val-unseen 1,839 episodes; code MIT, data CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US + Matterport ToU; RxR-CE multilingual (en/hi/te)
findings.relevance: Every SR/SPL number in this note is on this benchmark; Parcel's instruction-navigation evals should report the same action granularity and metrics to be comparable.

findings.claim: RxR is 10x larger than R2R (126k instructions in English/Hindi/Telugu) and uniquely provides word-level pose traces time-aligning each instruction word to the annotator's viewpoint, released under CC-BY.
findings.source_title: Room-Across-Room (RxR) dataset repository (Ku et al., EMNLP 2020)
findings.numbers: 126k instructions, 126k follower demonstrations; 161 GB full download; pose traces 18.6 GB; 1.1M grounded landmarks; 1M model-generated instructions; annotations CC-BY 4.0
findings.relevance: The only large supervision format where language is time-locked to viewpoint; the template for Parcel's synthetic (speech-turn, act-token, state-digest) traces.

findings.claim: Iterative VLN showed that implicit transformer memory does not carry across consecutive instructions in a persistent environment (t-nDTW 61 -> 45) while map-building agents benefit from persistence, motivating an explicit map/plan store for multi-command sessions.
findings.source_title: Iterative Vision-and-Language Navigation (IVLN)
findings.numbers: Tours up to 100 R2R episodes; IR2R 375 tours (76.6 episodes/tour), IR2R-CE 414 tours (48.1 episodes/tour); after 10 episodes >50% of the next target path already seen; HAMT SR 63 / nDTW 71 / t-nDTW 61, TourHAMT t-nDTW 45; MAP-CMA iterative maps t-nDTW 48 val-unseen, SR 39-41; unstructured CMA variants t-nDTW 38
findings.relevance: Supports keeping Parcel's LiDAR occupancy grid + historical plan queue as the 'global history' store rather than stretching Model A's context.

findings.claim: CVDN is the canonical dialog-conditioned navigation dataset (2050 human-human dialogs, 7415 NDH instances) and its baselines reached only 2.1 m goal progress vs 9.6 m for the oracle, with no streaming continuous-environment successor; live speech coupled to motion remains unbenchmarked.
findings.source_title: Vision-and-Dialog Navigation (CVDN)
findings.numbers: 2050 dialogs, 83 Matterport houses, >7k trajectories; 7415 NDH instances (4742/382/907/1384); 81.6 words per dialog vs R2R 29; paths 25.0+-12.9 vs R2R 6.0+-0.85; seq2seq full history val-unseen 2.10 m, test 2.35 m; shortest-path 9.58 / 9.76 m
findings.relevance: Establishes that Parcel's conversational-navigation eval must be built in-house; nothing off-the-shelf scores mid-task amendments with a live speaker.

findings.claim: Mobility VLA (Google) uses Gemini 1.5 Pro's 1M-token context to reason over a full 948-frame demonstration tour and a COLMAP topological graph, achieving 80-85% end-to-end success on reasoning-required and multimodal instructions in an 836 m2 office, but each high-level call takes 10-30 s and the model is closed.
findings.source_title: Mobility VLA: Multimodal Instruction Navigation with Long-Context VLMs and Topological Graphs (CoRL 2024)
findings.numbers: Tour ~16 min = 948 frames @ 1 Hz (phone tour 224 frames @ 3 Hz); graph edges within 2 m and <90 deg; low-level waypoint (dx,dy,dtheta) via MPC at 0.19+-0.047 s/step; VLM 10-30 s per call; 57 instructions: RF 80%, RR 80%, SO 40%, MM 85%; 900 sim trials 90%; wheeled mobile manipulator; CC BY 4.0 paper, closed model
findings.relevance: Shows the hosted-model role Parcel's OpenAI Realtime lane can play (whole-history reasoning) and why it must sit above, not inside, the motion loop.

findings.claim: VLMnav turns a frozen Gemini Flash into a zero-shot end-to-end navigation policy by overlaying numbered candidate arrows (depth-filtered, polar r/theta) on the image and keeping a 2-D explored-voxel map, reaching 50.4% ObjectNav success on HM3D versus 24.6% for PIVOT.
findings.source_title: End-to-End Navigation with Vision Language Models: Transforming Spatial Reasoning into Question-Answering (VLMnav)
findings.numbers: HM3D ObjectNav SR 50.4 / SPL 0.210 (prompt-only 29.8 / 0.107, PIVOT 24.6 / 0.106, no-nav 33.2); GOAT SR 16.3 / SPL 0.066; 131 deg FOV, 25 deg pitch, r_i <- min(2/3 r_i, r_max); disabling sliding drops SR 12.9 points; sim only; CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: A cheap fallback for the hosted lane to pick a local motion candidate from an annotated frame; also a warning that zero-shot VLM policies rely on sim 'sliding' and would collide on a real dog.

findings.claim: Zero-shot GPT-4 navigators (NavGPT -> DiscussNav -> MapGPT) climbed from 34% to ~44% SR on nav-graph R2R by adding expert discussion and an online linguistic topological map, and MapGPT cut per-step prompt cost to 672 input tokens; the only real deployment (DiscussNav, Turtlebot4) managed 25% on 20 instructions.
findings.source_title: MapGPT: Map-Guided Prompting with Adaptive Path Planning for VLN (ACL 2024), with NavGPT (arxiv 2305.16986v3) and DiscussNav (ar5iv 2309.11382) comparisons
findings.numbers: NavGPT GPT-4: SR 34 / SPL 29 / OSR 42 / NE 6.46 / TL 11.45 (BLIP-2 ViT-G FlanT5XL captions of 24 views, Faster R-CNN objects <3 m, GPT-3.5 summariser); DiscussNav: SR 43 / SPL 40 / OSR 61 / NE 5.32, real Turtlebot4 Lite 25% vs NavGPT 10%; MapGPT GPT-4V: SR 43.7 / SPL 34.8 / OSR 57.6 / NE 5.63 on 783 val-unseen, REVERIE (500) SR 31.6, tokens/step 672 in / 115 out vs NavGPT 2,465 / 317; simulator only
findings.relevance: Defines the ceiling and cost of a hosted-LLM-as-planner (Model B without a trained Model A); the linguistic topological map is a good serialization for the plan queue Parcel sends to the hosted voice.

findings.claim: LOVON is a plug-and-play open-vocabulary object-navigation stack for Unitree Go2/B2/H1-2 (MIT-licensed, weights released) that maps an LLM plan plus YOLO-11 detections to [vx, vy, theta] velocities via a 3.3M-parameter transformer trained on 1M generated samples, with a 5-state execution logic for target loss and blur filtering.
findings.source_title: LOVON: Legged Open-Vocabulary Object Navigator
findings.numbers: DeepSeek R1 planner; YOLO-11 detector; L2MM d=256, 4 layers, 8 heads, ff 1024, 3.30M params; 1M samples 4:1 split, ~1 h on RTX 3080 Ti; T_blur = 150 (+15% qualified frames); Gym-Unreal SR 1.00 (ParkingLot/UrbanCity/SnowVillage), mean episode length 499.75; RealSense D435i default; real results qualitative only
findings.relevance: Cheapest reproducible Go2 velocity-command baseline; its state machine (run-to-object / search-lost-object / maintain) is a ready-made narration vocabulary for Model B.

findings.claim: QUART/QUART-Online show that a quadruped VLA emitting 12-dim tokens (base velocities plus gait, height, pitch, foot parameters) can be brought from 2 Hz to 50 Hz controller-synchronous inference by discretizing action chunks with a learned codebook, raising average success from 0.37 to 0.68.
findings.source_title: QUART-Online: Latency-Free Large Multimodal Language Model for Quadruped Robot Learning (with QUAR-VLA, ECCV 2024)
findings.numbers: Fuyu-8B; 12-dim action tokens (vx, vy, wz, gait theta1-3, f, hy, pitch, foot width, foot height, terminate), 256 bins; QUART 2 Hz; QUARD 259K sim + 3K real episodes; sim SR: distinguish 66, go-to 60, obstacle 53, tunnel 41, crawl 32, unload 12; real 13/20 with 256K:3K mix; WR-2 quadruped + D435; QUART-Online ACD codebook 512, chunks 1/5/10, 50 Hz, 2.5x token speedup, 10x chunk speedup, 0.37 -> 0.68 avg, 0.99 on go-to unseen language
findings.relevance: Direct precedent for Parcel's discrete act-token codec on a quadruped and for including gait/pose tokens (gestures, poses) in the same vocabulary as motion.

findings.claim: LocoVLM grounds camera+text into a 300-entry LLM-synthesized locomotion-style database on a Unitree Go1, with a <100 ms VLM advisory driving a 50 Hz style-conditioned RL policy on a Jetson Xavier NX and 87% instruction-following accuracy.
findings.source_title: LocoVLM: Grounding Vision and Language for Adapting Versatile Legged Locomotion Policies
findings.numbers: GPT-4o skill DB of 300 descriptors (gait period, 4-D phase offsets, max velocity); BLIP-2 encoder on laptop RTX 3070 Ti, <100 ms; PPO in Isaac Gym, 50 Hz policy on Jetson Xavier NX, motors 200 Hz; retrieval 72/100 text vs 87/100 text-as-image; zero-shot to Unitree H1; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
findings.relevance: Model for expressive, narratable gait styles ('trotting happily') as a low-dimensional conditioning vector rather than raw joint control.

findings.claim: UrbanVLA runs a Qwen2-based VLA on a Unitree Go2 with four cameras at 2 Hz, consuming route instructions resampled to 20 waypoints over 40 m and emitting SE(2) trajectories, reaching 91% SocialNav success in MetaUrban and >500 m real urban routes from a remote RTX 4090.
findings.source_title: UrbanVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model for Urban Micromobility
findings.numbers: 2 Hz; 4 RGB cameras (front/left/right/rear); D=40 m, d=2 m -> 20 waypoints; 2,400 sim episodes (~40 h) + ~8 h real teleop + Sekai video; 8 H100 x 12 h = 96 GPU-h; MetaUrban SocialNav SR 91% test / 88% unseen, SNS 0.87 / 0.85; real routes >500 m qualitative; remote RTX 4090 via Web-ADK; CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Only fetched Go2 outdoor VLA; confirms 2 Hz slow-lane cadence and remote-GPU deployment as the current norm.

findings.claim: TartanGround is the largest legged/wheeled ground-robot perception dataset (photorealistic Unreal/AirSim, 10 Hz, 6 stereo pairs, LiDAR, semantic occupancy, ~15 TB) but contains no language and is CC BY-NC-SA, so it is useful for pretraining perception/occupancy heads, not for VLN supervision.
findings.source_title: TartanGround: A Large-Scale Dataset for Ground Robot Perception and Navigation (IROS 2025)
findings.numbers: HTML v1: 878 trajectories (440 omni-wheeled, 198 diff-drive, 240 legged via ANYmal D), 63 environments, 1.44M samples; abs page (updated): 910 / 70 / 1.5M; 17.3M RGB images; ~15 TB; 10 Hz; SurroundOcc IoU 12.91-22.15 urban vs 6.39-16.97 natural; SLAM rel. trans. error ORB-SLAM3 0.152-0.563, DPVO 0.010-0.089, MAC-VO 0.008-0.016 m/frame; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
findings.relevance: Candidate source for occupancy/depth pretraining that matches Parcel's LiDAR + camera sensor suite; license blocks commercial fine-tunes.

findings.claim: 'What Limits VLN?' finds monocular video-LLM navigators are brittle to the visual perturbations a walking dog produces (motion blur and viewpoint oscillation cut StreamVLN-class SR from 57% to 35% and 20%) and that training-data scale correlates weakly with success; its stereo StereoNav reached 81.1% SR on R2R-CE and 60.6% real-world vs 24.3% for StreamVLN.
findings.source_title: What Limits Vision-and-Language Navigation? (StereoNav)
findings.numbers: LLaVA-based SR 57.0 -> 35.3 (motion blur) -> 20.1 (viewpoint oscillation); Qwen-based SPL 56.8 -> 4.2 under blur; directional-ambiguity score 51.7 (failed) vs 77.3 (successful); StereoNav R2R-CE SR 81.1 / SPL 68.3 with external data; real 4 scenarios macro SR 60.6% vs StreamVLN 24.3%; oscillation degradation 37.0% vs 64.7%
findings.relevance: Argues for stereo/depth input and gait-consistent sim rendering in Parcel's Model A, and against betting on data scale alone.

findings.claim: VLN-Cache gives a training-free 1.52x per-step speedup on InternVLA-N1 by geometrically remapping and reusing KV entries between frames (using depth + relative pose) with only a 1.2-point SR loss, showing KV reuse is a viable memory/latency mechanism for streaming navigators.
findings.source_title: VLN-Cache: Enabling Token Caching for VLN Models with Visual/Semantic Dynamics Awareness
findings.numbers: A100-40GB BF16, R2R-CE val 1,839 episodes; per-step 637 -> 419 ms; token reuse ~31%; 12.3 GFLOPs saved (18.3% of attention); SR 64.3 -> 63.1, SPL 58.5 -> 57.6; ~11.2 MB cache per frame; CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Parcel has LiDAR odometry and depth, so the same geometric KV reuse is available to cut Model A latency on the Orin.

findings.claim: Slow Brain / Fast Planner shows how to fuse a 1-3 s cloud VLM into a 5-20 Hz local planner without blocking: decay the VLM's influence with exp(-dt/tau) (tau 3-5 s) and stream queries at 1 Hz; success stays above 80% out to 5 s of latency while a naive hold collapses past 2 s, and real sidewalk takeovers fell 75%.
findings.source_title: Slow Brain, Fast Planner: Latency-Resilient VLM-Augmented Urban Navigation
findings.numbers: Planner 5-20 Hz, 64 anchors -> K=18, ~4 s horizon (20 waypoints @ 5 Hz); VLM 1-3 s/query (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite median 1.7 s, Gemini 3 Flash 8.1 s; 4G 1.5-3.0 s); 1 Hz streaming; Score Fusion >80% SR out to 5 s, Probability Fusion ~78% at 5 s, VLM Hold collapses past 2 s; takeovers 3.49 -> 0.87 per 100 m; longest autonomous segment 111.7 m; VLM ADE 1.16 m vs planner 1.64 m; ~5,000 snapshots (3,000 normal / 2,000 hard); CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: Gives Model B's 'keep / revise / queue' arbitration a concrete form: a staleness-weighted fusion of hosted-model guidance into Parcel's 10 Hz local planner.

design_implications: Make Model A the slow lane (1-4 Hz), not the 10 Hz loop: every real legged deployment fetched (StreamVLN ~3.7 Hz per 4-action turn, DualVLN S2 2 Hz, Robostral 0.5 Hz, TIC-VLA 0.5 Hz, UrbanVLA 2 Hz) pairs a 7-8B video-LLM with a 10-50 Hz motion generator (DiT 30 Hz, diffusion 10 Hz, RL policy 50 Hz). Parcel's existing 10 Hz duplex frame clock + act-token codec is the fast lane; Model A should write a goal/latent (DualVLN-style pixel goal + latent tokens, or NaVILA-style mid-level text) into it.

Adopt LiveVLN's runtime contract in the act-token codec: a committed guard prefix sized from measured sense+inference latency that the executive never revokes, plus a revisable tail Model A may overwrite; condition the next inference on the committed prefix. Add LiveVLN's continuity metrics (waiting ratio, visible gap, pause count) to the nav eval next to SR/SPL, because a 'streaming' model on a real Unitree still idled 30.5% of the time without this.

Memory design for 'last 1 minute' vs 'global history': use StreamVLN/Uni-NaVid-style sliding-window KV cache (8 turns) with compressed older frames (64/4/1 tokens) and depth-guided token pruning or VLN-Cache-style geometric KV reuse (1.52x, -1.2 SR) for the recent window; keep Parcel's LiDAR occupancy grid + semantic grounding + historical plan queue as the persistent store, since IVLN showed implicit transformer memory does not carry across consecutive instructions (t-nDTW 61 -> 45) while map-based agents benefit.

Model B's 'keep / revise / queue' arbitration should be implemented as staleness-weighted fusion: decay hosted-model guidance with exp(-dt/tau), tau 3-5 s (Slow Brain / Fast Planner held >80% success out to 5 s latency), so a late hosted proposal never overrides a fresh local plan; serialize the plan queue to the hosted voice as a MapGPT-style linguistic topological map (672 tokens/step) rather than raw coordinates.

The narratable representation already exists as NaVILA's mid-level language actions ('move forward 75cm', 'turn right 30 degrees') and LOVON's execution states (run-to-object / search-lost-object / maintain / accomplish): have Model A emit a small discrete action vocabulary plus a one-line status token stream; Model B rewrites it into the hosted voice's narration. Include gait/pose tokens in the same vocabulary as QUART's 12-dim tokens and LocoVLM's style conditioning so gestures and poses are narratable too.

Sim-to-real for the Go2 hinges on rendering fidelity, not data scale: render the MuJoCo city at Go2 camera height (~0.5 m) with real gait oscillation and lighting variation, feed depth/LiDAR alongside RGB (RGB-only lost ~12 SR points in low light; motion blur cut SR 57 -> 35), and collect training traces through the same motion gateway used at deployment (VLN-PE: controller mismatch cost 5-8 SR points; consistent controller + cross-embodiment data gave the best results). Fine-tuning on a few hundred physics-sim episodes moved real Go2 SR from 7.1% to 28.6%.

Compute budget: all 7-8B navigators cited run on a remote RTX 4090 (DualVLN needs 20 GB) at 0.27-1.1 s per inference; the only Orin datapoint is TIC-VLA's 1B model at 4.8 s reasoning / 120 ms action on an Orin NX with 0.75 real SR. Plan for either a quantized 7-8B on the AGX Orin 64 GB (NaVILA W4A16 cut 595 -> 368 ms on a server GPU) with LiveVLN-style guards, or a ~1B Model A trained under randomized latency like TIC-VLA, and instrument sim-to-real with the actual round-trip.

Training data and licenses: start from Uni-NaVid (MIT code + HF weights; 3.6M samples across VLN/ObjectNav/EQA/human-following incl. 61% following SR) or NaVILA (Apache-2.0 code) if commercial use matters; StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1 weights and TartanGround are CC BY-NC-SA. No dataset couples live speech to motion (CVDN is dialog-history only; RxR has word-level pose traces), so Parcel must synthesize interleaved (speech-turn, act-token, StateDigest) traces in sim, using RxR's pose-trace format as the template, and build its own interruption/amendment benchmark on IVLN-style multi-instruction tours.
open_questions: StreamVLN and DualVLN real-world per-scenario Go2 success rates (hallway/bedroom/office, 20 trials each) are only in figures; need the PDF figure or InternNav eval logs to get exact numbers.
VLN-CE success radius: the ar5iv extraction mentions a 0.5 m threshold in the trajectory-transfer context; confirm the evaluation success threshold from the PDF before aligning Parcel's eval rows.
Uni-NaVid's real-robot platform (and whether the human-following demo used a quadruped) is in the unfetched supplementary material.
NaVILA weight license: code is Apache-2.0 on GitHub but the HF model card carries no license field; needs author confirmation before commercial fine-tuning.
No published latency for a 7-8B video-LLM at StreamVLN token counts on a Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB; only the Orin NX 1B (TIC-VLA) datapoint exists. Needs an in-house benchmark.
Whether Robostral Navigate's weights (8B VLM + 121M diffusion, 77.4 SR on R2R-CE, sim-only 2.4M trajectories) are released and under what terms is not stated in the paper.

No existing benchmark scores mid-task interruption or amendment with a live speaker while the robot moves; the nearest building blocks are LiveVLN's timing metrics, IVLN's multi-instruction tours and CVDN's dialog histories, so Parcel must define this benchmark itself.

results.claim: StreamVLN is the reference streaming VLN design: a LLaVA-Video (Qwen2-7B) video-LLM run as an online multi-turn dialogue over the camera stream, with a sliding-window KV cache of the last 8 dialogue turns, a slow-updating memory of 8 frames x 196 tokens, and depth-voxel token pruning; it emits 4 discrete actions per turn and was deployed on a Unitree Go2 (RealSense D455) from a remote RTX 4090.
results.evidence_quote: "We build StreamVLN based on the LLaVA-Video 7B model, which uses Qwen2-7B as the language model." / "Each interaction session consists of 8 dialogue turns, resulting in a total of 32 actions executed sequentially" / "increasing the memory size from 2*196 to 8*196 while keeping the window size fixed at 8 significantly improves navigation performance" / "Pruning is applied only on 8 memory frames, reducing memory tokens by 28% on R2R" ... "22% on RxR" / "We perform real world experiments based on a Unitree Go2 robotic dog. The robot is equipped with a upward facing camera (Intel RealSense D455) for RGB-D observations. We deploy StreamVLN on a remote workstation with an RTX 4090 GPU." / "The averge inference (0.27s for 4 actions) and communication (0.2s for indoor and 1.0s for outdoor environments) latency enable real-time physical deployment." / "For each method, we conducted 20 trials per scenario" / arXiv abs Comments: "Accepted to ICRA 2026" / GitHub README: "This work is under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License." / HF card mengwei0427/StreamVLN_Video_qwen_1_5_r2r_rxr_envdrop_scalevln_v1_3: 8B params, BF16.
results.correction: None needed. All listed numbers verified: R2R val-unseen SR 56.4 / SPL 50.2 / NE 4.90 / OS 63.6; prune+mem 57.4 / 51.1 / 4.73 (OS 65.5); RxR SR 54.4 / SPL 45.4 / nDTW 63.7 (paper and README); 450K MP3D + 300K ScaleVLN + 240K DAgger + 248K video VQA + 230K MMC4, ~1500 A100 GPU-hours. Two housekeeping notes: the discrete action set is 'TURN LEFT/RIGHT by 15 degrees, MOVE FORWARD by 25 centimeters, or STOP' with one token per action; the HF model card itself shows license '[More Information Needed]' — the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 statement lives in the GitHub README, and the HF repo name is mengwei0427/StreamVLN_Video_qwen_1_5_r2r_rxr_envdrop_scalevln_v1_3 (plus a _real_world variant).

results.claim: DualVLN / InternVLA-N1 splits navigation into a 2 Hz Qwen2.5-VL planner (System 2) that emits a pixel goal plus 4 latent query tokens, and a 30 Hz Diffusion-Transformer policy (System 1) that outputs 32-waypoint trajectories; the two run asynchronously so the fast lane handles dynamic obstacles while the slow lane reasons, and it is deployed on Turtlebot4, Unitree Go2 and Unitree G1.
results.evidence_quote: "System 2 (slow, 2 Hz) uses a 7B pretrained VLM to generate pixel goal and latent goal, while System 1 (fast, 30 Hz) is a lightweight diffusion-based policy." / "four learnable latent queries appended after the pixel goal prediction" / "compact Diffusion Transformer (DiT) design...with a hidden dimension of 384, 12 transformer layers, and 6 attention heads" / "32 dense waypoints" / "generates 32 trajectories in parallel within 0.03s using TensorRT" / "System 1, a lightweight diffusion-based policy model, transforms the grounded targets into continuous traversable trajectories, enabling robust collision avoidance in dynamic scenarios." / "Since the dual-system inference is performed asynchronously (Slow System 2, Fast System 1), the latent goal generated at time t remains fixed" / "wheeled (Turtlebot4), quadruped (Unitree Go2) and humanoid (Unitree G1) robots" / "The full model runs on a remote server with an RTX 4090 GPU, occupying 20GB memory." / "reduces trajectory token inference from 1.1s to 0.7s" / "20 trials per scenario per model" / HF card InternRobotics/InternVLA-N1: license CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, 8B params, BF16, base Qwen2.5-VL.
results.correction: None needed. Verified: R2R-CE val-unseen SR 64.3 / SPL 58.5 / NE 4.05 / OS 70.7; RxR-CE SR 61.4 / NE 4.58 / nDTW 70.0; VLN-PE zero-shot SR 51.60 / SPL 42.49; 'even using only 1% of the trajectories collected for System 2 already yields competitive performance'; '763K social navigation episodes across 60 MP3D scenes'. Note the arXiv page header license (CC BY 4.0) applies to the paper text; the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 is the HF weights license, as the claim states.

results.claim: Even 'streaming' navigators stall on real robots: LiveVLN measured StreamVLN/NaVILA-class models on a Unitree G1 at 30.5% idle time with 94.9% of rounds stop-and-go, and fixed it without retraining by a guarded handoff (committed guard buffer sized from measured sense+inference latency, plus a revisable tail), cutting waiting time 73-78% while preserving success.
results.evidence_quote: "The diagnostic study uses a controlled NaVIDA deployment on a Unitree G1 robot with a front-facing Intel RealSense D455f camera and monocular RGB input." / "Average waiting is 10.64 s per episode, corresponding to a 30.5% waiting ratio. The controller experiences 9.25 pauses over 9.75 inference rounds on average, so 94.9% of rounds are stop-and-go. Native blocking NaVIDA spends nearly one third of a typical episode in waiting time" / Ref [7]: "W. Zhu, Z. Zhang, X. Wang, H. Pan, T. Wang, T. Geng, R. Xu, and F. Zheng (2026) NaVIDA: vision-language navigation with inverse dynamics augmentation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2601.18188" (NaVILA is Ref [8], appearing only as a Table I baseline row) / "The runtime estimates the next sense-and-inference latency, releases the shortest prefix as the next guard buffer whose execution time covers that delay, and keeps the remainder as the revisable tail ... No backbone-specific retraining, architectural change, or fixed action horizon is required" / Table II: StreamVLN T_wait 7.32 -> 1.63 s, eta_wait 17.4% -> 4.4%, N_pause 6.75 -> 0.80, gap 0.96 -> 0.11; NaVIDA T_wait 10.64 -> 2.89 s, eta_wait 30.5% -> 10.3%, N_pause 9.25 -> 1.20, gap 1.09 -> 0.16 / Table I: StreamVLN† SR 56.4 -> +LiveVLN 57.2 (SPL 50.2 -> 50.0; RxR SR 54.4 -> 53.7); NaVIDA SR 61.4 -> 59.9 (SPL 54.7 -> 53.9; RxR 57.4 -> 56.7) / "Under matched checkpoints, LiveVLN cuts waiting time by more than 70% on both StreamVLN and NaVIDA ... while preserving task performance in both simulation and real-robot trials."
results.correction: The second navigator is NaVIDA (Zhu et al., 2026, arXiv:2601.18188, 'vision-language navigation with inverse dynamics augmentation'), not NaVILA; NaVILA is never run with LiveVLN and appears only as a Table I reference row (SR 54.0). All 'NaVILA' numbers in the claim (R2R 59.9 vs 61.4; waiting 10.64 -> 2.89 s, -72.8%) are NaVIDA's. The 30.5% waiting ratio / 94.9% stop-and-go / 10.64 s diagnostic was measured on NaVIDA alone; StreamVLN's native waiting ratio on the same G1 rig was 17.4% (7.32 s, 6.75 pauses per episode). Corrected statement: 'LiveVLN measured StreamVLN and NaVIDA on a Unitree G1 (RTX 5090 server, D455f, Wi-Fi jitter within 50 ms) at 17.4% and 30.5% waiting ratio respectively (NaVIDA: 94.9% of rounds stop-and-go) and, training-free, cut waiting time 77.7% / 72.8% via a guard buffer sized from a running sense+inference latency estimate (psi = l_SI + delta) plus a revisable tail, with SR within about 1.5 points (57.2 vs 56.4; 59.9 vs 61.4) and real-robot stop-within-2m 15/40 -> 16/40 and 12/40 -> 12/40.' Everything else in the claim holds.

results.claim: NaVILA (legged, Go2/H1/G1) shows language itself can be the action interface: an 8B VILA model outputs mid-level text actions ('move forward 75cm', 'turn right 30 degrees') that are cast to fixed velocity commands for a 50 Hz Isaac-Lab RL locomotion policy, reaching 88% on 25 real instructions at about 1 s per action.
results.evidence_quote: "A VLM is fine-tuned to output a mid-level action (VLA) in the form of language such as 'turn right 30 degrees', and a low-level visual locomotion policy ..." / abstract: "mid-level actions with spatial information in the form of language, (e.g., 'moving forward 75cm')" / "VLM outputs a fixed set of actionable words, such as {move forward, turn left, turn right, stop}, we casts these instructions to fixed command velocities {0.5 m/s, pi/6 rad/s, -pi/6 rad/s, 0} and execute with corresponding time durations to align with the specific VLM value." / "This control policy is trained in the Isaac Sim simulator using Isaac Lab and then directly deployed to the real-world robot." / The only frequency stated: "the robot is equipped with a LiDAR sensor mounted at the base of its head, broadcasting point clouds at a frequency of 15Hz." (no '50 Hz' in v1 HTML or v2 PDF) / "NaVILA's current wait time between each action is about 1 second ... the VLA inference time is approximately 0.6 seconds per sample." / "an 88% success rate on 25 instructions, including a 75% success rate on complex instructions" / "we test our NaVILA model on a Unitree Go2 robot and also a Unitree H1 robot within the benchmark" (H1 = VLN-CE-Isaac simulation) / GitHub README: "[RSS'25]", Apache-2.0; HF card a8cheng/navila-llama3-8b-8f shows no license.
results.correction: Two details are not in the source: (1) the paper never states a 50 Hz control rate for the locomotion policy — the only rates given are the LiDAR at 15 Hz, 60K FPS training throughput, and the VLA at 'roughly 1 FPS' (0.6 s inference, ~1 s wait per action including image transmission); drop '50 Hz' or source it elsewhere. (2) Robots: in the cited v1, real-world deployment is on the Go2 only; the H1 appears only in the VLN-CE-Isaac simulation benchmark (Go2 vision 50.2 vs blind 36.2; H1 45.3 vs 24.4); the G1 is not mentioned in v1 or v2 (v2 adds a Booster T1 humanoid 'without any retraining'; the project page lists Go2/G1/Booster T1). Corrected: 'NaVILA (Go2 real-world; H1 in Isaac sim; Booster T1 humanoid added in v2) ... cast to fixed velocities {0.5 m/s, pi/6 rad/s} for an Isaac-Lab PPO locomotion policy (rate unstated), reaching 88% on 25 real instructions x 3 trials at ~1 s per action (0.6 s VLA inference).' All benchmark numbers (R2R 54.0/49.0/5.22; RxR 34.3/28.2; 1,077 of 1,839 trajectories; W4A16 594.58 -> 367.80 ms; 8 frames real-world, 8-64 tested; 2K YouTube videos -> 20K trajectories; 'NaVILA-8B') verified.
