results.claim: The Go2 sim-to-real gap is dominated by camera height, lighting and locomotion-controller mismatch rather than data scale: on the physics-realistic VLN-PE platform NaVid's zero-shot success collapses from 22.4% (humanoid) to 4.7% on a 0.5 m quadruped, RGB-only models lose ~12 points in low light while RGB-D lose ~2-3, and 14 real Go2 episodes went from 7.1% to 28.6% SR after fine-tuning on physics-sim data.
results.evidence_quote: Table 5 ("Comparison of the CMA model using different combination of cross-embodiment training data"): row Quadruped | VLN-CE | val-unseen OS 7.84, SR 4.73, SPL 3.80; row Wheeled | VLN-CE | val-unseen SR 11.02; Table 1 row 6 NaVid (ZS) val-unseen SR 22.42 / "Fig. 5 evaluates NaVid's zero-shot performance on different robot types" — Figure 5 bar chart shows NaVid val-unseen SR approx. 40 (VLN-CE), 32 (Flash), 27 (Wheeled), 22 (Humanoid), 14-15 (Quadruped) / "The quadruped robot (about 0.5 m), with a significantly lower camera height, causes the model to nearly fail completely." / Table 6 val-unseen SR: NaVid 22.42 -> 9.95 (DL300) / 11.17 (CL); CMA 18.78 -> 17.37 / 17.04; RDP 21.98 -> 22.27 / 22.78 / Table 4 (collect w/ loco, eval w/ loco) val-unseen: FR 18.63, StR 3.12, SR 18.78, SPL 14.56 / Table 5 Humanoid rows: Humanoid-data 18.78/14.56; H+Q+W 19.30/16.97; H+Q+W+Flash 26.87/23.54 / "This improvement can be attributed both to increased data volume and to the benefits of multi-view learning" / Table 7: CMA not fine-tuned OS 14.29, SR 7.14; fine-tuned on VLN-PE OS 57.14, SR 28.57 / "fine-tuning small models (#3 and #5) using just 441 episodes from 3 scene leads to a significant performance boost"; Table 2 CMA-CLIP val-unseen SR 15.31 -> 22.46 / abstract: "significant performance degradation due to limited robot observation space, environmental lighting variations, and physical challenges like collisions and falls" / arXiv Comments: "Accepted by ICCV 2025".
results.correction: Three fixes. (1) Model attribution: the 4.73% quadruped and 11.02% wheeled SRs are Table 5 rows for CMA trained on VLN-CE, not NaVid. NaVid's per-embodiment results exist only in the Figure 5 bar chart, where its val-unseen SR on the quadruped is roughly 14-15% (humanoid 22.4%, wheeled ~27%). Corrected: 'zero-shot SR on the ~0.5 m quadruped collapses to 4.7% for VLN-CE-trained CMA (vs 16.0% on the humanoid) and to ~14% for NaVid (vs 22.4%)'. (2) Lighting: RGB-only NaVid loses 12.5 (DL300) / 11.3 (camera light) points; RGB-D CMA loses only 1.4 / 1.7 and RGB-D RDP loses nothing (+0.3 / +0.8), so 'RGB-D lose ~2-3' should be '<2 (RDP unchanged)'. (3) 'Rather than data scale' is not a paper claim: the abstract attributes the drop to observation space, lighting and collisions/falls, the 26.87/23.54 cross-embodiment result uses H+Q+W+Flash data (H+Q+W alone gives 19.30/16.97), and the paper credits that gain 'both to increased data volume and to the benefits of multi-view learning'. Also note: the VLN-CE-side numbers 25.99/32.08/40.67 are not printed in the text; Fig. 4 shows bars at ~25/~32/~40.5 with 'SR declines of 10%, 16%, and 18%', consistent with the claim's values. Controller (18.78 SR, FR 18.63%, StR 3.12%), real-Go2 (14 episodes, 7.14 -> 28.57 SR, OS 14.29 -> 57.14), 441-episode fine-tune (15.31 -> 22.46), and ICCV 2025 are confirmed.

sweeps.topic: Benchmarks a companion robot should be scored on for navigation, instruction following (incl. mid-task interruptions/amendments) and conversation: metric definitions, dataset sizes, current SOTA, offline runnability

findings.claim: R2R-CE / RxR-CE SOTA on a Unitree Go2-deployed model is SR 68.3 / SPL 65.2 (R2R-CE val-unseen) and SR 71.5 / SPL 66.8 / nDTW 76.1 (RxR-CE), but the model is an 8B LLaMA3 VLM that runs at ~10 s per reasoning step, 15 s end-to-end via a remote H20 server; a duplex 10 Hz Model A cannot be a VLM in the loop.
findings.source_title: MobileVLA-R1: Reinforcing Vision-Language-Action for Mobile Robots (ECCV 2026)
findings.numbers: R2R-CE val-unseen NE 4.05 / OS 69.7 / SR 68.3 / SPL 65.2 (NaVILA 54.0/49.0; StreamVLN 56.9/51.9; ETPNav 57.0/49.0); RxR-CE NE 3.92 / SR 71.5 / SPL 66.8 / nDTW 76.1 (NaVILA 49.3/44.0/58.8); LLaMA3-8B backbone, LoRA r=16; CoT data 18K/78K/38K; SFT 4xH20 96GB ~20K steps, GRPO 1xH20 1K steps; real Go2 86-100% success across workspace/corridor/outdoor; latency ~10 s per step, 15 s end-to-end
findings.relevance: Sets the SR bar for VLN-CE and the latency reality: the highest-SR nav model on Parcel's exact robot is two orders of magnitude slower than the 10 Hz frame clock.

findings.claim: A 0.5B-parameter topological VLN policy (ETP-R1) reaches R2R-CE val-unseen SR 65 / SPL 56 and test-unseen SR 64 / SPL 54, and RxR-CE SR 59.92 / nDTW 65.31 / SDTW 50.41 — small policies are sufficient for near-SOTA VLN-CE.
findings.source_title: ETP-R1: Evolving Topological Planning with Reinforcement Fine-tuning for VLN-CE
findings.numbers: 0.5B params; pretrain on 3.18M trajectories then SFT then GRPO; R2R-CE val-unseen NE 3.94 / OSR 72 / SR 65 / SPL 56 (G3D-LF 61/52, HNR 61/51, ETPNav 57/49); test-unseen NE 4.19 / SR 64 / SPL 54; RxR-CE val-unseen NE 5.22 / SR 59.92 / SPL 48.97 / nDTW 65.31 / SDTW 50.41
findings.relevance: Evidence that Model A can be small enough to run on the Orin while staying competitive on the canonical VLN metrics.

findings.claim: R2R-CE has 10,819 train / 778 val_seen / 1,839 val_unseen / 3,408 test episodes over 61/11/18 MP3D scenes (English only); RxR-CE has ~126K instructions in EN/HI/TE with CC-BY annotations; both run offline in Habitat-Sim with ~90 MP3D scenes under the MP3D ToU (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US); success radius 3 m, 0.25 m step.
findings.source_title: VLN-CE Data page + VLN-CE GitHub README + RxR GitHub README
findings.numbers: R2R-CE train 10,819 / val_seen 778 / val_unseen 1,839 / test 3,408 / EnvDrop 146,304; scenes 61/11/18/60; vocab 2,504; RxR 126K instructions, 3 languages, CC-BY; splits train 72.1MB, val_seen 12.9MB, val_unseen 12MB, test 1.9MB; Habitat-Sim/Lab 0.1.7; forward 0.25 m; success 3 m; MP3D CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US (see also https://github.com/jacobkrantz/VLN-CE and https://github.com/google-research-datasets/RxR)
findings.relevance: Sizes and licences for standing up a VLN-CE eval on the desktop sim; nDTW/SDTW defined by RxR.

findings.claim: HM3D-OVON (open-vocab ObjectNav): 15,661 instances / 379 categories / 181 scans; success = stop within 1 m within 500 steps; 2024 baselines SR 35-37 / SPL ~20 on val-unseen; 2026 SOTA Qwen-RobotNav-4B SR 53.1 / SPL 20.9 on unseen at 4.9 Hz on a Jetson Thor (FP8), trained on 15.6M samples (8B: 2,816 H100 GPU-hours).
findings.source_title: HM3D-OVON: A Dataset and Benchmark for Open-Vocabulary Object Goal Navigation (+ Qwen-RobotNav Technical Report)
findings.numbers: Train 145 scenes x 50k eps; val 36 scenes x 3k; categories 280 train / 79 seen / 50 synonyms / 49 unseen; Table III SR/SPL (seen|syn|unseen): DAgRL+OD 38.5/21.1 | 39.0/21.4 | 37.1/19.9; VLFM 35.2/18.6 | 32.4/17.3 | 35.2/19.6; RL 39.2/18.7 | 27.8/11.7 | 18.6/7.5; noise: DAgRL+OD -0.3 SR vs VLFM -6.1; Qwen-RobotNav-4B 57.7/60.1/53.1 SR, SPL 24.4/25.1/20.9; 8B 56.1/57.8/51.2; Jetson Thor FP8 on-device 204 ms (4.9 Hz), remote 196 ms (5.1 Hz) (https://arxiv.org/html/2606.18112); HM3D licence academic non-commercial (https://aihabitat.org/datasets/hm3d/)
findings.relevance: The comparable open-vocab benchmark for Parcel's SigLIP-2 semantic grounding + search; SPL ~20 is the honest efficiency ceiling; the Jetson number is the nearest on-robot VLM-policy latency datum.

findings.claim: GOAT-Bench (lifelong multimodal nav, 5-10 sequential goals per episode specified by category / language / image): paper-era val-unseen SR 29.5 / SPL 11.3 (SenseAct-NN skill chain; monolithic RL 12.3 / 6.8; Modular GOAT 24.9 / 17.2); 2026 zero-shot VLM + 3D scene memory (HGR) reaches SR 64.14 / SPL 50.1 on full val and 72.41 / 56.22 on a 278-subtask subset.
findings.source_title: GOAT-Bench: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal Lifelong Navigation (+ Hypothesis Graph Refinement 2026)
findings.numbers: Train 725k episodes (145 scenes x 5k); val 36 scenes x 10 episodes (50-100 subtasks each); val-unseen 36 categories 1,282 goals; val-seen-synonyms 31 categories 877 goals; success within 1 m (HTML renders '11m', likely typo) within 500 actions/subtask; SR/SPL: Modular GOAT 24.9/17.2, CoW 16.1/10.4, SenseAct-NN skill chain 29.5/11.3, monolithic 12.3/6.8; HGR full val 64.14/50.1 vs 3D-Mem 62.9/44.7; subset 72.41/56.22 (https://arxiv.org/html/2604.04108)
findings.relevance: Closest benchmark to a queue of historical global plans across modalities; monolithic end-to-end RL was the worst family, memory-based modular pipelines the best.

findings.claim: Social navigation must be scored with Personal Space Compliance (1.0 m threshold = 0.3 m human radius + 0.25 m robot + margin) and human-collision rate: Falcon SOTA on Social-HM3D is SR 55.15 / SPL 55.15 / PSC 89.56 / H-Coll 42.96, while Habitat 3.0's own SocialNav RL baseline reports 97% finding success with a 0.51 collision rate.
findings.source_title: From Cognition to Precognition: A Future-Aware Framework for Social Navigation (Falcon / Social-HM3D) + Habitat 3.0
findings.kind: primary paper (PDF read) + primary paper (arXiv HTML)
findings.numbers: Social-HM3D 844 scenes, Social-MP3D 72 scenes, up to 6 ORCA humans; Table II (Suc/SPL/STL/PSC/H-Coll %): A* 46.14/46.14/46.12/90.56/53.50; ORCA 38.91/38.91/38.44/90.55/47.52; Proximity-Aware 20.11/18.57/19.51/92.91/33.99; Falcon 55.15/55.15/54.94/89.56/42.96; MP3D Falcon 55.05/55.04/54.80/90.01/42.19; Habitat 3.0: find-and-follow at 1-2 m, metrics S / SPS / F / CR, RL 97% S, CR 0.51+-0.03, expert 100%, CR 0.52; 1190 FPS; HSSD 37 train / 10 test scenes; 12 avatar shapes (https://arxiv.org/html/2310.13724)
findings.relevance: Owner-following is literally the Habitat 3.0 SocialNav task; PSC/H-Coll expose that SOTA still collides with a human in 42% of episodes.

findings.claim: BARN scores constrained-space navigation as s_i = 1_success x OT_i / clip(AT_i, 2OT_i, 8OT_i) (max 0.5 since the bound moved from 4OT to 2OT); ICRA 2024 sim winner scored 0.4762 vs baselines 0.1656-0.4354 and then won only 6/9 physical trials; every surviving stack was hybrid learning + classical + explicit safety layer.
findings.source_title: Lessons Learned From the Third BARN Challenge at ICRA 2024 (IEEE RAM, Sept 2024) + BARN Challenge 2026 page
findings.numbers: Jackal, 2D LiDAR, 2 m/s; 300 public envs + 50 hidden x 10 trials; sim 2024: LiCS-KI 0.4762, AIMS 0.4723, EIT-NUS 0.3795, MLDA_EEE 0.2476; physical: LiCS-KI 6/9 (avg 30/35 s), MLDA_EEE 5/9, AIMS 5/9, EIT-NUS 0/9; 120 cardboard boxes, 3 courses, 5 trials, top 3 count; winners 2025 RRSL 7/9, RobotiXX 3/9, UVA AMR 1/9; 2026 IN2BOT / EW-Glab / Team Robo (https://people.cs.gmu.edu/~xiao/Research/BARN_Challenge/BARN_Challenge26.html)
findings.relevance: Template for a time-weighted, collision-gated local-motion metric for Model A's local movements and for a safety layer independent of the learned policy.

findings.claim: On EmbodiedBench (1,128 tasks, 4 sims, 24 MLLMs) the best models average only ~50% success and low-level EB-Manipulation tops out at 28.9% (GPT-4o); on EmbodiedEval (328 tasks, 125 scenes, LEGENT/Unity) humans score 97.26% vs GPT-4o 25.00% — MLLM planners are far from human on interactive embodied instruction following.
findings.source_title: EmbodiedBench (ICML 2025) + EmbodiedEval (2025)
findings.numbers: EmbodiedBench: EB-ALFRED 300 / EB-Habitat 300 / EB-Navigation 300 / EB-Manipulation 228; six subsets ~50 each; SR (ALFRED/Habitat/Nav/Manip/avg): GPT-4o 56.3/59.0/57.7/28.9/50.5; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 64.0/68.0/44.7/25.4/50.5; Gemini-1.5-Pro 62.3/56.3/24.3/21.1/41.0; InternVL3-78B 39.0/55.0/53.7/26.3/43.5; sims AI2-THOR, Habitat 2.0, VLMBench; local models via LMDeploy, 48 GB GPU guidance, Docker, headless X. EmbodiedEval: human 97.26%, GPT-4o 25.00% (GcS 32.42%), Qwen-VL-Max 28.07%, Gemini-1.5-Pro 19.26%, LLaVA-OV-72B 12.80%, InternVL2-8B 8.23%; needs display/Xorg, ~20 GB, MIT (https://arxiv.org/html/2501.11858)
findings.relevance: Calibrates expectations for a hosted-VLM planner over Parcel's task executive and shows both suites are runnable on a Linux desktop GPU.

findings.claim: Situated Instruction Following (SIF) is the nearest benchmark to 'the instruction's referent changes mid-task': when the human moves (S_hum) even an oracle-perception LLM planner drops to SPL 29 vs 81 on static pick-and-place, and with learned perception SPL is 19 / 11 / 15 (PnP / S_obj / S_hum); ambiguity handling is the failure mode.
findings.source_title: Situated Instruction Following (ECCV 2024)
findings.numbers: 240 val + 240 test tasks (40 seen / 40 unseen per type x 3 types); 10 houses; Spot model, 0.17 m step; SPL primary; Table 6 Val Seen SPL: Oracle+oracle 100/100/98; Oracle+learned 47/44/59; Prompter oracle 70/29/29, learned 17/10/11; Reasoner oracle 81/60/29, learned 19/11/15; Table 9 Reasoner SR (GT vision) S_hum clear 15 vs ambiguous 75, S_obj 72 vs 77
findings.relevance: Defines a testable 'situated' amendment axis (object moved / human moved) for Parcel's transactional goal amendment; no spoken interruptions though.

findings.claim: IHBench is the only fetched benchmark that scores spoken mid-task interruptions with a typed taxonomy (Normal, Impatient, Correction, Topic Switch, Filler, Pushback): the best hosted realtime model (GPT Realtime 2) reaches task-fulfilment win .728 and recovery-quality pass .624, best open model Qwen3-Omni-30B .304 / .676, filler (backchannel) handling is 7-31% for GPT vs 62-68% for Gemini 2.5, and task fulfilment decays -0.030 per conversation turn; its rubric judge agrees with humans at kappa 0.75 / 0.70.
findings.source_title: IHBench: Evaluating Post-Interruption Recovery in Voice Agents with Structured Workflows
findings.numbers: 45 conversations, 10 domains, 428 interruption points, 30.1 msgs avg; 27 configs (17 closed, 10 open), 3 epochs, 1000-iter bootstrap; Table 1 TF/RQ: GPT Realtime 2 (medium) .728/.624; (xhigh) .702/.613; GPT Realtime 1.5 .654/.655; Gemini 3 Flash (think) .632/.605; GPT Realtime .597/.680; Gemini 2.5 Flash (think) .586/.704; Gemini 2.5 Flash .488/.679; Gemini 3.1 Flash Live .419/.611; Qwen3-Omni-30B .304/.676; filler pass GPT 7-31%, Gemini 2.5 62-68%, Gemini 3.x 13-32%; slope -0.030/turn (open-weight 3.3x faster, closed -0.016); human kappa 0.75 TF / 0.70 RQ; data on HF bosonai/ihbench
findings.relevance: Direct template for Model B's revise / keep / queue injection eval: interruption point + type + type-specific pass criteria, and a validated judge protocol.

findings.claim: Full-Duplex-Bench measures the timing behaviours Model B's narration must satisfy — pause-handling takeover rate, backchannel timing (JSD), response latency, and interruption handling — and shows the field is far from human: Gemini Live pause TOR 0.255 at 1.30 s latency vs Moshi TOR 0.985 at 0.27 s; v1/v1.5 run offline locally; v2 adds an LLM examiner with Fast/Slow pacing and 1-5 rubric scores (GPT-Realtime correction 4.02 / entity 4.51 / safety 4.44 vs Moshi 2.88 / 2.76 / 3.67) validated at r = 0.59-0.69 vs humans.
findings.source_title: Full-Duplex-Bench v1 (ASRU 2025) + Full-Duplex-Bench v2 + GitHub README
findings.numbers: 727 samples: Candor 216 pause + 119 turn-taking; ICC 55 backchannel; synthetic 200 interruption + 137 pause; pauses 0.4-1.0 s; metrics TOR, backchannel freq, JSD, latency, GPT-4o 0-5 score; results (pause TOR / bc TOR / latency / int TOR / GPT-4o): dGSLM 0.934/0.935/0.352s/0.917/0.201; Moshi 0.985/0.980/0.265s/1.000/0.765; Freeze-Omni 0.642/0.481/0.953s/0.867/3.615; Gemini Live 0.255/0.310/1.301s/0.891/3.376; v2 (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.07838): GPT-Realtime examiner, Gemini 2.5 Flash judge on Parakeet ASR, Fast: Freeze-Omni 2.74/2.62/3.94, Moshi 2.88/2.76/3.67, GPT-Realtime 4.02/4.51/4.44; Slow: 3.50/2.86/4.27, 3.46/3.84/3.51, 3.94/4.12/4.53; r=0.59-0.69; README: v1/v1.5 offline local, v2 WebRTC, v3 tool use under disfluency (https://github.com/DanielLin94144/Full-Duplex-Bench)
findings.relevance: Gives Parcel a runnable offline timing scorer for 'Sure, I'll check the sofa' (turn-taking latency) and 'Done! Should I go back?' (robot-initiated turn, TOR), plus the examiner pattern for the sim-to-real conversation rig.

findings.claim: Talking Turns provides an offline supervised turn-taking judge (ROC-AUC 92.0 on Switchboard, 91 OOD) and shows current systems take the floor 2x too often and almost never backchannel: human turn-change 15.9% vs Moshi 32.7% / cascade 37.1%; backchannel 0.30% vs 0.01%; floor-taking success 63.6% vs 17.4% (Moshi) / 59.4% (cascade).
findings.source_title: Talking Turns: Benchmarking Audio Foundation Models on Turn-Taking Dynamics (Apple)
findings.numbers: Judge trained on Switchboard 2000/300/138 conversations; ROC-AUC continuation 93.3, backchannel 89.4, turn change 90.8, interruption 91.3, silence 95.1, overall 92.0; OOD Columbia Games 91.5, Fisher 91.0; ~4 h human-AI dialogue, 11 participants; systems Moshi, cascade (VAD+Whisper+SmolLM+MeloTTS), GPT-4o+Whisper, SALMONN, Qwen2-Audio; understanding acc 56.7-66.3%, prediction 46.5-62.2%
findings.relevance: A no-API judge for narration timing that can score Parcel's duplex frame-clock outputs against human-human statistics.

findings.claim: VoiceBench (6,783 spoken instructions, 7-9 subsets) shows pipeline ASR+LLM still matches or beats end-to-end speech models and that spoken input is fragile: low-resource accents cost 15-35%, mispronunciation -20.34%, and some models' safety refusal drops from >=95% (text) to 37-57% (speech); the 2026 leaderboard tops at 89.88 (LFG-3) with Whisper-v3+GPT-4o at 87.80 and GPT-4o-Audio at 86.75.
findings.source_title: VoiceBench: Benchmarking LLM-Based Voice Assistants (TACL 2026) + leaderboard
findings.kind: primary paper (arXiv HTML) + leaderboard page + repo
findings.numbers: AlpacaEval 636 (repo: 199), CommonEval 200, SD-QA 553, OpenBookQA 455, MMSU 3,074, IFEval 345, AdvBench 520, + WildVoice 1,000, BBH 1,000; metrics GPT-4o 1-5 judge / accuracy / IFEval / refusal; paper overall: Whisper+GPT-4o 87.23, GPT-4o-Audio 86.42, Whisper+LLaMA 79.06, Qwen2-Audio 55.35, LLaMA-Omni 37.51, VITA 34.68, Mini-Omni2 31.32, Moshi 27.47; degradation mispronunciation -20.34%, disfluency -12.55%, repetition -9.30%, grammar -2.68%; leaderboard LFG-3 89.88, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni 89.39, Ultravox-GLM-4P7 88.86, Whisper-v3+GPT-4o 87.80, GPT-4o-Audio 86.75, GPT-4o-mini-Audio 82.84 (https://matthewcym.github.io/VoiceBench/)
findings.relevance: Justifies keeping a cascaded owner-voice-command path for Model B and adds accent/noise/disfluency robustness rows to the conversation eval.

findings.claim: AudioBench (8 tasks, 26 datasets, 400+ h, 100k+ samples) validates a fully local judge: Llama-3-70B-Instruct correlates >0.85 with GPT-4-as-judge, and no single audio LLM wins across speech, audio-scene and paralinguistic tasks (cascades win speech-heavy tasks; AudioLLMs win emotion/gender).
findings.source_title: AudioBench: A Universal Benchmark for Audio Large Language Models (NAACL 2025)
findings.numbers: ASR x9, SQA x4, SI x2, AQA x3, AC x2, emotion x3, accent x1, gender x2; (SALMONN / Qwen-Audio-Chat / WavLLM / Whisper+LLaMA3): LibriSpeech-clean WER 2.10/3.20/1.83/2.25; other 4.80/6.07/3.71/4.16; CN-College-Listen 65.43/74.50/85.25/60.85; OpenHermes-Audio 22.40/44.80/63.0/11.00; ALPACA-Audio 21.60/52.60/70.8/9.60; AudioCaps METEOR 6.70/19.89/7.95/27.70; IEMOCAP emotion 45.91/49.30/34.43/27.34; VoxCeleb1 gender 70.51/99.12/53.41/70.56; accent 37.65/29.19/39.33/45.70
findings.relevance: Lets the conversation-quality scorer drop its hosted-judge dependency (local 70B judge) and adds paralinguistic (emotion) rows relevant to a companion.

findings.claim: Long-term conversational memory is far from solved and its metrics are noisy: LoCoMo (50 conversations, ~305 turns / 9.2K tokens each, 7,512 questions) gives human F1 87.9 vs GPT-4-turbo 32.1 (RAG 41.4); PersonaMem (180+ histories, ~6,000 MC queries at 32k/128k/1M tokens, 7 personalisation question types) has frontier models at ~50%, with 'suggest new ideas / recommendations / generalise' at 30-50%.
findings.source_title: LoCoMo (Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents) + PersonaMem (Know Me, Respond to Me)
findings.numbers: LoCoMo: 19.3 sessions avg (max 35), 304.9 turns, 9,209.2 tokens; QA 7,512 = single-hop 2,705 / multi-hop 1,104 / temporal 1,547 / open-domain 285 / adversarial 1,871; F1 human 87.9, GPT-4-turbo 32.1, GPT-3.5-16K 37.8, RAG 41.4; 24.2 events/conv; repo ships locomo10.json (10 convs). PersonaMem (https://arxiv.org/html/2504.14225): 10/20/60 sessions = 32k/128k/1M; 15 scenarios; 128k accuracy GPT-4.5 ~52, GPT-4.1 ~52, Gemini-2.0-Flash ~50, o4-mini ~50, o1 ~48, Claude-3.7 ~48, DeepSeek-R1 ~47, Llama-4-Maverick ~43; easiest 60-70%, hardest 30-50%
findings.relevance: PersonaMem's offline multiple-choice format is the right shape for testing whether the whisperer's StateDigest + global history lets the narrator remember owner preferences; LoCoMo only for temporal questions.

findings.claim: tau2-bench shows that user simulators become reliable only when tied to the environment (telecom simulator 16% error / 6% critical vs 40-47% for prompt-only retail/airline) and that moving from no-user to dual-control costs frontier agents 18-25 pp pass^1; pass^1 -> pass^4 gaps of 8-12 pp mean single-trial scores are unreliable. MIT-licensed, LiteLLM, local models allowed.
findings.source_title: tau2-bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment (+ repo, taubench.com)
findings.numbers: Retail 115, airline 50, telecom 114 tasks (2,285 generated); Dec-POMDP dual control; user error telecom 16%/6%, retail 40%/12%, airline 47%/13%; GPT-4.1 pass^1/pass^4 retail 74/82, airline 56/68, telecom 34/45; o4-mini ~50/~62; Claude 3.7 ~45-49/~60-62; no-user->dual-control drop GPT-4.1 -18 pp, o4-mini -25 pp; leaderboard 2026 tau2: Qwen3.5-397B-A17B 87.9, Gemini 3.0 Pro 85.4, Claude Opus 4.5 85.3; tau3-Voice Pine Voice Preview 75.4; MIT; `tau2 run --agent-llm ... --user-llm ...` (https://github.com/sierra-research/tau2-bench, https://taubench.com)
findings.relevance: Design rule for the 'LLM converses with the robot while it navigates' rig: give the simulated owner the robot's StateDigest/map (dual control) and report pass^k over >= 4 trials.

findings.claim: LLM-as-judge scores must be reported chance-corrected: across 21 judges / 9 providers / ~541k judgments, raw agreement overstates Cohen's kappa by 33.8-41.3 pp on MT-Bench ('85% agreement => kappa ~0.48'), position bias reaches 0.192 even for judges with test-retest >0.95, and verbosity bias is negligible (<0.011); reference-anchored QA judging reaches kappa 0.72-0.96 vs human majority.
findings.source_title: Reliability without Validity: A Systematic, Large-Scale Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge Models (+ LLMs-as-Judges in Free-Form QA, WiNLP 2025)
findings.kind: primary papers (arXiv HTML; ACL Anthology PDF read)
findings.numbers: 21 judges, 9 providers, MT-Bench/JudgeBench/RewardBench, 118 runs, ~541,000 judgments; kappa deflation 33.8-41.3 pp (MT-Bench), 23.7 (JudgeBench), 10.4 (RewardBench); test-retest 0.888-0.992; position bias 0.002-0.192; 7/16 judges >=1.5x flip-rate degradation; verbosity <0.011; MVVP: kappa, AB+BA swaps, >=3 runs, >=2 benchmarks. WiNLP (https://aclanthology.org/2025.winlp-main.37.pdf): 100 samples/dataset; PA human 82-99% vs judges 72-96%; single-judge kappa 0.63-0.93; ensemble kappa 0.72-0.96 (TruthfulQA 0.72-0.79, TriviaQA 0.79-0.96, HotpotQA 0.88-0.96)
findings.relevance: Parcel's conversation-quality scorer (grounding 2/10, personal 3/13) needs a kappa-based validity audit before it is used as a training or gating signal.

findings.claim: Competition sim-to-real records warn that simulation rank does not transfer: OVMM's winner went 10.8% (sim) -> 33.3% (real) while the next two teams (3.2%, 2.4% sim) scored 0% real; heuristic/RL baselines were 0.8% / 0.0%; winners credited error detection and recovery over perception accuracy.
findings.source_title: Towards Open-World Mobile Manipulation in Homes: Lessons from the NeurIPS 2023 HomeRobot OVMM Challenge
findings.numbers: 61 teams, 79 final submissions; metrics overall success, partial success (find object / grasp / find receptacle / place), steps; baselines heuristic 0.8%, RL 0.0%; sim UniTeam 10.8%, Rulai 3.2%, KuzHum 2.4%; real UniTeam 33.3%, Rulai 0.0%, KuzHum 0.0%
findings.relevance: Argues for building the Go2 sim-to-real rig around recovery/retry instrumentation and reporting sim and physical numbers side by side.

design_implications: Model A must be a small policy (ETP-R1 shows 0.5B reaches R2R-CE SR 65 / SPL 56); the best Go2-deployed VLN model (MobileVLA-R1, SR 68.3) runs at ~10-15 s per step and the fastest Jetson VLM nav policy is ~5 Hz on a Thor, so the VLM/hosted model can only update the global plan asynchronously while the 10 Hz act-token loop is served by Model A. Report Model A latency on the Orin as a first-class metric next to SR/SPL/nDTW.

Evaluate Model A on HM3D-OVON val-unseen and GOAT-Bench val-unseen (both offline in Habitat) so Parcel's SR 0.20 is placed against known baselines (2024 modular SR 35-37, 2026 SR 53-64); expect SPL ~20 on open-vocab search unless an explicit 3D scene memory is added — GOAT's monolithic end-to-end RL was the worst family (SR 12.3).

Build the mid-task interruption/amendment eval as an IHBench-style scenario set over the existing 5x5 instruction-nav matrix: typed interruption points (Normal/Correction/Topic-Switch/Filler/Pushback/Impatient mapped to revise/keep/queue), 2-4 type-specific pass criteria, task-fulfilment vs a reference, and a rubric judge validated to kappa >= 0.7; add SIF-style situated cases (object moved, owner moved) where oracle planners drop to SPL ~29.

Score Model B's narration with Full-Duplex-Bench v1/v1.5 metrics offline (pause-handling TOR, response latency, backchannel JSD, interruption TOR) and a Talking-Turns supervised judge (ROC-AUC 92); the target window for 'Sure, I'll check the sofa' is under ~1 s and robot-initiated turns ('Done! Should I go back?') must not barge in. Use the Full-Duplex-Bench v2 examiner pattern (LLM examiner, Fast vs Slow pacing, 1-5 rubrics) as the template for the sim-to-real 'LLM converses with the robot while it navigates' rig.

In the conversation-during-navigation harness, couple the simulated owner to the environment (give it the robot's StateDigest and map, dual control as in tau2-bench telecom: 16% simulator error vs 40-47% prompt-only) and report pass^k over >= 4 trials; budget for an 18-25 pp drop versus scripted commands.

Audit the conversation-quality scorer with the Minimum Viable Validation Protocol before using it for training or gating: chance-corrected kappa (85% raw agreement is only kappa ~0.48), AB/BA swaps for position bias, >= 3 runs, >= 2 benchmarks; a local Llama-3-70B judge is acceptable (corr > 0.85 with GPT-4 on AudioBench) and removes the hosted dependency from the eval loop.

Score owner-following with Habitat 3.0 SocialNav (find-and-follow at 1-2 m: finding success, SPS, following rate) plus Falcon's PSC (1.0 m) and H-Coll; do not rely on Habitat 3.0's collision rate (baseline 97% success with 51% collisions).

Keep a cascaded ASR+LLM path for owner voice commands: VoiceBench shows pipelines match or beat end-to-end speech models and are more robust to accents (-15 to -35% for low-resource accents), mispronunciation (-20%), and speech-form safety bypass (refusal 37-57%); add these perturbations as rows in the conversation eval.

Use PersonaMem-style multiple-choice memory probes (32k/128k contexts, 7 question types) to test whether the global history + StateDigest lets the narrator remember owner preferences; frontier models sit at ~50%, so this is a differentiator, not a solved input.

Plan the Go2 sim-to-real setup around error detection/recovery and a safety layer independent of Model A: OVMM winners transferred only via recovery logic (10.8% sim -> 33.3% real, runners-up 0%), and every BARN physical finisher was a hybrid stack with an explicit safety check; report sim and physical numbers side by side.

Licensing for the offline desktop stack: MP3D scenes (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US + ToU) and HM3D (academic non-commercial) are fine for internal evals but not for commercial training data; RxR annotations CC-BY; tau2-bench and EmbodiedEval MIT; only VoiceBench's open-ended subsets, Full-Duplex-Bench v1's interruption score and v2's examiner require hosted models, and each can be swapped for a local judge with re-validation.
open_questions: What SR / SPL does Parcel's current grid planner + SigLIP-2 grounding + search/recovery achieve on HM3D-OVON val-unseen and GOAT-Bench val-unseen through the product code path? Needed to place the frozen-matrix SR 0.20.

Can a 0.5B ETP-R1-class or Qwen-RobotNav-2B policy run at >= 5 Hz on the Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB at FP8/INT8 (the published 4.9 Hz figure is on a Jetson Thor), and how much SR is lost versus the 8B models?

No fetched benchmark scores spoken interruption of a moving robot with a navigation-state-dependent rubric; IHBench (structured workflows) and SIF (moving humans) are the nearest halves. Does anything closer exist (searches exhausted this session)?

GOAT-Bench success radius: the arXiv HTML renders '11m'; confirm 1 m in the PDF before configuring an evaluator. Likewise the VLN-CE README extraction returned a 30 degree turn angle; verify the YAML (common configs use 15 degrees).
The 'dialogue kappa = 0.57' LLM-judge figure surfaced by search was not found in the fetched WiNLP paper; its source is unknown and it should not be cited until located.
Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5 overlap-event numbers (side conversation, ambient speech, listener backchannel) were not extracted; they matter for a household with several people.

Whether a companion robot should backchannel or take the floor at human-human rates (Talking Turns human reference: 15.9% turn change, 0.30% backchannel) is a product decision; the benchmarks measure human-likeness, not companion appropriateness.

LoCoMo later-work 'accuracy' numbers (86-94% in search summaries) are on the 10-conversation subset with an LLM-judge metric, not the paper's F1; a consistent metric must be chosen before comparing memory systems.

results.claim: R2R-CE / RxR-CE SOTA on a Unitree Go2-deployed model is SR 68.3 / SPL 65.2 (R2R-CE val-unseen) and SR 71.5 / SPL 66.8 / nDTW 76.1 (RxR-CE), but the model is an 8B LLaMA3 VLM that runs at ~10 s per reasoning step, 15 s end-to-end via a remote H20 server; a duplex 10 Hz Model A cannot be a VLM in the loop.
results.evidence_quote: Table 2 (R2R-CE val-unseen): MobileVLA-R1 NE 4.05 / OS 69.7 / SR 68.3 / SPL 65.2; NaVILA 54.0/49.0; StreamVLN 56.9/51.9; ETPNav 57.0/49.0. Table 3 (RxR-CE): MobileVLA-R1 NE 3.92 / SR 71.5 / SPL 66.8 / nDTW 76.1; NaVILA 49.3/44.0/58.8. Text: "LLaMA3-8B language backbone" with LoRA "r=16, α=32"; "Training is conducted on 4×H20 (96 GB) GPUs"; "On this setup, one forward pass of MobileVLA-R1 takes about 10 seconds per decision step, and the end-to-end closed loop (including perception I/O and network transmission) requires roughly 15 seconds per control step." Table 4 (real Go2) SR: workspace 0.93/0.91, corridor 1.00/0.86, outdoor 1.00/0.96. Dataset: "18K episode-level samples, 78K step-level samples, and ... 38K CoT annotations"; ~20K SFT steps, 1K GRPO steps.
results.correction: All numbers in the claim check out against the arXiv HTML (v1, 22 Nov 2025). Two caveats: (1) the source_title's '(ECCV 2026)' venue is not stated anywhere on the arXiv abs/HTML page (no Comments field; the only ECCV mention is a 2024 reference), so treat the venue as unverified; (2) 'a duplex 10 Hz Model A cannot be a VLM in the loop' is the author's inference, not a statement in the paper.

results.claim: HM3D-OVON (open-vocab ObjectNav): 15,661 instances / 379 categories / 181 scans; success = stop within 1 m within 500 steps; 2024 baselines SR 35-37 / SPL ~20 on val-unseen; 2026 SOTA Qwen-RobotNav-4B SR 53.1 / SPL 20.9 on unseen at 4.9 Hz on a Jetson Thor (FP8), trained on 15.6M samples (8B: 2,816 H100 GPU-hours).
results.evidence_quote: HM3D-OVON: "over 15k annotated instances of household objects across 379 distinct categories" (Table I: 15,661); "181 unique, photo-realistic virtual scans of real-world environments"; "we generate 50k episodes per scene for the 145 training scenes, and 3k episodes per scene for the 36 validation scenes"; "Success is defined as the agent invoking stop within 1m of a goal object within 500 time steps." Table III val-unseen SR/SPL: DAgRL+OD 37.1/19.9, VLFM 35.2/19.6, RL 18.6/7.5; noise: DAgRL+OD drops "up to 0.3% and 3.0%", VLFM "up to 6.1% and 5.4%". Qwen-RobotNav (arXiv 2606.18112) Table 5: 4B seen 57.7/24.4, synonyms 60.1/25.1, unseen 53.1/20.9; 8B 56.1/28.5, 57.8/28.8, 51.2/24.0; "trained on 15.6M samples"; 8B "trained with a global batch size of 256 for a total of 2,816 H100 GPU hours"; Jetson Thor FP8 on-device "204 ms" ("4.9 Hz"), remote "196 ms (5.1 Hz)". aihabitat.org: "HM3D is free and available here for academic, non-commercial research."
results.correction: Numbers are correct as written. One nuance for the 'SPL ~20 efficiency ceiling' framing: the Qwen-RobotNav-8B reaches SPL 24.0 on val-unseen (28.5 seen / 28.8 synonyms), so the 4B's 20.9 is not the best SPL in that report; the numbers field's '8B 56.1/57.8/51.2' are SR only. The 4B model's GPU-hours are not stated (only the 8B's 2,816).

results.claim: IHBench is the only fetched benchmark that scores spoken mid-task interruptions with a typed taxonomy (Normal, Impatient, Correction, Topic Switch, Filler, Pushback): the best hosted realtime model (GPT Realtime 2) reaches task-fulfilment win .728 and recovery-quality pass .624, best open model Qwen3-Omni-30B .304 / .676, filler (backchannel) handling is 7-31% for GPT vs 62-68% for Gemini 2.5, and task fulfilment decays -0.030 per conversation turn; its rubric judge agrees with humans at kappa 0.75 / 0.70.
results.evidence_quote: Table 1 (audio input, 3 epochs; judge GPT-5.4-mini): GPT Realtime 2 (medium)† .728±.03 / .624±.04; GPT Realtime 2 (xhigh)† .702/.613; GPT Realtime 1.5 .654/.655; Gemini 3 Flash† .632/.605; GPT Realtime .597/.680; Gemini 2.5 Flash† .586/.704; Gemini 2.5 Flash .488/.679; Gemini 3.1 Flash Live .419/.611; open-weight block: Gemma 4 12B Instruct† .511±.03 / .550±.04; Gemma 4 12B Instruct .505/.540; MiMo-Audio-7B† .445/.519; Voxtral-Small-24B .308/.593; Qwen3-Omni-30B .304±.03 / .676±.04; Kimi-Audio-7B .220/.519. "all evaluated GPT-family audio models continue an utterance correctly after a backchannel less than a third of the time (filler pass rate between 7% and 31%), and the Gemini 2.5 family is markedly better (62%–68%) although the newer Gemini 3.x line regresses sharply (13%–32%)." "The mean per-model slope is −0.030 per additional turn"; open-weight "mean −0.053" vs closed "mean slope of −0.016". Judge agreement: "The judges agree with each other. The second judge is Gemini 3 Flash (with thinking) ... the two judges' 3-epoch verdicts agree at the sample level in the 'substantial' range (Cohen's κ = 0.75 on TF and 0.70 on RQ)"; "The judge agrees with humans ... the judge agrees with humans slightly more often than two humans agree with each other (κ = 0.45–0.51 vs. 0.43 on TF and 0.41–0.44 vs. 0.40 on RQ), so it is statistically indistinguishable from an additional annotator." Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/bosonai/ihbench (PDF).
results.correction: Two details are wrong. (1) Kappa 0.75 / 0.70 is JUDGE-vs-JUDGE agreement (GPT-5.4-mini vs Gemini 3 Flash thinking), not judge-vs-human. Judge-vs-human agreement is κ = 0.45–0.51 on TF and 0.41–0.44 on RQ, which the authors present as on par with human–human agreement (0.43 / 0.40). Corrected statement: 'its rubric judge agrees with a second LLM judge at κ 0.75 / 0.70 and with human annotators at κ 0.45–0.51 / 0.41–0.44 (human–human 0.43 / 0.40).' (2) Qwen3-Omni-30B is not the best open-weight model on task fulfilment: Gemma 4 12B Instruct (thinking) leads open-weight TF at .511 (.550 RQ), followed by Gemma 4 12B .505 and MiMo-Audio-7B (thinking) .445; Qwen3-Omni-30B (.304 TF) is the best open-weight model on recovery quality (.676). Everything else (taxonomy, 45 conv / 10 domains / 428 points / 30.1 msgs, 27 configs = 17 closed + 10 open, 3 epochs, 1000-iter bootstrap, the GPT Realtime 2 .728/.624, filler rates, −0.030 slope, HF link) is supported.

results.claim: Full-Duplex-Bench measures the timing behaviours Model B's narration must satisfy — pause-handling takeover rate, backchannel timing (JSD), response latency, and interruption handling — and shows the field is far from human: Gemini Live pause TOR 0.255 at 1.30 s latency vs Moshi TOR 0.985 at 0.27 s; v1/v1.5 run offline locally; v2 adds an LLM examiner with Fast/Slow pacing and 1-5 rubric scores (GPT-Realtime correction 4.02 / entity 4.51 / safety 4.44 vs Moshi 2.88 / 2.76 / 3.67) validated at r = 0.59-0.69 vs humans.
results.evidence_quote: v1 (arXiv 2503.04721v3; abs page: "Accepted by ASRU 2025"): Candor pause handling 216, smooth turn-taking 119; ICC backchannel 55; synthetic user interruption 200, pause handling 137; pauses "between 0.4 and 1.0 seconds"; metrics TOR, backchannel frequency, JSD ("ranges from 0 (perfect alignment) to 1 (complete divergence)"), latency ("time (in seconds) between the end of the user's speech and the start of the model's response"), GPT-4o score 0–5. Table III (pause TOR / bc TOR / latency / interruption TOR / GPT-4o): dGSLM 0.934/0.935/0.352/0.917/0.201; Moshi 0.985/0.980/0.265/1.000/0.765; Freeze-Omni 0.642/0.481/0.953/0.867/3.615; Gemini Live 0.255/0.310/1.301/0.891/3.376. v2 (arXiv 2510.07838): examiner GPT-Realtime, judge "Gemini (gemini-2.5-flash-preview-09-2025)", ASR Parakeet-TDT; Table 1 Correction/Entity/Safety (Fast/Slow): FreezeOmni 2.74/3.50, 2.62/2.86, 3.94/4.27; Moshi 2.88/3.46, 2.76/3.84, 3.67/3.51; GPT-Realtime 4.02/3.94, 4.51/4.12, 4.44/4.53; "Agreement between the automated LLM judge and human annotators" on "120 evaluation sessions": r = 0.6137 / 0.6807 / 0.5877 / 0.6330 / 0.6914, "moderate to strong agreement across all metrics (Pearson's r = 0.59–0.69)". README: v1/v1.5 "evaluate models based on pre-recorded static datasets in an offline, server-client inference manner"; v2 "real-time audio conversations (via WebRTC or WebSocket) between your target model (the Examinee) and an automated AI evaluator"; v3 "Tool Use for Full-Duplex Voice Agents Under Real-World Disfluency" (papers: 2503.04721, 2507.23159, 2510.07838, 2604.04847).
results.correction: None. All numbers, the ASRU 2025 venue, the judge-vs-human nature of the r = 0.59–0.69 validation, and the README version descriptions are confirmed.

results.claim: tau2-bench shows that user simulators become reliable only when tied to the environment (telecom simulator 16% error / 6% critical vs 40-47% for prompt-only retail/airline) and that moving from no-user to dual-control costs frontier agents 18-25 pp pass^1; pass^1 -> pass^4 gaps of 8-12 pp mean single-trial scores are unreliable. MIT-licensed, LiteLLM, local models allowed.
results.evidence_quote: Tasks: retail 115, airline 50, telecom 114 (2,285 generated). User simulator errors: telecom "16% error rate" / "6% critical errors"; retail "40%" / "12%"; airline "47%" / "13%". Figure 3 (pass^k, k=1..4) gpt-4.1: retail 0.74/0.64/0.58/0.53, airline 0.56/0.46/0.42/0.40, telecom 0.34/0.26/0.22/0.19; text: "gpt-4.1 pass^1 drops from 74%/56% for retail and airline respectively to 34% for telecom ... In the case of claude-3.7-sonnet, the pass^1 score for telecom (49%) is on par with airline. However, as k increases, the pass^k scores decline more rapidly for telecom compared to airline"; intro: "42% for o4-mini" on telecom. Ablation (Figure 4 left: gpt-4.1 default 0.34 vs no-user 0.52; o4-mini 0.42 vs 0.67): "shifting from no user operation (No-User) to a collaborative setup (Default) where the agent must guide the user results in a substantial drop in pass^1 (18% drop for gpt-4.1 and 25% drop for o4-mini)." "All LLM API calls are implemented using the Litellm package [3]." Repo README: License MIT; "uses LiteLLM — any supported provider works"; example `tau2 run --domain airline --agent-llm gpt-4.1 --user-llm gpt-4.1 --num-trials 1 --num-tasks 5`. taubench.com: tau2 Qwen3.5-397B-A17B 87.9%, Gemini 3.0 Pro 85.4%, Claude Opus 4.5 85.3%; tau3-Voice Pine Voice Preview 75.4%.
results.correction: The user-simulator error rates, task counts, the 18/25 pp No-User→Default drop (Figure 4 bar values confirm these are percentage points: 0.52→0.34 and 0.67→0.42), LiteLLM, the MIT repo licence and the leaderboard figures are all supported. The pass^k numbers are not: pass^k is the probability that all k trials succeed, so it FALLS with k. Figure 3 gives gpt-4.1 pass^1→pass^4 of 74→53 (retail), 56→40 (airline), 34→19 (telecom), i.e. gaps of 15–21 pp, not 8–12 pp; the claim's pass^4 values 82/68/45 (and o4-mini ~62, Claude ~60–62) appear nowhere in the paper. o4-mini telecom pass^1 is 42%, not ~50% (the ~50% wording in the text is loose; Figure 3 and the intro give 42%). Claude 3.7 pass^1 is 79/50/49 with pass^4 roughly 60/31/25. Corrected statement: 'pass^1→pass^4 drops of 15–21 pp for gpt-4.1 mean single-trial scores overstate reliable performance.' Also note the arXiv paper itself is CC BY 4.0; MIT applies to the GitHub repo. 'Local models allowed' is supported only indirectly via the README's 'any [LiteLLM-]supported provider works'.

results.claim: LLM-as-judge scores must be reported chance-corrected: across 21 judges / 9 providers / ~541k judgments, raw agreement overstates Cohen's kappa by 33.8-41.3 pp on MT-Bench ('85% agreement => kappa ~0.48'), position bias reaches 0.192 even for judges with test-retest >0.95, and verbosity bias is negligible (<0.011); reference-anchored QA judging reaches kappa 0.72-0.96 vs human majority.
results.evidence_quote: Abstract: "21 judges from nine providers across MT-Bench, JudgeBench, and RewardBench, evaluated under three protocols (agreement, consistency, bias audit) over 118 runs and approximately 541,000 individual judgments." Results 4.1: "exact match overstates chance-corrected agreement by between 33.8 and 41.3 percentage points across the 21 models" (Figure 1 caption rounds to 41.2); JudgeBench mean deflation 23.7 pp, RewardBench 10.4 pp; "a judge reporting '85% agreement' on MT-Bench has κ≈0.48". "The least position biased model, Gemini 2.5 Pro (pb=0.002) and most position biased model Qwen 3 8B (pb=0.192)"; Table 6 row "Qwen 3 8B | 0.992 | 0.995 | 0.189"; Figure 1 caption: "high test–retest reliability (≥0.95) coexists with severe position bias (>0.10) for Qwen 3 8B and Gemini 2.5 Flash". Test-retest min 0.888 (GPT-5.4-mini, JudgeBench), max 0.992. "All 21 judges evaluated under the bias-audit protocol register a verbosity bias below 0.011 on MT-Bench". "seven of the sixteen judges evaluated under the consistency protocol show a position flip-rate increase of at least 1.5×". WiNLP 2025 (Badshah & Sajjad, 'Reference-Guided Verdict: LLMs-as-Judges in Automatic Evaluation of Free-Form QA'): "we only utilize 100 random samples from each" dataset; Table 1 PA (%) human 82–99 vs LLM judges 72–96; Table 2 single-judge κ vs human majority 0.63–0.93; Human-LLMs ensemble κ: TruthfulQA 0.79/0.72/0.78, TriviaQA 0.91/0.96/0.79, HotpotQA 0.94/0.96/0.88.
results.correction: None. Every number checks out; the only wrinkle is that the paper's Figure 1 caption says 33.8–41.2 pp while Section 4.1, Table 2 and the conclusion say 33.8–41.3 pp (rounding), so the claim's 41.3 matches the body text.

sweeps.topic: Navigation with dialogue: datasets, benchmarks and models where the agent talks while navigating, asks for help mid-task, or must absorb spoken/typed instruction changes and interruptions mid-task (CVDN, RobotSlang, Talk the Walk, HANNA/VNLA, Just Ask, WAY, TEACh, DialFRED, Alexa Arena, SIF, DialNav/RAINbow, QAsk-Nav, TANDEM, InstructNav, EmbodiedBench, CoNav/CoNavBench, HA-VLN 2.0, IVLN, OpenEQA, InterruptBench, P^3, YAY Robot, ELLSA, DuplexSLA/DuplexOmni/VideoFDB, NaVILA, Woofs-to-Words)

findings.claim: Every canonical dialogue-navigation dataset is typed, turn-based and evaluated 'from dialog history' (offline replay of a human-human chat); none evaluates spoken interruptions while the robot is moving. CVDN's Navigator stops, types, waits for the Oracle, then moves; the NDH benchmark replays that history.
findings.source_title: Vision-and-Dialog Navigation (CVDN / NDH), CoRL 2019
findings.numbers: 2050 human-human dialogs; >7k trajectories; 83 Matterport houses; 7415 NDH instances; ~6 utterances/dialog (up to 26), ~5% with no exchange; >90% of dialogs have egocentric references; >10% conversational repair; 1 step ≈ 2.25 m; $1.25/HIT, >$7k total. Seq2seq full-history mixed-supervision goal progress: val seen 6.16 m, val unseen 1.83-2.10 m, test unseen 2.27-2.35 m vs shortest-path 9.52/9.58/9.76 m and random 0.42/1.09/0.83 m.
findings.relevance: Sets the baseline data format Parcel would depart from; NDH 'goal progress in metres' and the dialog-history conditioning are directly reusable as Model A evaluation metrics; Matterport3D needs a separate license.

findings.claim: RobotSlang is the one classic dataset where human-human dialogue is genuinely simultaneous with physical robot motion (a Driver pilots a real robot while chatting with a Commander), but it is typed chat and its released LDH/NDH tasks are again from dialog history; physical transfer was never validated.
findings.source_title: The RobotSlang Benchmark: Dialog-guided Robot Localization and Navigation, CoRL 2020
findings.numbers: 169 trials/dialogs in 116 mazes; ~5k utterances; >1k minutes of camera+control streams; 28 messages and 200 words per dialog (CVDN: 81.6 words); 6.5 min per dialog; 3 targets per trial; splits 120/26/28 trials, 360/78/84 NDH; NDH seq2seq test Topological Distance 3.38 ± 1.15 m vs immediate-stop 4.33 m; >10% of trials need re-localization; human LDH error 0.446 m.
findings.relevance: Shows live-dialog-while-driving makes dialogs 2.5x more verbose than stop-and-ask; Parcel's narration budget should assume this density.

findings.claim: Talk the Walk grounds ~10k human dialogues in 360° street imagery where the tourist chats and moves simultaneously; natural-language localization and full-task performance remain far below humans.
findings.source_title: Talk the Walk: Navigating New York City through Grounded Dialogue
findings.numbers: >10k successful dialogues; 5 neighbourhoods, ~10x10 grid each; human success 76.74%; >62 acts per success; guide ~9 / tourist ~8 utterances; vocab >10K; single-utterance NL localization 16.17% test (random 6.25%); emergent MASC 69.85% at T=3; full task: human 76.74%, best NL model 50.00%, best emergent 88.33% under perfect perception.
findings.relevance: Canonical evidence that concurrent talk+move dialog is collectable at scale with crowd workers; a template for Parcel's sim data-collection UI.

findings.claim: Letting the agent ask for help mid-navigation (agent-initiated clarification) multiplies success in unseen environments by 4-6x in HANNA and VNLA, with learned ask policies beating fixed schedules at fewer requests.
findings.source_title: Help, Anna! Visual Navigation with Natural Multimodal Assistance via Retrospective Curiosity-Encouraging Imitation Learning (EMNLP 2019); with VNLA CVPR 2019 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.04155)
findings.numbers: HANNA: 68 Matterport3D envs, 51 train envs, <9,000 instructions (reusing R2R's 21,567); test SR no-assistance 17.21% seen / 8.10% unseen → learned 88.37% / 47.45% with 2.9 / 5.8 requests per task; RandomAsk 37.05% (6.8 req), AskEvery5 34.42% (7.1 req); language adds +15.17 pts over image-only in unseen (31.88 → 47.45); perfect-interpretation skyline 83.56% unseen. VNLA ASKNAV (289 object labels, 26 rooms, 61/11/18 env split): test unseen SR NONE 6.36 → LEARNED 34.50 (teacher 34.95); seen 28.39 → 52.09.
findings.relevance: Model B must support robot-initiated questions with a learned 'when to ask' head, not only owner-initiated commands; the ask budget is a tunable Parcel hyperparameter.

findings.claim: Just Ask shows a confusion-triggered ask policy on R2R lifts unseen success from 0.47 to 0.81 with ~2 questions per episode, and that learned ask actions trade success for fewer questions monotonically.
findings.source_title: Just Ask: An Interactive Learning Framework for Vision and Language Navigation (AAAI 2020)
findings.numbers: val unseen SR: base 0.471 (0 questions); Model-Confusion ε=0.1 0.562 (0.56 q), ε=0.5 0.807 (1.99 q); ASA r_ask=0.1 0.732 (1.92 q), r_ask=0.5 0.494 (0.15 q); human-guided exploration beats pre-exploration by 5% (0.554 vs 0.504); ~1.5% ask rate at r_ask=0.5.
findings.relevance: A cheap, trainable 'ask when action distribution is flat' trigger that Parcel can implement on Model A's act-token logits.

findings.claim: WAY (6k dialogs) shows the Observer navigating while answering questions, and localization-from-dialog is still less than half of human performance; DiaLoc's per-turn predictions improve steadily with more turns.
findings.source_title: Where Are You? Localization from Embodied Dialog (EMNLP 2020); DiaLoc (https://arxiv.org/html/2403.06846)
findings.numbers: ~6k (6,134) dialogs, 87 Matterport3D environments; LED best model 32.7% success within 3 m unseen vs 70.4% human; DiaLoc Acc5 valUnseen 40.41% vs LingUNet 33.33% (+7.08), multi-shot 47.15% vs 36.30% (+10.85).
findings.relevance: Model B's narration should include self-localization descriptions ('I'm in the hallway by the door') so a remote/hosted model can track the dog; per-turn refinement is the right decoding mode.

findings.claim: TEACh interleaves utterances and actions in 3,047 human-human sessions, but its EDH/TfD benchmarks replay dialog history, and the Episodic Transformer baseline stays near 10% SR (TfD < 2%); dialog-act annotation (TEACh-DA) adds up to 2 points.
findings.source_title: TEACh: Task-driven Embodied Agents that Chat (AAAI 2022); TEACh-DA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.12953); repo https://github.com/alexa/teach
findings.numbers: 3,047 successful sessions of 4,365 (74.17% human success); 12 task types, 438 variants, 109 scenes; >45k utterances, 8.40 Commander + 5.25 Follower per session; 131.8 ± 109.7 Follower actions/session; EDH splits 5758 / 654+2188 / 696+2370; E.T. EDH SR val seen 9.05, val unseen 13.49, test unseen 9.62 (+H 12.5 seen); TfD val unseen SR 0.48, test unseen 0.17; TEACh-DA 39.5k utterances annotated, +2 pts SR. Licenses: code MIT, images Apache 2.0, data CDLA-Sharing 1.0.
findings.relevance: TEACh-DA's dialog-act inventory is a ready-made tag set for Model B's narration context; TfD numbers show long-horizon dialog-conditioned execution is still nearly unsolved.

findings.claim: DialFRED demonstrates that letting an embodied agent ask location/appearance/direction questions nearly doubles success (18.3 → 33.6 unseen) at 0.71 questions per episode, and that asking every step buys little more at 30x the questions.
findings.source_title: DialFRED: Dialogue-Enabled Agents for Embodied Instruction Following (RA-L 2022)
findings.numbers: 25 sub-goal task types; 34,253 train / 1,296 val-seen / 1,363 val-unseen tasks; 53K human-annotated QA (AMT, 2 annotators per sub-goal, Fleiss κ 0.13); templated oracle; SR seen/unseen, NQ: instruction-only 25.4/18.3 (0); all QAs 43.4/32.0 (3.24); random QA 39.9/27.9 (0.81); RL-begin 47.3/32.7 (0.37); RL-anytime 47.8/33.6 (0.71); ask-every-step 51.9/34.7 (21.39); removing 50% of location answers shifts questioner to 28% fewer location / 81% more direction questions; episode cap 1000 steps / 10 failed actions.
findings.relevance: Gives Parcel the reward shape (r_suc=1.0, per-question and invalid-question penalties) and the evidence that a cost-aware questioner is the right Model B component.

findings.claim: Alexa Arena ships a dialog-enabled instruction-following dataset where each mission has multiple human instruction sets and clarification QA pairs flagged for necessity, under non-commercial licenses.
findings.source_title: Alexa Arena: A User-Centric Interactive Platform for Embodied AI (NeurIPS 2023 D&B); README + trajectory-data README
findings.numbers: 3k+ game missions; 3 sets of human language instructions per mission; 2 sets of QA per instruction set with a 'question_necessary' flag; template-based synthetic instructions per trajectory; executable non-commercial, datasets CC BY-NC 4.0; recommended 8 vCPU / 1 GPU / 32 GiB / 200 GiB.
findings.relevance: The 'question_necessary' annotation is a cheap supervision signal for a when-to-ask head; licensing rules it out as a training base for a product.

findings.claim: Situated Instruction Following is the cleanest measurement of intent that changes while the robot acts (the human receptacle starts moving at task start): success collapses from 81% static to 29% dynamic even with oracle perception.
findings.source_title: Situated Instruction Following (2024)
findings.numbers: Habitat 3.0; 240 val + 240 test tasks; PnP / S_obj / S_hum; 10 houses (6 train, 4 test); human speed 0.08 m/step; agent step 0.17 m; SR with oracle perception: Prompter 70/29/29, Reasoner 81/60/29, Oracle 100/100/98.
findings.relevance: Parcel's 'following' and 'go to the owner' behaviours must be evaluated under a moving human; SIF's PnP/S_obj/S_hum split is a ready template.

findings.claim: DialNav (2025) adds a remote Guide who cannot see the Navigator and a learned 'Decision Head' for when to ask; RAINbow (2026) shows that auto-converting R2R/RxR/CVDN into 238K multi-turn dialog episodes at $0.0016 each doubles unseen success.
findings.source_title: Advancing DialNav through Automatic Embodied Dialog Augmentation (RAINbow); DialNav: Multi-turn Dialog Navigation with a Remote Guide (https://arxiv.org/html/2509.12894)
findings.numbers: RAIN: 2,231 episodes, 83 Matterport3D scans (1,401 from CVDN + 838 new), 1.87 QA/episode, Q 27.63 words, A 42.24 words; baseline SR 27.0 seen / 13.9 unseen, OSR 34.5, SPL 25.4; human ratings 4.48 / 4.28 of 5. RAINbow: 238K episodes; concatenate 2-4 paths (endpoints ≤1 m, detour ratio <1.3), LLaVA captions, GPT-4o-mini reformatting; $0.0016/episode vs $3.75 manual (~2,000x); SR val seen 30.77 → 58.24, val unseen 14.52 → 29.05, SPL 51.65; LE −2.56 m; 90.0% goal alignment, naturalness 4.76 vs 4.83 human.
findings.relevance: The recipe Parcel should copy to synthesize dialog-and-interruption training data from its own headless-city / MuJoCo trajectories at negligible cost; DTC/NSC/LE are the metrics to log.

findings.claim: 2026 interactive-navigation benchmarks (QAsk-Nav/CoIN, TANDEM) now score question-asking quality with per-question costs, and small models run interaction 150x faster than LLM-heavy baselines.
findings.source_title: Ask When It Pays: Cost-Aware Open-Ended Interaction for Instance Goal Navigation (TANDEM); with Benchmarking Interaction, Beyond Policy (QAsk-Nav, https://arxiv.org/html/2604.00265v1)
findings.numbers: TANDEM: 500 episodes (150 easy/200 medium/150 hard) from 22,905 episodes / 262 scenes / 70 categories; question penalties Appearance 0.182, Region 0.162, Direction 0.240, Confirmation 0.103; 35.3 SR@1.5, 21.4 Weighted SR; exploration reduction 47.5% hard vs 21.9% easy; backbones Qwen3.5-8B, GPT-5.4, Gemini3-Flash. QAsk-Nav: ~28K reasoning traces (15.98k/6.38k/5.03k), ~1,400 QA episodes; Light-CoNav SR 0.451 vs AIUTA 0.303, finish 0.332 vs 0.199, 1.15 s vs 177.83 s runtime; 1.50x unseen nav gain with 3x fewer params, 70x faster.
findings.relevance: Provides a Weighted-SR-style metric that charges Model B for each clarification, and evidence that an on-Orin-sized questioner is viable.

findings.claim: Zero-shot LLM navigation (InstructNav) and MLLM embodied benchmarks (EmbodiedBench) evaluate no dialogue or interruption at all, and frontier models still score ~30-58% on navigation-type tasks.
findings.source_title: EmbodiedBench (ICML 2025); InstructNav (CoRL 2024, https://arxiv.org/html/2406.04882)
findings.numbers: EmbodiedBench: 1,128 tasks (EB-ALFRED 300, EB-Habitat 300, EB-Navigation 300, EB-Manipulation 228), 6 capability subsets; GPT-4o 57.7% EB-Navigation, 28.9% EB-Manipulation; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 64.0% ALFRED / 68.0% Habitat; long-horizon subset −30+ pts; no vision −40-70% on low-level tasks. InstructNav: GPT-4 (0613) + GPT-4V; R2R-CE zero-shot SR 31%, SPL 24, NE 6.89 m; HM3D ObjNav SR 58.0%, SPL 20.9; DDN SR 30.0%; TurtleBot 4 real robot; no latency reported.
findings.relevance: Do not expect the hosted voice model to plan navigation; Model A must own motion, and the dialogue/interruption axis is absent from all mainstream embodied MLLM benchmarks.

findings.claim: Human-aware VLN benchmarks already validate on the exact Parcel platform (Unitree Go2-EDU with RGB-D + LiDAR among 2-4 moving people) and show that even strong agents reach only ~0.2 SR with >0.5 collision rate before any dialogue is added; CoNav has no dialogue and lists it as future work.
findings.source_title: HA-VLN 2.0: Open Benchmark and Leaderboard for Human-Aware Navigation (2025); HA-VLN 2024 (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.19236); CoNav (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.02425)
findings.numbers: HA-VLN 2.0: 16,844 instructions (avg 112 words vs 27 R2R-CE; vocab 5,032); HAPS 2.0 486 SMPL motion sequences, 910 human models / 428 regions / 90 scans; continuous-env unseen: BEVBert NE 5.51 m SR 0.21 CR 0.55, ETPNav SR 0.17 CR 0.58; real Go2-EDU in 4 indoor spaces with 2-4 volunteers. HA-VLN 2024: HAPS 145 activities → 435 motions, HA-R2R 21,567 instructions (29 → 69 words); unseen SR VLN-CM 0.12 (TCR 0.99), VLN-DT 0.11 (TCR 0.37). CoNav: 20,293 train / 4,962 eval episodes, 49 scenes, 107 activities, Habitat 3.0; FASR 19.8%, RASR 23.2%, CR 20.1%; 'No dialogue'.
findings.relevance: Defines Parcel's sim-to-real protocol (Go2-EDU, moving volunteers, collision counts) and the realistic ceiling for Model A's navigation SR in crowded homes.

findings.claim: InterruptBench formalizes user interruptions as Addition / Revision / Retraction injected at 60% of trajectory length and finds even the strongest LLM adapts successfully only ~55% of the time, with token overhead dominating the cost of adaptation.
findings.source_title: When Users Change Their Mind: Evaluating Interruptible Agents in Long-Horizon Web Navigation (InterruptBench)
findings.numbers: 165 WebArena-Lite tasks, 5 domains; 6 backbones; post-interruption success at k=30 (Addition): Claude Opus 4.5 ~55%, Sonnet ~44%, Haiku ~38%, DeepSeek-V3.1 ~30%, Qwen3-Coder-480B ~26%, Mistral-Large-3 ~23%; multi-turn (3 interruptions) Opus 41.82%; injection at 60% of baseline trajectory length; 'token overhead dominates adaptation cost'.
findings.relevance: Supplies the injection taxonomy (maps to the owner's revise/keep/queue) and the eval recipe for Parcel's mid-task amendment benchmark; also warns that a hosted LLM alone will not handle amendments reliably.

findings.claim: Real-robot systems that accept a new instruction mid-task (P^3 snapshot-and-resume scheduler; YAY Robot spoken corrections every ~4 s) show large gains from corrections but still low absolute success on interrupted tasks.
findings.source_title: P^3: Toward Versatile Embodied Agents (2025); Yell At Your Robot (https://arxiv.org/html/2403.12910)
findings.numbers: P^3: Jetson AGX Orin mobile dual-arm; 'current job is snapshot with its targets and partial progress, then later reinstated at the same step'; 11 competing tasks; simple competing 92.86%; interrupted task 42.86% vs RoboOS 35.71%; Qwen-VL-Max active perception 56.15%; 97.2% LLM-human scoring agreement. YAY: ALOHA, high-level policy re-queried every 4 s; base 15-20% full-task success; corrections +25-50% (bag), +30-45% (trail mix), +15-25% (plates); after fine-tuning +20-45% / +15-20% / +15-25%; 1170 trajectories, 41,517 skill segments, 1054 commands.
findings.relevance: P^3's task-memory snapshot is the concrete semantics for Parcel's 'queue' verb on the global-plan history; YAY's override-then-finetune loop is a template for learning from owner corrections in sim.

findings.claim: ELLSA is the closest existing thing to Parcel's Model A: a full-duplex speech+vision+action model that stops an ongoing action on a spoken interruptive command 94.3% of the time and speaks while acting, but only for tabletop manipulation (LIBERO), not navigation.
findings.source_title: End-to-end Listen, Look, Speak and Act (ELLSA)
findings.numbers: SA-MoE: Speech Expert = Mamba (32 blocks, 2048 hidden) + LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct; Action Expert = Emu3-Base + FAST tokenizer; CosyVoice2-0.5B TTS; interruptive-command success 94.3%; LIBERO 89.4% avg (SPATIAL 90.8 / OBJECT 95.8 / GOAL 86.4 / LONG 84.4); speaking-while-acting: speech QA 68.9% while manipulation 93.3%; latency per 1-s block 854 ms speech-to-speech, 786 ms speech-to-action (A100); training ASR 481k, QA 729k, 3,386 LIBERO + 1,693 defective-instruction samples.
findings.relevance: Proves the architecture class is trainable and that interruption robustness comes from explicit 'defective/interrupting instruction' training data; Parcel would extend it from arm actions to act-token locomotion on a 100 ms clock.

findings.claim: Full-duplex spoken LMs now emit interrupt/backchannel/pause labels and tool calls on an action channel synchronized with speech at sub-second latency, with interruption handled natively in the backbone rather than by a VAD module.
findings.source_title: DuplexSLA: A Full-Duplex Spoken Language Model with Synchronized Speech, Language, and Action; DuplexOmni (https://arxiv.org/html/2606.09186v1); VideoFDB (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.30256)
findings.numbers: DuplexSLA: 160 ms chunks; user audio 2 feats/chunk (80 ms), assistant TA4 (1 text + 4 audio tokens, 40 ms), action channel ≤10 tokens/chunk; 7B backbone from Step-Audio 2 mini; ~550k h pretrain (320k h duplex) + ~50k h post-train (36k h interrupt/backchannel/pause, 14k h tools); 2,100-case bench: Interrupt 99.33% / 0.40 s, Backchannel 98.33% / 0.32 s, Pause 93.33% / 0.27 s, Normal 96.00% / 0.27 s; tool call 85.56% at 0.64 s vs ASR+LLM 91.33% at 2.77 s. DuplexOmni: 480 ms slices, latency 0.506 s, 72.6% ToR Full DuplexBench, ~3.02M conversations, 128 H20 GPUs. VideoFDB: 237 clips, 11 dynamics; closed models 2.73-3.17 vs human 4.20; MiniCPM-o 4.5 3.40, 73% TOR-Alignment, 720 ms.
findings.relevance: Gives Model A/B a concrete channel layout (speech stream + rate-limited action/representation stream on one token clock) and the latency bar (interrupt-to-hold ≤0.4 s) for the tight speech-motion coupling the owner wants.

findings.claim: On the Go2 itself, NaVILA runs a language-action VLA at ~1 FPS above a real-time locomotion policy with 88% real-world success, and 'From Woofs to Words' shows a Go2 guide dog that clarifies before navigating and verbalizes scenes during navigation (with Wizard-of-Oz motion) is rated highly by blind users.
findings.source_title: From Woofs to Words: Towards Intelligent Robotic Guide Dogs with Verbal Communication; NaVILA (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.04453)
findings.numbers: Woofs: Unitree Go2; Vosk ASR → GPT-4 → ASP planner → TTS; scene verbalization on region-boundary crossing or long silence; 7 legally blind participants (1 excluded), ages 40-68; Likert utility 4.83, helpfulness 4.83, communication ease 4.50, safety 3.83; simulation 94.8% on 77 tasks, −5.2% at 30% character noise; plan info saves ~47 s. NaVILA: VLA ~1 FPS on RTX 4090; R2R-CE val-unseen SR 54.0% / SPL 49.0% / NE 5.22 m; RxR-CE SR 49.3%; 25 real instructions, Go2 88% (75% complex); 2K YouTube videos → 20K trajectories.
findings.relevance: Directly informs Model B narration triggers (region boundaries, silence) and the two-rate deployment pattern (slow language model over fast locomotion) on Parcel's Orin.

findings.claim: Persistent-memory VLN (IVLN) and open-vocabulary EQA (OpenEQA) show that cross-episode spatial memory helps while frontier VLMs remain near-blind on spatial questions; NIABench frames the inverse problem of a robot that must help without interrupting the human.
findings.source_title: OpenEQA (CVPR 2024) via Meta AI blog + project page; IVLN (https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03087); Assistance Without Interruption / NIABench (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.01368)
findings.numbers: OpenEQA: >1,600 questions, >180 environments, 7 categories, EM-EQA vs A-EQA, LLM-Match; human 85.9% vs GPT-4V 48.5% (gap 37.4); MIT license. IVLN: tours up to 100 R2R episodes, ~400 tours in 80 scenes (IR2R, IR2R-CE); implicit transformer memory 'not sufficient', map-persistent agents win. NIABench: 2,000 train episodes, 7 test tasks, 4 rooms, 118 objects / 800 atomic actions; NiaRR 29.4 human steps saved, 95.0% SuccessAcc.
findings.relevance: Parcel's 'global history' should be a persistent map + plan queue (IVLN); OpenEQA-style questions are a natural conversational-benchmark family for the hosted voice narrating from Model A's representation; NIABench supplies a 'do not interrupt the owner' metric.

design_implications: Own the gap explicitly: no existing dataset or benchmark evaluates spoken amendments/interruptions while a mobile robot is moving. Define a Parcel 'Interrupt-Nav' benchmark rather than adopt one: inject spoken Addition / Revision / Retraction (InterruptBench taxonomy, mapped to queue / revise / keep-or-cancel) at a controlled fraction (e.g., 40-70%) of each trajectory, with separate splits for owner-initiated vs agent-initiated turns.

Model A clock and channel layout: keep the 10 Hz act-token clock as the motion rate and aggregate 2-5 ticks per speech chunk (DuplexSLA 160 ms, DuplexOmni 480 ms, ELLSA 1 s are the published points); give the 'representation for narration' output a rate-limited action-style channel (DuplexSLA caps at 10 tokens/chunk with overflow spilling into later chunks) so narration never stalls locomotion.

Make interruption native in the codec: add HOLD / RESUME / ABORT / BACKCHANNEL act tokens and train on synthetic 'defective / interrupting instruction' episodes (ELLSA used 1,693 such samples to reach 94.3% interrupt success; DuplexSLA used ~36k h of interrupt/backchannel/pause audio). Target interrupt-to-hold latency ≤0.4 s (DuplexSLA) and speech-to-action <0.8 s per block (ELLSA).

Model B must include a cost-aware agent-initiated questioner, not only a command-injection path: asking multiplies unseen success 2-6x (DialFRED 18.3→33.6 at 0.71 q/ep; HANNA 8.10→47.45; VNLA 6.36→34.50; Just Ask 0.471→0.807), while asking every step buys ~+1-4 SR at 30x the questions. Reuse DialFRED's reward shape and TANDEM's per-question-type penalties (0.10-0.24) as a Weighted-SR metric.

Global plan queue semantics: adopt P^3's task-memory rule ('snapshot with targets and partial progress, reinstated at the same step') for the 'queue' verb, and log DialNav's Dialog Turn Count / Navigation Step Count / Localization Error alongside NDH goal-progress-in-metres, SPL and HA-VLN collision rate.

Narration context from Model A → hosted voice: tag each narration packet with a TEACh-DA style dialog act (Acknowledge, Confirm, RequestForInstruction, Instruction) plus a trigger reason (region-boundary crossing, goal reached, blocked, long silence — the 'Woofs to Words' triggers) and a self-localization phrase (WAY/DiaLoc show remote listeners need it); let the hosted model render wording only.

Data: synthesize dialogue-and-interruption episodes from Parcel's existing headless-city / MuJoCo trajectories using the RAINbow recipe (concatenate 2-4 paths, caption at dialog points, LLM-reformat into multi-turn dialog; $0.0016/episode, doubled unseen SR), then TTS the owner turns and mix reSpeaker recordings at walking-noise SNR so the model sees audio, not text.

Set realistic acceptance bars: strongest human-aware VLN agents reach SR ~0.21 with collision rate ~0.55 on HA-VLN 2.0 unseen; GPT-4o gets 57.7% on EmbodiedBench navigation; Claude Opus 4.5 adapts to text interruptions ~55%; P^3's interrupted real-robot task is 42.86%. Parcel's current SR 0.20 on its frozen matrix is in that band; do not gate the program on beating frontier LLMs that have never been evaluated on this axis.

Sim-to-real protocol: copy HA-VLN 2.0's Go2-EDU validation (fixed instruction set, 2-4 free-moving volunteers, RGB-D + LiDAR, collision counts) and NaVILA's two-rate deployment (~1 FPS language-action model above a real-time locomotion policy); add the Woofs-to-Words user-study questionnaire (utility, communication ease, safety) for the conversational layer.

Persistent memory: IVLN shows implicit transformer memory across a tour is insufficient while map-persistent agents benefit; Parcel's 'global history' stream should be a persistent spatial map + historical plan queue, with the 'last 1 minute' stream as the token-level context.
open_questions: No source measures ASR/duplex robustness to the robot's own locomotion and fan noise while walking; Parcel must characterize reSpeaker SNR on a moving Go2 before trusting any published interrupt-latency number.

ELLSA is the only full-duplex speech+action model with an interruption number (94.3%) and it is manipulation-only (LIBERO); whether the same architecture holds for navigation act-tokens at 10 Hz is untested anywhere.

Alexa Arena's paper-level statistics (scene count, mission success rates, clarification-type distribution) were not extracted because the NeurIPS/arXiv PDFs exceed the fetch limit; only README-level numbers (3k+ missions, 3 instruction sets, 2 QA sets each) are cited.
OpenEQA numbers (human 85.9% vs GPT-4V 48.5%) come from Meta's blog and project page, not the CVPR PDF (HTTP 403).
SPRING (AAAI 2023) was seen only in search snippets and appears to be a situated-conversation QA agent, not a navigation benchmark; it was not read and is not cited.
CoNavBench/DeCoNav dialogue is robot-to-robot; no 2025-2026 benchmark was found with human spoken dialogue during long-horizon multi-robot navigation.
InstructNav and most LLM-navigation papers report no per-step latency; the cost of a GPT-4-class planner in the loop on an Orin is unknown from the literature.

Web-search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200) after the main sweep; 'Yell At Your Robot', OpenEQA and CoNavBench were reached via known URLs, but a second sweep for very recent (mid-2026) spoken-VLN-on-legged-robot work could not be run.

results.claim: Every canonical dialogue-navigation dataset is typed, turn-based and evaluated 'from dialog history' (offline replay of a human-human chat); none evaluates spoken interruptions while the robot is moving. CVDN's Navigator stops, types, waits for the Oracle, then moves; the NDH benchmark replays that history.
results.evidence_quote: "Pairs of workers were connected to one another via a chat interface. ... The dialog begins with the Navigator's turn. On the Navigator's turn, they could navigate, type a natural language question to ask the Oracle, or guess that they had found the goal room. ... On the Oracle's turn, they could view an animation depicting the next 5 hops through the navigation graph towards the goal room according to a shortest path planner and communicate back to the Navigator via natural language." NDH: "An agent, given a target object and a dialog history between humans cooperating to find that object, must infer navigation actions towards the goal in unexplored environments." Numbers all verified in the PDF text: "We collect 2050 human-human navigation dialogs, comprising over 7k navigation trajectories punctuated by question-answer exchanges, across 83 MatterPort houses"; "We extract 7415 NDH instances from the 2050 navigation dialogs"; "Dialogs average about 6 utterances each ... up to 26 utterances. Some dialogs have no exchanges (about 5%)"; "over 90% of all dialogs, contain egocentric references"; "More than 10% of dialogs exhibit conversational repair" (Table 2: Repair 12.5% of dialogs); "On average, 1 step corresponds to 2.25 meters"; "Each HIT paid $1.25 per worker, the entire dataset collection cost over $7k." Table 3 Mixed-supervision Goal Progress: Val Seen 6.16; Val Unseen 1.83 (2.10 with nav history); Test Unseen 2.27 (2.35); Shortest Path 9.52/9.58/9.76; Random 0.42/1.09/0.83.
results.correction: Every CVDN-specific statement and every number is verified verbatim (the WebFetch summarizer's first pass hallucinated '10,047 dialogs / 90 houses / $0.20 per HIT' — the PDF text contradicts it). What the source cannot support is the universal 'every canonical dataset ... none evaluates spoken interruptions': the CVDN paper only describes CVDN/NDH. Restate as: 'CVDN (and the other datasets checked in this batch — HANNA/VNLA, DialFRED, RAIN/RAINbow) are text-based, turn-based, and evaluated offline from dialog or help history; none of them evaluates spoken interruptions while the robot is in motion.' Note the paper itself acknowledges older *spoken* human-human navigation corpora (HCRC Map Task, SCARE, CReST) that are 'substantially smaller' — so 'typed' is not literally true of all predecessor corpora, though it is true of the VLN-era datasets.

results.claim: Letting the agent ask for help mid-navigation (agent-initiated clarification) multiplies success in unseen environments by 4-6x in HANNA and VNLA, with learned ask policies beating fixed schedules at fewer requests.
results.evidence_quote: HANNA Table 3 (test splits): "No assistance 17.21 [SR seen] ... 0.0 [requests] | 8.10 [SR unseen] ... 0.0"; "Learn to interpret assistance (ours) 88.37 ... 2.9 | 47.45 ... 5.8"; "Perfect assistance interpretation 90.99 ... 2.5 | 83.56 ... 3.2". Table 5 (unseen SR / requests per task): "NOASK 8.10 / 0.0; RANDOMASK 37.05 / 6.8; ASKEVERY5 34.42 / 7.1; Learned (ours) 47.45 / 5.8". Table 4: "Target image only 84.95 / 31.88; + Language instruction 88.37 / 47.45"; text: "the improvement from language on TEST UNSEENALL (+15.17%) is substantially [larger]". Setup: "HANNA features 68 Matterport3D environments"; "training set of 51 environments and less than 9,000 language instructions"; R2R "contains 21,567 natural language instructions". VNLA (arxiv.org/pdf/1812.04155) Table 2, ASKNAV test unseen SR: "NONE 6.36 ± 0.00; FIRST 20.00 ± 0.10; RANDOM 25.05 ± 0.31; LEARNED 34.50 ± 0.23; TEACHER 34.95 ± 0.33"; test seen: "NONE 28.39 ... LEARNED 52.09 ... TEACHER 52.26"; "We use the same environment splits as [2]: 61 training, 11 development, and 18 test ... we obtain 289 object labels and 26 room labels."
results.correction: All numbers verified in the PDF text. Multipliers: HANNA unseen 8.10 → 47.45 = 5.9x; VNLA unseen 6.36 → 34.50 = 5.4x, so '4-6x' holds (more precisely ~5.4-5.9x). Two nuances: (1) 'agent-initiated clarification' is loose — in both papers the agent emits a help-request signal and receives a subgoal instruction (VNLA: language subgoal; HANNA: language + target image); it does not formulate a natural-language question. (2) The 'fewer requests than fixed schedules' comparison is documented in HANNA (Learned 5.8 vs AskEvery5 7.1 vs RandomAsk 6.8 requests/task); VNLA's Table 2 reports SR, room-finding SR and nav error but no per-policy request counts.

results.claim: DialFRED demonstrates that letting an embodied agent ask location/appearance/direction questions nearly doubles success (18.3 → 33.6 unseen) at 0.71 questions per episode, and that asking every step buys little more at 30x the questions.
results.evidence_quote: Table I (Seen SR / Unseen SR / NQ): "1 Instruction only 25.4 18.3 ... 0; 2 All QAs 43.4 32.0 ... 3.24; 3 Random QA 39.9 27.9 ... 0.81; 5 RL begin 47.3 32.7 ... 0.37; 6 RL anytime 47.8 33.6 ... 0.71". Table III: "RL anytime (Fixed 1) 51.9 34.7 ... 21.39; RL anytime (Fixed 5) 47.8 33.6 ... 0.71; RL anytime (Fixed 10) 46.3 32.4 ... 0.36; RL anytime (MC) 47.1 33.0 ... 0.31" with caption "We manipulate the number of steps the performer rolls out before the questioner can ask the next question. For (Fixed 1), we modify the rewards (rinvalid = −0.01, rq = −0.002) to promote question asking." Text: "reducing the number of steps between questions leads to slightly better performance, but it also requires the oracle to answer significantly more questions." Rewards: "reward for task completion rsuc = 1.0, penalty for each step rstep = −0.01, penalty per question asked rq = −0.05, penalty per invalid question rinvalid = −0.1." Dataset: "we arrive at 25 sub-goal types"; "34,253 tasks in the training fold, 1,296 tasks in the validation seen fold and 1,363 tasks in the validation unseen fold"; "53K human-annotated task-relevant questions and answers"; "For each sub-goal, we ask two different annotators"; "(Fleiss' κ = 0.13)"; oracle "provides templated answers"; "We terminate the episode when it exceeds 1000 steps or has more than 10 failed actions"; "the questioner asks 28% fewer location questions and 81% more direction questions instead."
results.correction: All numbers verified. One precision note: 'asking every step' is the paper's 'RL anytime (Fixed 1)' setting — the questioner is *allowed* to ask after every performer step and the question penalties were relaxed (rq = −0.002, rinvalid = −0.01) to promote asking; it averages 21.39 questions/episode (30.1x the 0.71 of Fixed 5), not literally one question per step. The gain is +1.1 SR points unseen (33.6 → 34.7), consistent with 'buys little more'.

results.claim: DialNav (2025) adds a remote Guide who cannot see the Navigator and a learned 'Decision Head' for when to ask; RAINbow (2026) shows that auto-converting R2R/RxR/CVDN into 238K multi-turn dialog episodes at $0.0016 each doubles unseen success.
results.evidence_quote: DialNav (arxiv.org/html/2509.12894, 16 Sep 2025): "DialNav is a cooperative navigation task between Navigator and Remote Guide, where Guide is not aware of Navigator's location but only familiar with the environment." On asking: "[we] tested 3 approaches; Fixed-Interval [28], where questions are asked at regular navigation step intervals, Confidence Thresholding [42, 13], ... and Decision Head [29], which learns questioning timing from RAIN using action decision features. The baseline model adopts Decision Head." Ref [29] = "Kunal Pratap Singh, Luca Weihs, ... Roozbeh Mottaghi. Ask4help: Learning to leverage an expert for embodied tasks. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 35:16221–16232, 2022." RAIN: "Our dataset includes 1,401 navigation tasks from CVDN [31] and 838 additional tasks generated following the same scheme"; "Each episode contains an average of 1.87 QA pairs ... questions and answers in RAIN average 27.63 [and 42.24 words]". RAINbow (arXiv:2606.19948v1, 18 Jun 2026): "construct the RAINbow dataset, a large-scale training dataset with 238K episodes for DialNav. Our pipeline converts existing VLN datasets into multi-turn dialog"; "In Rainbow, the average numbers of dialog turns, trajectory nodes, question words, and answer words are 2.71, 19.54, 30.43, and 43.17, respectively (compared to 1.88, 26.03, 27.48, and 42.53 in RAIN). The reformatting step using GPT-4o-mini incurred a total cost of about USD 400, equating to USD 0.0016 per episode. This makes our generation pipeline about 2,000 times more cost-effective than manual annotation in RAIN (USD 3.75 per episode)." Results: "Together, these advances improve performance of the holistic navigation-dialog loop by more than two-fold: success rate increases from 30.77 to 58.24 (+89%) on Val Seen and from 14.52 to 29.05 (+100%) on Val Unseen." Table 5: "the new localization model reduces localization error (LE) by 2.56m in Val Seen and 3.02m in Val Unseen compared to the baseline."
results.correction: Two details are off.
