(1) DialNav did not introduce the Decision Head: it is Ask4Help's decision head (Singh et al., NeurIPS 2022), evaluated as one of three *existing* when-to-ask strategies (Fixed-Interval, Confidence Thresholding, Decision Head) and adopted for the baseline. Restate: 'DialNav adopts a learned Decision Head from Ask4Help.' (2) The 14.52 → 29.05 unseen doubling is the *combined* effect of the RAINbow data plus two further advances ('Dual-Strategy Training' and a VLN-pretrained localization model — 'Together, these advances ... By combining these complementary solutions'), not the data alone; and the 'LE −2.56 m' in the numbers field is the localization-model ablation (Table 5), not a dataset effect. Everything else checks: 238K (238,028) episodes at USD 0.0016 vs USD 3.75 manual (~2,000x), multi-turn (2.71 turns/episode avg), R2R/RxR/CVDN sources, LLaVA-1.5-7B captions + GPT-4o-mini, remote Guide without the Navigator's location, RAIN 2,231 episodes / 83 scans / 1,401 CVDN + 838 new / 1.87 QA per episode / SR 27.0 seen 13.9 unseen / OSR 34.5 / SPL 25.4 / ratings 4.48 and 4.28. Trivial: RAINbow's Table 7 lists RAIN at 1.88 turns vs DialNav's 1.87.

results.claim: Human-aware VLN benchmarks already validate on the exact Parcel platform (Unitree Go2-EDU with RGB-D + LiDAR among 2-4 moving people) and show that even strong agents reach only ~0.2 SR with >0.5 collision rate before any dialogue is added; CoNav has no dialogue and lists it as future work.
results.evidence_quote: HA-VLN 2.0: "We deploy our trained agents on a Unitree Go2-EDU quadruped, equipped with Intel Realsense D435i RGB-D camera, MID360 3D LiDAR, and IMU for onboard perception and control. As Fig. 7 (b) illustrates, experiments are conducted in four indoor spaces (office, living room, hallway, lobby), each populated by 2–4 free-moving volunteers." Table 1 (HA-VLN-CE Results Across Validation (Seen/Unseen) and Test Splits), val-unseen block, NE | TCR | CR | SR: "BEVBert (An et al., 2023) ... 5.51 | 4.71 | 0.55 | 0.21"; "ETPNav (An et al., 2025) ... 5.43 | 6.94 | 0.58 | 0.17"; text: "BEVBert's SR increases from 0.19 to 0.27 in seen split and from 0.15 to 0.21 in unseen." Dataset: "16,844 curated instructions (train/val_seen/val_unseen/test: 10,819/778/1,839/3,408)"; "average instruction length increases from 27 to 112 words, with the vocabulary expanding from 2,616 to 5,032"; "HAPS 2.0 dataset, featuring 486 SMPL-based motion sequences across 26 region types"; "up to 910 human models across 428 regions in 90 buildings". HA-VLN 2024 (arxiv.org/html/2406.19236): "145 human activity descriptions converted into 435 detailed 3D human motion models"; "21,567 human-like instructions"; "average instruction length increased from 29 to 69 words"; Table 8 unseen rows: VLN-DT (100%) SR 0.11 TCR 0.37; VLN-CM (25%) SR 0.12 TCR 0.99. CoNav (arxiv.org/html/2406.02425): "20,293 training episodes", "4,962 evaluation episodes", "49 environments", "107 possible activities", Habitat 3.0; FASR 19.8, RASR 23.2, CR 20.1; "In the future, we will expand our work to introduce dialogue information to improve the robustness and success rate of navigation."
results.correction: Verified. Two scoping notes: (a) only HA-VLN 2.0 uses the Go2-EDU + D435i RGB-D + MID360 LiDAR rig; the 2024 HA-VLN paper's real robot was 'a Unitree quadruped robot equipped with a stereo fisheye camera, ultrasonic distance sensors, and an IMU' on a Jetson TX2, so 'benchmarks' (plural) validating on that exact platform should read 'HA-VLN 2.0'. (b) The 5.51/0.21/0.55 and 0.17/0.58 rows are the val-unseen split for agents trained on HA-VLN-CE; the test-split rows are slightly lower (BEVBert SR 0.18, CR 0.58; ETPNav SR 0.16, CR 0.58), still consistent with '~0.2 SR, >0.5 CR'. The HA-VLN 2024 numbers in the claim's numbers field pick VLN-DT at 100% data and VLN-CM at 25% data — both rows exist but are not the same data-proportion condition.

results.claim: InterruptBench formalizes user interruptions as Addition / Revision / Retraction injected at 60% of trajectory length and finds even the strongest LLM adapts successfully only ~55% of the time, with token overhead dominating the cost of adaptation.
results.evidence_quote: "We formalize three realistic interruption types, including addition, revision, and retraction, and introduce InterruptBench, a benchmark derived from WebArena-Lite"; "We inject interruptions at a relative position (60% by default) of the baseline trajectory length obtained from the corresponding no-interruption run."; "For the Addition scenario, Opus reaches approximately 50% by k=10 and 55% by k=30, while Sonnet reaches roughly 40% and 44%, and Haiku reaches approximately 33% and 38%."; "Token overhead dominates adaptation cost. Table 1 shows that efficiency differences are driven primarily by token overhead rather than by additional actions."; multi-turn: "Opus achieving the highest overall performance (41.82% at n=3)"; WebArena-Lite "selects 165 representative tasks for human verification as the evaluation set" across five domains (Reddit, GitLab, CMS, Map, OneStopShop); six backbones: Claude-Haiku-4.5, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Claude-Opus-4.5, Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B, DeepSeek-V3.1, Mistral-Large-3.
results.correction: Verified verbatim. Precision notes: the '~55%' is Opus 4.5's post-interruption success at k=30 in the *Addition* scenario (Revision and Retraction curves differ; Retraction has 'notably stronger baselines'); 60% is the default, and Table E.3 also sweeps {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8}. The DeepSeek ~30% / Qwen ~26% / Mistral ~23% values in the numbers field are read off Figure 2 rather than stated in prose (only the Claude family values appear in text).

sweeps.topic: Interruptible task planning for LLM/robot agents: how a running plan is revised, kept, or queued when a new instruction arrives; plan histories as memory; benchmarks that score interruption handling

findings.claim: Hi Robot splits control into a slow high-level VLM (emits an intermediate language command plus an optional verbal reply) and a fast low-level VLA (pi0); the high level is re-invoked about every second and immediately on any user interjection, and its replies are grounded in the current image. Synthetic 'situated interjections' are generated by prompting a VLM with (image, skill label) to imagine the user utterance and robot reply.
findings.numbers: High level re-invoked every ~1 s or immediately on user intervention; ~40% higher instruction accuracy than a GPT-4o high level; 20 trials/task/method; PaliGemma-3B for both levels; inference on 1-2 RTX 4090; tasks: table bussing, sandwich making, grocery shopping (single-arm, dual-arm, mobile).
findings.relevance: Direct precedent for the Model A (continuous policy) / Model B (language reasoner that also speaks) split, with the concrete rule 'owner speaks -> re-infer Model B now' and a sim-friendly recipe for synthesizing mid-task interjection training data.
findings.source_title: Hi Robot: Open-Ended Instruction Following with Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Models

findings.claim: YAY Robot lets a spoken correction temporarily override the high-level policy's language command, which is otherwise re-queried at a fixed 4 s cadence, while a 50 Hz low-level language-conditioned policy keeps executing; corrections are logged with 2 s of prior context and reused to fine-tune the high level.
findings.kind: primary paper (arXiv HTML + project page fetched)
findings.numbers: High-level queried every 4 s; low-level data at 50 Hz; baselines 0% (bag packing, 3 items), 20% (trail mix), 60% (plate cleaning); on-the-fly corrections +25-50 pp, +30-45 pp, +15-25 pp; fine-tuning on corrections +20% average per stage (20-45 / 15-20 / 15-25 pp); data 1170/317/265 trajectories (41,517/7,008/3,236 skill segments).
findings.relevance: The cleanest published mechanism for 'Model B injects a steerable override into Model A for a bounded window, then reverts', and evidence the same utterances double as training labels.
findings.source_title: Yell At Your Robot: Improving On-the-Fly from Language Corrections

findings.claim: A two-LLM coordinator/worker robot with working, declarative (one persistent log per task), and procedural memory can be interrupted mid-task, switch to another task, and later resume from the stored snapshot ('If the task gets interrupted ... the interaction history is kept safe'; on resume it 'retrieves previous actions, environment state, and task state at the interruption point').
findings.numbers: NICOL robot; 50 trials per condition; GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 vs Llama-3-70B (8-bit, A100), temp 0.2; standalone 92-100% / 86-98%; consecutive-with-memory 92-100% / 98-100%; intervened (interrupt then resume) with memory: Separate 75/96, Arrange 100/82, Point 98/98, Recipe 92/92, Tower 98/98%.
findings.relevance: Template for Parcel's task stack: per-goal snapshot (actions, env state, progress) kept on suspend and re-injected on resume; gives an interrupt/resume success number to beat.
findings.source_title: Robots Can Multitask Too: Integrating a Memory Architecture and LLMs for Enhanced Cross-Task Robot Action Generation

findings.claim: InterruptBench formalizes mid-task user interruptions as Addition / Revision / Retraction of intent, injects them at 60% of the baseline trajectory, and scores effectiveness and efficiency; even frontier models succeed on only ~20% of interrupted long-horizon web tasks and often 'continue with stale assumptions'.
findings.numbers: 165 human-verified WebArena-Lite tasks, 5 domains; single-interruption success Claude-Opus-4.5 21.21/20.00/23.64% (add/rev/retract), Sonnet-4.5 15.15/13.94/15.76, Haiku-4.5 12.12/9.70/11.52, Qwen3-480B 11.52/7.27/10.91, DeepSeek-V3.1 12.12/9.09/11.52, Mistral-Large-3 11.52/5.45/9.70; multi-turn Opus 5.45% (0 interruptions) -> 41.82% (3); token inflation +37.6 to +1,699 tokens/episode, action delta -0.99 to +0.82; both-fail overhead Haiku +2,624, Sonnet +1,128, Opus +351 tokens.
findings.relevance: Provides the interruption taxonomy, injection protocol, and paired effectiveness/efficiency metrics Parcel should add as an axis to its 5x5 instruction-navigation matrix; sets a realistic (low) baseline expectation.
findings.source_title: When Users Change Their Mind: Evaluating Interruptible Agents in Long-Horizon Web Navigation (InterruptBench)

findings.claim: EchoChain evaluates full-duplex voice models on state-update reasoning when the user interrupts mid-utterance, and names three failure modes: contextual inertia (acknowledge but do not apply the update), interruption amnesia (apply then revert), and objective displacement (abandon the original task). All models pass fewer than half of interrupted conversations, and a half-duplex control shows interruption handling itself causes most failures.
findings.numbers: 200 interrupted conversations; models GPT-realtime-2025-08-28, Gemini Live 2.5 flash native audio, Grok Voice Agent, Amazon Nova Sonic 2; Mean Pass Rate <50% for all, best Grok 48.5%; paired half-duplex control: total failures drop 40.2%; cloned-voice validity chi2=0.92, p=0.63.
findings.relevance: The three failure classes map one-to-one onto revise/keep/queue errors for Model B and give Parcel a ready failure rubric for its conversation-quality scorer.
findings.source_title: EchoChain: A Full-Duplex Benchmark for State-Update Reasoning Under Interruptions

findings.claim: Inner Monologue closes the loop by appending success detection, scene description and human feedback to the LLM planner's context; the planner replans around failures, proposes alternative goals when one is infeasible, and 'switches tasks twice' when a human changes the goal mid-episode.
findings.kind: canonical paper (arXiv abs + ar5iv full text + project page fetched)
findings.numbers: Sim tabletop seen: CLIPort 16.0%, IM object 40.5%, +success 43.5%, +scene 48.5%; unseen: CLIPort 0.0%, IM 34.5/37.5/42.5%; real tabletop 45% (object-only) -> 90% (object+success); real kitchen (120 evals): SayCan 60.8% -> IM 83.3% without disturbance, 30.8% -> 60.4% with adversarial disturbances.
findings.relevance: Canonical evidence that feeding human mid-task feedback into a running plan context yields goal switching without training, and that closed-loop feedback roughly doubles success under disturbance.
findings.source_title: Inner Monologue: Embodied Reasoning through Planning with Language Models

findings.claim: SayCan scores skills by LLM usefulness x learned affordance value and is open-loop: it 'is not easily able to react to situations where individual skills fail' and has no mechanism for instruction changes during execution.
findings.numbers: 101 instructions, 7 families; PaLM-SayCan mock kitchen plan 84% / execute 74%; real kitchen 81% / 60%; FLAN-SayCan 70% / 61%; 540B PaLM.
findings.relevance: Baseline against which Inner Monologue's closed-loop gains are measured; illustrates why an open-loop plan scorer cannot serve as Model B.
findings.source_title: Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances

findings.claim: Reflexion stores natural-language self-reflections in a bounded episodic buffer and triggers reflection with a simple stuck heuristic (same action and response >3 cycles, or >30 actions), raising ALFWorld completion from ~104/134 to 130/134 over 12 trials.
findings.numbers: ALFWorld 130/134 vs ReAct ~104/134 (+22% absolute) over 12 consecutive trials; HotPotQA +20%; HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80%; memory bounded to Omega = 1-3 reflections ('truncate to the last 3 self-reflections').
findings.relevance: Gives Model B a cheap self-initiated revision trigger (stuck detector) and a bounded reflection memory that keeps prompts small.
findings.source_title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

findings.claim: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with actions so the model can 'induce, track, and update action plans as well as handle exceptions'.
findings.numbers: ALFWorld +34% absolute success over imitation/RL baselines; WebShop +10%.
findings.relevance: The base loop nearly every LLM replanner (Reflexion, InterAct, ITP) builds on; the 'thought' slot is where a revise/keep/queue decision naturally lives.
findings.source_title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

findings.claim: ITP handles a new user request mid-execution by building a new prompt from (completed steps, task guidelines, new request) appended to the chat history and regenerating the remaining plan ('replan accordingly with precision based on the new request, task guidelines and previously executed steps').
findings.numbers: High-level replanning 10/10 user requests vs Code-as-Policies 5/10; dishwashing 10/10; 10 VirtualHome tasks; real-robot milk-tea making; GPT-4; no latency reported.
findings.relevance: Minimal 'revise' implementation: state = completed-steps ledger + chat history; the plan tail is regenerated by one LLM call.
findings.source_title: Interactive Task Planning with Language Models (ITP)

findings.claim: CoMuRoS lets the user 'give new commands, interrupt ongoing tasks, or change intention anytime during execution' via chat; suspended tasks are marked INTERRUPTED and explicitly re-included in the replanned sequence, and a retraction ('I don't want it anymore') is classified as a relevant event that redirects a Unitree Go2 to return the item.
findings.numbers: Hardware: object recovery 9/10, formation transport 8/8, human-assisted recovery 5/5; 22 sim scenarios x 3 tasks (~20 robots); replanning set 5 scenarios, correctness 1.0; Grok 3 correctness 0.91, allocation 0.96, classification 0.96, IoU 0.97, executability 0.98; 8 LLMs; temp 0.5; robots include Unitree Go2; no planning-latency numbers.
findings.relevance: An explicit suspend / re-queue / retract state machine demonstrated on the same quadruped Parcel targets.
findings.source_title: LLM-Based Generalizable Hierarchical Task Planning and Execution for Heterogeneous Robot Teams with Event-Driven Replanning (CoMuRoS)

findings.claim: RT-H inserts a language-motion layer between task and action; in correction mode a human can 'enter a new language motion correction, keep running the previously entered language motion correction, or exit correction mode', re-queried at a fixed frequency, and only 30 correction episodes per task suffice to learn from interventions.
findings.numbers: PaLI-X 55B; 100K demos (70K kitchen + 30K diverse); 8 evaluation tasks; RT-H beats RT-2 by 15% on average; human corrections raise precise tasks by 60-70%; 30 correction episodes per task; corrections yield near-perfect success.
findings.relevance: Enumerates the keep / replace / exit semantics of a correction channel that Model B must expose to the owner's voice.
findings.source_title: RT-H: Action Hierarchies Using Language

findings.claim: A flat language-conditioned policy trained on ~600K language-labelled trajectories can be guided by real-time human language mid-motion toward long-horizon goals ('nudge the green star down and left a bit').
findings.kind: canonical paper (arXiv abs + project page fetched)
findings.numbers: 93.5% success on 87,000 unique language strings; ~600,000 trajectories (Language-Table); behavioral cloning. (A 5 Hz control rate appears only in a search snippet, unverified.)
findings.relevance: Lower bound for 'speech tightly coupled to movement' with no separate planner; shows the data scale at which flat real-time language following works.
findings.source_title: Interactive Language: Talking to Robots in Real Time

findings.claim: LLM-BT keeps the plan as a behavior tree and, on a failed condition, searches an action-template library for actions whose post-conditions satisfy the failed node, builds a fallback subtree, and inserts it with raised priority when it conflicts with existing nodes, so environmental changes are absorbed without a full replan.
findings.numbers: Cargo sorting 5 cases x 20 non-professional users: 18/17/16/18/18 of 20 (~85%); household service 15/14/15/16/17 of 20 (~75%); failures mostly 'unclear requirements expressed by users' (10; 16/100), parser failures 6/84, 1 unsolvable disturbance.
findings.relevance: A 'keep the plan, patch the step' mechanism; user-ambiguity dominates failures, arguing for Model B clarification before revision.
findings.source_title: LLM-BT: Performing Robotic Adaptive Tasks based on Large Language Models and Behavior Trees

findings.claim: LLM-HBT extends behavior trees at runtime: when a condition node fails, an LLM allocator returns a robot assignment and action subtree that either replaces the failed node locally or is delegated to another robot while the original 'temporarily suspends execution at fi while monitoring its status'.
findings.numbers: 60 tasks across 3 simulated scenarios (quadruped; +drone; +arm); scenario 3 baselines 40% vs LLM-HBT 100%; real cafe: 10/10 repeated trials with a wheeled-legged robot + arm.
findings.relevance: BT-native suspend-at-node / resume-on-status is a clean way to implement 'queue' semantics inside Model A's plan executor.
findings.source_title: LLM-HBT: Dynamic Behavior Tree Construction for Adaptive Coordination in Heterogeneous Robots

findings.claim: JARVIS-1 stores plan histories as a multimodal key-value memory (key = task + observation at creation, value = the plan that was successfully executed), retrieves candidates by text-embedding threshold then re-ranks by visual similarity, and grows the memory via self-proposed exploration.
findings.numbers: 200+ Minecraft tasks, 11 groups; diamond pickaxe 6.22% vs 2.5% (VPT-RL, 20 min), 12.5% at 60 min; vs DEPS: Wood 88.84 vs 80.23, Stone 88.69 vs 69.27, Iron 34.63 vs 16.92, Diamond 8.99 vs 2.42%; 425 successful trajectories after 4 epochs.
findings.relevance: Concrete schema for Parcel's 'global plans stored as a historical queue': (goal, StateDigest) -> plan, retrieved by situation similarity when a new goal arrives.
findings.source_title: JARVIS-1: Open-World Multi-task Agents with Memory-Augmented Multimodal Language Models

findings.claim: RavenClaw manages dialogue with a runtime dialog stack (discourse structure) plus an expectation agenda (what the system expects to hear), supporting hierarchical task decomposition, user-initiated topic shifts, suspension and resumption, and distributed error handling; deployed in LARRI, RoomLine and Let's Go!.
findings.numbers: Multiple deployed systems (LARRI, RoomLine, Let's Go! bus information); no task-success numbers in the fetched text.
findings.relevance: Mature engineering pattern for deciding whether an utterance is a sub-dialogue (push), a focus shift (suspend), or a barge-in on the current task — the expectation agenda is what Model B should expose to the voice lane.
findings.source_title: The RavenClaw dialog management framework: Architecture and systems

findings.claim: The information-state approach defines dialogue management as informational components (including plan/QUD stacks), dialogue moves, update rules and a control strategy, implemented in TrindiKit as a dialogue move engine.
findings.kind: canonical paper (Semantic Scholar API record fetched; 609 citations)
findings.numbers: 609 citations (Semantic Scholar); Natural Language Engineering 2000.
findings.relevance: Model B's revise/keep/queue is an update-rule set over a small information state; this is the formalism to write it in.
findings.source_title: Information state and dialogue management in the TRINDI dialogue move engine toolkit

findings.claim: Alexa Conversations trains dialogue components from a simulator seeded by a few dialogues plus API/entity specs and supports 'users changing their mind during conversation' out of the box rather than via hand-authored flows.
findings.kind: industry paper (NAACL 2021, Amazon Science page fetched)
findings.numbers: >50% improvement in turn-level action-signature prediction accuracy on movie-ticket booking from the dialogue simulator.
findings.relevance: Industrial precedent that mind-changes should be generated in simulation at training time — matches Parcel's train-in-sim plan for Model B.
findings.source_title: Alexa Conversations: An extensible data-driven approach for building task-oriented dialogue systems

findings.claim: DiagGPT runs an explicit LLM-operated topic stack with actions load/push, finish (pop), stay, jump to an existing topic, and create new topic, managed by a Topic Manager agent.
findings.numbers: 20 scenarios; completion 1.0, success 1.0; rounds 7.0 vs GPT-4 7.7; response quality 9.0/10; comparison score 11.5 vs 8.5.
findings.relevance: A ready vocabulary of stack operations for Model B's goal queue (push / finish / jump / create).
findings.source_title: DiagGPT: An LLM-based and Multi-agent Dialogue System with Automatic Topic Management for Flexible Task-Oriented Dialogue

findings.claim: An LLM-powered social robot that classifies user interruptions by intent (cooperative agreement / assistance / clarification, disruptive) and responds with acknowledge-and-continue, answer-then-resume-planned-content, or yield handled 93.69% of interruptions; failures correlate with lower perceived inclusion.
findings.numbers: 21 participants (M age 22.38); 104/111 interruptions handled (93.69%); intent classification 88.78%; 76.03% of interruptions disruptive (n=92; 45.65% opinion questions), agreement 18, clarification 9, assistance 2; rho(42)=-0.43, p=.005 between unhandled interruptions and perceived inclusion; most failures from speech recognition errors.
findings.relevance: Gives Model B's narration side a tested policy: keep talking vs yield vs answer-then-resume, with a 'resume previously planned content' primitive.
findings.source_title: Interruption Handling for Conversational Robots

findings.claim: When a robot interleaves a new investigative task into an assigned delivery, users rate it as more competent when tasks are not interleaved; interleaving is most acceptable when the reason (another person's request) is communicated and least when it is a long detour motivated by curiosity.
findings.kind: HRI user study (abstract via Semantic Scholar API; HRI 2022 TOC fetched)
findings.numbers: Three motive framings (another person's request / curiosity / no information); HRI 2022, DOI 10.1109/HRI53351.2022.9889307.
findings.relevance: Argues for 'queue' (finish then switch) as the default and for Model B to narrate why it reorders goals when it does interleave.
findings.source_title: You're delaying my task?! The Impact of Task Order and Motive on Perceptions of a Robot

findings.claim: tau-Voice evaluates full-duplex voice agents on verifiable tasks with a 200 ms tick orchestrator, seeded user simulators, and a rule that agents must yield within 2 s of a user interruption; voice agents keep only 30-45% of text-model capability under realistic audio.
findings.numbers: 278 tasks (retail 114, airline 50, telecom 114); 200 ms ticks; yield deadline 2 s; GPT-5 text 85%; voice clean 31-51%, realistic 26-38%; retail ablations accents -10 pp avg (-18 xAI, -1 Google), turn-taking -7 pp, noise -4 pp; latency OpenAI 0.90 s, xAI 1.15 s, Google 1.14 s; responsiveness 100/83/69%; agent interrupt rate 84/14/21%; selectivity 57/54/6%; 79-90% of failures agent-caused.
findings.relevance: Harness design (tick clock, seeded simulator, yield deadline) that Parcel's 10 Hz duplex frame clock can mirror for sim-to-real conversation-while-navigating evals.
findings.source_title: tau-Voice: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Voice Agents on Real-World Domains

findings.claim: Full-Duplex-Bench measures user-interruption takeover rate and stop latency for spoken dialogue models; the best model stops within about a quarter second while API models take over a second.
findings.numbers: 200 synthetic user-interruption samples; user-interruption TOR / stop latency: Moshi 1.000 / 0.257 s, Freeze-Omni 0.867 / 1.409 s, Gemini Live 0.891 / 1.183 s, dGSLM 0.917 / 2.531 s; smooth turn-taking latency Moshi 0.265 s, Gemini Live 1.301 s.
findings.relevance: Sets the stop-latency bar for Parcel's narration when the owner barges in (<0.3 s achievable, >1 s typical for hosted APIs).
findings.source_title: Full-Duplex-Bench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Full-duplex Spoken Dialogue Models on Turn-taking Capabilities

findings.claim: SID-Bench separates true interruptions from backchannels and scores false-interruption rate, interruption-response latency and a combined penalty time; a small audio-encoder + Qwen-0.6B detector reaches sub-half-second response with ~14% false interruptions, about 3x better penalty than prior systems.
findings.numbers: 3,700 instances (~10 h): beginning 1,000, middle 1,200, uninterrupted 1,000, noise 200, silence 300; SID-model IRL 0.444 s EN / 0.338 s ZH, FIR 0.140/0.138, APT 0.921/0.656; Moshi IRL 2.517 s, FIR 0.010; FSMN-VAD FIR 0.906; K=3 decision smoothing.
findings.relevance: The semantic barge-in gate Model B needs before deciding revise vs keep: quantifies the latency / false-alarm trade-off.
findings.source_title: Semantic-Aware Interruption Detection in Spoken Dialogue Systems: Benchmark, Metric, and Model (SID-Bench)

findings.claim: PACE fixes 'generative context mis-anchoring' in full-duplex voice by tracking the client playback boundary and, on interruption, re-injecting only the last 5 s of audio the user actually heard, so follow-ups like 'how do I get there?' resolve against spoken, not merely generated, content.
findings.numbers: GCM-Bench 108 cases (12 scenarios x 3 delays x 3 operations); referent-anchoring accuracy 25.0% -> 96.3% (+71.3 pp); Elaborate 2.78 -> 94.44, Next 61.11 -> 97.22, Repeat 11.11 -> 97.22; Full-Duplex-Bench turn-obedience 100%, interruption latency 771 -> 830 ms (+59 ms).
findings.relevance: Model B's narration ledger must be playback-aligned: 'go back to the door' must resolve against what the owner heard the robot say, not what Model B generated.
findings.source_title: PACE: A Playback-Aligned Context Engine for LLM-Based Full-Duplex Voice Dialogue

findings.claim: tau2-bench adds dual control (user also acts on the environment) and shows agents lose 18-25 points when an active user is present versus solving alone; neither tau-bench nor tau2-bench scripts explicit mid-task mind-changes.
findings.numbers: 115 retail / 50 airline / 114 telecom tasks (telecom sampled from 2,285); telecom pass^1 Claude 3.7 Sonnet 49%, GPT-4.1 34%, o4-mini ~50%; GPT-4.1 retail 74%, airline 56%; no-user -> dual-control drop GPT-4.1 -18%, o4-mini -25%; tau-bench gpt-4o <50%, pass^8 <25% retail.
findings.relevance: Shows the conversational-agent benchmarks Parcel might borrow do not yet test intent revision; InterruptBench/EchoChain fill that gap.
findings.source_title: tau2-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment

findings.claim: AgentBoard introduces a fine-grained progress-rate metric (subgoal-averaged or best matching score) alongside success, revealing that open-weight agents plateau after ~6 steps while GPT-4 keeps progressing over 30 steps.
findings.numbers: 9 tasks, 1,013 environments; embodied subset progress/success: GPT-4 65.5/43.3%, Claude2 34.1/24.6, GPT-3.5 35.6/17.2, Llama3-70B 29.6/12.7; GPT-4 overall progress 70.0%.
findings.relevance: Progress rate is the right partial-credit metric for episodes whose goal is amended midway (the original subgoals should still count).
findings.source_title: AgentBoard: An Analytical Evaluation Board of Multi-turn LLM Agents

findings.claim: ProgPrompt expresses plans as Python with assert-based precondition checks and recovery actions, so a step can be repaired locally ('if not, the agent first executes find(salmon)') without regenerating the plan.
findings.numbers: VirtualHome SR 0.34+/-0.08 (GPT-3) vs 0.00 for the prior language planner; no comments 0.18+/-0.04; no feedback 0.28+/-0.04; real robot 4 tasks with 1-3 distractors.
findings.relevance: Local repair-in-place is the cheapest form of 'keep' for Model A's plan executor.
findings.source_title: ProgPrompt: Generating Situated Robot Task Plans using Large Language Models

findings.claim: RoCo re-plans through dialog when validators (text parsing, IK feasibility, collision check) reject a plan and appends the feedback to each agent's prompt; a human can take one of the agent roles in real-world trials.
findings.numbers: RoCoBench success: Sweep Floor 0.95, Pack Grocery 0.44, Move Rope 0.65, Arrange Cabinet 0.75, Make Sandwich 0.80, Sort Cubes 0.93; 1.0-3.5 average re-plan attempts; human-in-the-loop sorting 9/10 and 8/10 (~5.3-5.5 steps).
findings.relevance: Shows replanning converges in 1-3 rounds when validators are cheap and feedback is textual — a budget for Model B's revise loop.
findings.source_title: RoCo: Dialectic Multi-Robot Collaboration with Large Language Models

design_implications: Adopt the Hi Robot / YAY cadence: Model A runs continuously (Parcel's 10 Hz frame clock); Model B runs at 1-4 s and is re-invoked immediately on any owner utterance; a Model B correction temporarily overrides Model A's high-level command for a bounded window (skill length ~4 s) and then reverts unless renewed (RT-H keep/replace/exit semantics).

Implement revise / keep / queue as information-state update rules over: current goal, plan tail, completed-steps ledger (ITP), per-goal snapshot on suspend (actions, env state, progress; Robots Can Multitask Too), and a goal stack with push / finish / jump / create operations (DiagGPT, RavenClaw dialog stack + expectation agenda, CoMuRoS INTERRUPTED flag).

Gate Model B with three cheap classifiers: (1) semantic barge-in vs backchannel (<0.5 s, ~14% false-interrupt is achievable per SID-Bench); (2) intent type addition / revision / retraction (InterruptBench) mapped to queue / revise / cancel; (3) a stuck detector (Reflexion: same action and response >3 cycles or >30 steps) that can trigger self-initiated revision.

Store the global-plan history as a JARVIS-1-style key-value memory keyed by (goal text, StateDigest at creation) with the executed plan and outcome as value; retrieve by situation similarity when a new goal arrives; keep only 1-3 reflections in the prompt (Reflexion). The 'queue' is the same store filtered to status=suspended.

Make Model B's narration ledger playback-aligned (PACE): record what was actually spoken before an interruption so references like 'go back to the door' resolve against what the owner heard; use acknowledge-and-continue / answer-then-resume / yield strategies from Cao et al. 2025 and narrate the reason whenever the queue is reordered (Carter et al. 2022).

Generate interruptions in simulation rather than by hand: synthesize situated interjections from (observation, skill label) as in Hi Robot and Alexa Conversations, inject them at a fixed fraction of the trajectory (InterruptBench uses 60%), and log each correction with 2 s of prior context (YAY) so it doubles as a Model B training label.

Add an interruption axis to the 5x5 instruction-navigation matrix: addition / revision / retraction x single / multi-turn, scored on success, progress rate (AgentBoard), efficiency overhead vs the uninterrupted run (InterruptBench), yield latency against a 2 s deadline (tau-Voice) and stop latency (Full-Duplex-Bench), plus EchoChain failure classes (inertia / amnesia / displacement).

Set expectations from the numbers: closed-loop feedback roughly doubles success under disturbance (SayCan 30.8% -> Inner Monologue 60.4%); interrupt-then-resume with per-task memory reaches 75-100% on simple tasks; on-the-fly language corrections add +15-50 pp; but frontier LLM agents handle only ~20% of interrupted long-horizon tasks and voice agents keep 30-45% of text capability under realistic audio, so the initial Parcel baseline will be low.
open_questions: No fetched source reports a wall-clock 'latency to switch goal' for an LLM replanner on a mobile robot (ITP, CoMuRoS, LLM-BT give none); the only latency numbers are for voice stop/yield (0.26-2.5 s) and policy cadences (1-4 s). Parcel must measure this itself in sim.

Model Interruption Bench (OpenReview) could not be fetched (host verification wall); its protocol (interrupt on an error step, stay silent otherwise) is known only from a search snippet and should be read before being cited.

The XLand 'goal intervention' evaluation (goal changed after the first third of a 1.5x episode) is snippet-only; whether an end-to-end trained policy generalizes to mid-episode goal switches without a planner remains unverified here.

No benchmark scores interruption handling for *navigation* specifically; InterruptBench is web navigation, EchoChain/tau-Voice are voice-only, AgentBoard has no interruptions. Parcel's interruption axis on the headless-city matrix would be novel.

Robots Can Multitask Too and LLM-BT show that per-task memory and BT patching work on tabletop tasks with 5-10 s skills; whether the same suspend/resume snapshot is sufficient for a mobile goal whose world state drifts while suspended (doors, people) is untested.
Interactive Language's 5 Hz control rate and LLM-Planner's 15.36% unseen success appear only in search snippets, not in the fetched pages.

How to weight retraction vs revision when the owner's utterance is ambiguous (LLM-BT attributes most failures to unclear user requirements) — clarification-first policies were not benchmarked against immediate replanning in any fetched source.

results.claim: Hi Robot splits control into a slow high-level VLM (emits an intermediate language command plus an optional verbal reply) and a fast low-level VLA (pi0); the high level is re-invoked about every second and immediately on any user interjection, and its replies are grounded in the current image. Synthetic 'situated interjections' are generated by prompting a VLM with (image, skill label) to imagine the user utterance and robot reply.
results.evidence_quote: "we rerun high-level inference and recompute ℓ̂_t either when one second has elapsed, or when a new interaction with the user takes place" ... "When the system receives a user intervention, the high-level inference is triggered immediately to recompute ℓ̂_t. The high-level policy has the option to include a verbal utterance u_t in the command ℓ̂_t, which can be confirmations or clarifications from the robot." ... "the responses of the high-level policy are contextual, because it observes not only the prompt ℓ_t, but also the current image observations." ... "The low-level policy is the π0 VLA (Black et al., 2024), which is trained by finetuning PaliGemma-3B with an additional flow matching 'action expert'" ... "we prompt p^gen with both the visual context I^1_t,...,I^n_t and the skill label ℓ̂_t (e.g., pick up the lettuce). p^gen then imagines an appropriate interaction that might have led to ℓ̂_t in a real user interaction: it generates possible user prompts ℓ_t ... and corresponding robot utterance u_t" ... "Hi Robot averages over 40% higher instruction accuracy than GPT-4o" ... "Each evaluation consists of 20 trials per task per method." ... "the low-level and high-level policies use the same base VLM as a starting point, namely the PaliGemma-3B VLM" ... "we utilize one to two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 consumer-grade GPUs" ... "three robotic platforms, including single-arm, dual-arm, and dual-arm mobile robots ... cleaning messy tables, making sandwiches, and grocery shopping"
results.correction: None needed. Only wording nuance: the paper says 'over 40% higher instruction accuracy than GPT-4o' (not '~40%'), and the GPT-4o comparison is on the Instruction Accuracy metric scored by a blinded human evaluator, not task success.

results.claim: YAY Robot lets a spoken correction temporarily override the high-level policy's language command, which is otherwise re-queried at a fixed 4 s cadence, while a 50 Hz low-level language-conditioned policy keeps executing; corrections are logged with 2 s of prior context and reused to fine-tune the high level.
results.evidence_quote: "During post-training, the high-level policy is queried at fixed intervals, specifically every 4 seconds as the average skill length, to generate language instructions for the robot." ... "The user's verbal interventions temporarily override the high-level policy's output, directly influencing the low-level policy to enable on-the-fly adaptation: π_deploy(a_t|o_{t-k:t}) = π_L(a_t|o_t, l_user) if intervention; π_L(a_t|o_t, l_H) otherwise" ... "The demonstration data includes these camera feeds and the robots' joint positions at 50Hz." ... "considering the human reaction time, the system also saves data from 2 seconds prior to the intervention for more context. This data is then used to fine-tune the high-level policy" ... Table I (Base Policy column): "Bag Packing ... 3 items 0 ... Trail Mix Preparation ... 3 ingredients 20 ... Plate Cleaning ... Clean 12 gummies 60" ... "significant improvements in success rates at each stage when incorporating real-time language corrections: 25%-50% in Bag Packing, 30%-45% in Trail Mix Preparation, and 15%-25% in Plate Cleaning." ... "finetuning with our approach improves success rates at each stage by 20%-45% in Bag Packing, 15%-20% in Trail Mix Preparation, and 15%-25% in Plate Cleaning." ... Fig. 5 caption: "Our system demonstrates a 20% improvement in success rates over the base policy across three long-horizon bi-manual manipulation tasks"; project page: "enhance the autonomous policy's performance at each stage of the tasks by 20% on average through fine-tuning." ... Table III: "Trajectories 1170 317 265 ... Skill Segments 41517 7008 3236"
results.correction: All numbers verified. One precision note: the paper states 50 Hz as the rate of the demonstration data (camera feeds + joint positions), not explicitly as the execution rate of the low-level policy; phrase it as 'low-level policy trained on 50 Hz data' to stay literal.

results.claim: A two-LLM coordinator/worker robot with working, declarative (one persistent log per task), and procedural memory can be interrupted mid-task, switch to another task, and later resume from the stored snapshot ('If the task gets interrupted ... the interaction history is kept safe'; on resume it 'retrieves previous actions, environment state, and task state at the interruption point').
results.evidence_quote: "If the task gets interrupted, i.e., the robot is asked to switch to another one, the interaction history is kept safe. When the robot continues the interrupted task, it retrieves essential information like previous actions, environment state, and task state at the interruption point." ... "We store this memory persistently as log files, one file per task. Similar to working memory, declarative memory is specialized to one task" ... "We conducted a total of 50 trials for each experiment using two LLMs: ChatGPT-3.5-Turbo-0125 and Llama 3." ... "we utilized the 8-bit quantized version of Llama 3 ... a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with 80 GB of VRAM" ... "The temperature was set to 0.2". CONTRADICTING numbers — TABLE IV (columns: Success Rate [w/o, with memory], Task Retention [w/o, with], Env. Retention [w/o, with]): "Separate GPT 3.5 0.78 0.80 0.58 0.75 0.60 0.98 Llama 3 0.19 0.96 0.15 0.99 0.66 0.98 Arrange GPT 3.5 0.62 1.00 ... Llama 3 0.19 0.82 ... Point GPT 3.5 0.60 0.98 ... Llama 3 0.28 0.98 ... Recipe GPT 3.5 0.14 0.92 ... Llama 3 0.18 0.88 0.42 0.92 ... Tower GPT 3.5 0.42 0.98 ... Llama 3 0.15 0.98"; TABLE III (consecutive): "Separate GPT 3.5 0.70 0.84 0.61 0.92 ... Tower ... Llama 3 0.58 0.92 0.68 0.98"
results.correction: Architecture, memory design, and the interrupt/resume quotes are verbatim-correct; NICOL, 50 trials, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 vs 8-bit Llama-3-70B on an A100, temp 0.2, and the standalone ranges (GPT 92-100%, Llama 86-98%) all check. Four numbers are wrong because task-retention values were read as success rates: intervened-with-memory success is Separate 80/96 (not 75/96) and Recipe 92/88 (not 92/92); Arrange 100/82, Point 98/98, Tower 98/98 are correct. Consecutive-with-memory success ranges are GPT 84-100% (Separate = 0.84, not 0.92) and Llama 92-100% (Tower = 0.92, not 0.98). Also note the interruption protocol: every task is paused at 50% progress and resumed in a second round.

results.claim: InterruptBench formalizes mid-task user interruptions as Addition / Revision / Retraction of intent, injects them at 60% of the baseline trajectory, and scores effectiveness and efficiency; even frontier models succeed on only ~20% of interrupted long-horizon web tasks and often 'continue with stale assumptions'.
results.evidence_quote: SUPPORTING: "We inject interruptions at a relative position (60% by default) of the baseline trajectory length obtained from the corresponding no-interruption run." ... "analyzing both their effectiveness in adapting to updated intents and their efficiency in recovering from mid-task changes" ... "a curated evaluation set of 165 human-verified tasks" covering "five diverse domains" ... "Even capable web agents often continue with stale assumptions, fail to reconcile the environment state with the updated intent" ... Table 2 (multi-turn): "Claude-Opus-4.5 5.45 21.21 36.36 41.82" ... "the average action overhead ranges from -0.99 (Opus) to +0.82 (Sonnet), while the average token overhead spans from +37.6 (Qwen) and +88.5 (Mistral) to +670.9 (Sonnet) and +1699.1 (Haiku)" ... "Haiku (+2624 tokens in F/F) and Sonnet (+1128 tokens in F/F), and remains evident even for Opus (+351 tokens in F/F)". CONTRADICTING the ~20% single-interruption figures: "For the Addition scenario, Opus reaches approximately 50% by k=10 and 55% by k=30, while Sonnet reaches roughly 40% and 44%, and Haiku reaches approximately 33% and 38%. Open-weight backbones plateau at lower levels; for instance, Qwen reaches approximately 26%, DeepSeek 30%, and Mistral 23% at k=30." Table 1 (Addition, # cases S/F F/S S/S F/F): "Claude-Opus-4.5 ... 1 70 21 73" => interrupted-run success (F/S+S/S)/165 = 55.2%. Table 2 caption: "Converged performance under multiple interruption updates ... more interruptions correspond to more user-provided information" (0-interruption baseline 5.45%).
results.correction: Taxonomy, 60% injection point, 165 tasks / 5 domains, effectiveness+efficiency framing, the 'stale assumptions' quote, the multi-turn Opus 5.45% -> 41.82% trajectory, and all token/action overhead figures are correct. The per-model 'single-interruption success 21.21/20.00/23.64 ...' numbers and the headline '~20%' are wrong: the paper never reports those per-scenario figures (15.76 and 10.91 do not appear anywhere; 23.64 is Qwen at n=3; 20.00 and 9.70 are domain cells in Table E.3). Single-interruption success derived from the paper's own paired-outcome counts (Tables 1, B.1, C.1; add/rev/retract) is Opus 55.2/53.9/51.5%, Sonnet 44.2/41.2/38.8%, Haiku 38.2/37.0/37.6%, Qwen 26.7/26.1/28.5%, DeepSeek 29.7/26.1/29.7%, Mistral 21.8/17.6/19.4%, matching the Section 4.1 prose (Opus ~55% at k=30). The 21.21% figure is Opus at n=1 in the multi-turn protocol, where the initial query is deliberately underspecified (0-interruption baseline 5.45%) and each interruption adds required information. Corrected headline: 'frontier models recover to roughly 50-55% success after a single interruption, open-weight models ~20-30%; in the multi-turn underspecified protocol the best model reaches only 21% after one update and 42% after three.' Also note the paper is internally inconsistent about the Qwen model: setup text says 'Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B (abbreviated as Qwen3-480B-A35B)' while every table labels it 'Qwen3-235B-A22B'.

results.claim: EchoChain evaluates full-duplex voice models on state-update reasoning when the user interrupts mid-utterance, and names three failure modes: contextual inertia (acknowledge but do not apply the update), interruption amnesia (apply then revert), and objective displacement (abandon the original task). All models pass fewer than half of interrupted conversations, and a half-duplex control shows interruption handling itself causes most failures.
results.evidence_quote: "In contextual inertia, the model receives the new information but continues generating as if nothing changed. In interruption amnesia, the update is initially incorporated but later overwritten as generation proceeds. In objective displacement, the model pivots entirely to the interruption, abandoning the original task." ... Fig. 1: "(Contextual Inertia) The assistant acknowledges the interruption but fails to correctly revise its prior reasoning." ... "Table 1 summarizes the results across 200 interrupted conversations for GPT-realtime-2025-08-28, Gemini Live-2.5-flash-native-audio, Grok Voice Agent, and Amazon Nova Sonic 2." ... "The mean pass rate (MPR) measures the fraction of conversations in which a model satisfies every rubric criterion" ... "Across all four models, MPR remains below 50% ... The highest MPR is observed for Grok Voice Agent at 48.5%." (Table 1 MPR: Nova 26.5, Gemini 16.5, GPT-realtime 45.0, Grok 48.5) ... "X^2=0.92 (p=0.63), providing no evidence of a directional preference for either voice type". CONTRADICTING 'most failures': "In a paired half-duplex control, total failures drop by 40.2% relative to interrupted runs, indicating that many errors are driven by state-update reasoning under interruption rather than task difficulty alone." ... "with 48 sampled conversations across all 4 models, 92 failures were detected for the interrupted conversations, while 55 failures were detected for the non-interrupted conversations. This corresponds to a net 40.22% reduction in total failures, indicating that a substantial share of errors are related to the interruption event."
results.correction: Taxonomy and definitions, 200 conversations, the four models, MPR < 50% for all with Grok best at 48.5%, and the cloned-voice chi-square (0.92, p=0.63) all verify. 'Interruption handling itself causes most failures' overstates the paper: the half-duplex control removes 40.2% of failures (92 -> 55 in 48 paired conversations), which the authors describe as 'many errors' / 'a substantial share', not a majority; roughly 60% of failures persist without any interruption. Corrected statement: 'a paired half-duplex control cuts total failures by 40.2%, attributing a substantial share (not most) of failures to the interruption itself.'

sweeps.topic: Hosted real-time speech model (OpenAI Realtime / gpt-realtime, Gemini Live) as the voice of a locally-planned robot: tool latency, barge-in, context injection, 2026 pricing, robot integrations, open alternatives

findings.claim: OpenAI bills Realtime audio at 1 token per 100 ms of input and 1 token per 50 ms of output; gpt-realtime-2/2.1 cost $32 per 1M audio-input tokens ($0.40 cached) and $64 per 1M audio-output tokens, so listening costs $0.0192/min and speaking $0.0768/min before context re-reads; the mini tier is $10/$0.30/$20.
findings.source_title: OpenAI docs — Managing Realtime API costs (pricing cross-checked at https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing)
findings.numbers: 1 tok/100 ms in, 1 tok/50 ms out => 600 tok/min heard, 1,200 tok/min spoken; gpt-realtime-2.x audio $32 in / $0.40 cached / $64 out per 1M; text $4/$0.40/$24; image $5; mini audio $10/$0.30/$20, text $0.60/$0.06/$2.40; 32k model with 4,096 max output => 28,224 input tokens; retention_ratio default 1.0, recommended 0.8; editing earlier items busts the prefix cache
findings.relevance: Sets the always-on listening budget for a companion dog (~$1.15/h listening alone on OpenAI) and forces local VAD gating plus append-only context for Model B's StateDigest injection.

findings.claim: The Realtime API exposes every mechanism Model B needs: server VAD with interrupt_response/create_response switches (keep VAD, decide locally), conversation.item.truncate for barge-in on WebSocket (automatic on WebRTC/SIP), out-of-band responses (response.create with conversation:'none', custom input array, metadata), per-response instruction/tool overrides, function_call_output items, session.update at any time, and a hard 60-minute session cap.
findings.source_title: OpenAI docs — Realtime conversations guide
findings.numbers: max session 60 min; audio chunk <= 15 MB; voice locked after first audio; truncate fields item_id/content_index/audio_end_ms; input:[] ignores all context
findings.relevance: Defines the exact API surface for turning Model A's event stream into narration context and for injecting owner commands as validated tool calls without letting the vendor VAD drive motion.

findings.claim: gpt-realtime (GA 2025-08-28) added asynchronous function calling in which the model keeps talking while a tool runs and emits placeholder utterances instead of hallucinating results; the GA model had a 32,768-token window (4,096 max response, 28,672 input, 16,384 for instructions+tools), idle_timeout_ms on server VAD, and a sideband server connection for tools/instructions.
findings.source_title: OpenAI developer blog — Developer notes on the Realtime API
findings.numbers: 32,768 window; 4,096 max response; 28,672 max input; 16,384 instructions+tools; session 60 min (was 30); model gpt-realtime-2025-08-28; async FC GA-only
findings.relevance: Async function calling is the mechanism that lets 'Sure, I'll check the sofa' be spoken in the same turn while Model A starts moving and the completion arrives seconds later as a second event.

findings.claim: gpt-realtime-2 (2026-05-07) and gpt-realtime-2.1 (2026-07-06) carry a 128,000-token context window, 32,000 max output tokens, configurable reasoning effort, knowledge cutoff 2024-09-30, and tier-1 rate limits of 200 RPM / 40K TPM; 2.1 claims improved interruption behavior and >=25% lower p95 latency via caching.
findings.source_title: OpenAI model card — gpt-realtime-2.1 (release notes at https://community.openai.com/t/new-realtime-models-on-the-api-gpt-realtime-2-1-and-gpt-realtime-2-1-mini/1385896)
findings.numbers: 128,000 context; 32,000 max output; tier1 200 RPM/40K TPM ... tier5 20,000 RPM/15M TPM; p95 latency -25%; same $32/$64 audio pricing; GPT-Realtime-Translate $0.034/min, GPT-Realtime-Whisper $0.017/min
findings.relevance: Context budget for a 1-minute window + global history injection is now ample; the binding constraints are price per audio token and the 60-minute session, not the window.

findings.claim: A backend can attach a second WebSocket to a client's WebRTC or SIP Realtime session via the call_id returned in the SDP Location header (wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id=...), and that sideband connection can monitor the session, update instructions and respond to tool calls while the client only streams audio.
findings.source_title: OpenAI docs — Webhooks and server-side controls
findings.numbers: 1 audio connection + 1 control connection per session; SIP webhook realtime.call.incoming
findings.relevance: Lets the robot's audio endpoint (mic array/speaker) and Model B's context-injection process be separate processes on the Orin, matching Parcel's existing gateway/whisperer split.

findings.claim: Gemini Live supports NON_BLOCKING function declarations whose results are delivered with scheduling INTERRUPT (speak now), WHEN_IDLE (wait until current speech ends) or SILENT (absorb without speaking); by default function calling is sequential and 'execution pauses until the results of each function call are available'.
findings.source_title: Gemini API docs — Live API tool use
findings.numbers: 3 scheduling modes; async FC launched 2025-04-09 (changelog); code execution and Google Maps not supported on Live models
findings.relevance: These three scheduling semantics are exactly the revise/keep/queue narration policy Model B needs (arrival => INTERRUPT, progress => WHEN_IDLE, routine StateDigest => SILENT).

findings.claim: Gemini Live audio-only sessions are limited to 15 minutes (2 minutes with video) unless context-window compression is enabled, each connection lives ~10 minutes, resumption handles stay valid 2 hours, and a GoAway message with timeLeft precedes disconnection; audio is 16 kHz PCM in / 24 kHz out and is tokenised at 32 tokens per second.
findings.source_title: Gemini API docs — Live API session management (token rate at https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens)
findings.numbers: 15 min audio-only; 2 min audio+video; ~10 min connection; 2 h resumption; 32 audio tok/s; 263 video tok/s; 3.1 Flash Live context 131,072 in / 65,536 out; 2.5 native audio 131,072 / 8,192
findings.relevance: Session cycling with a carried-over text summary is unavoidable on Gemini; Model B's representation must be serialisable to text to survive reconnects.

findings.claim: Gemini 3.1 Flash Live costs $3.00 per 1M audio-input tokens (or $0.005/min), $12.00 per 1M audio-output tokens ($0.018/min), $0.75/$4.50 text in/out and $1.00 ($0.002/min) for video — roughly 4x cheaper than gpt-realtime-2.x per audio minute.
findings.source_title: Gemini Developer API pricing
findings.numbers: $0.005/min in, $0.018/min out (3.1 Flash Live); 2.5 Flash native audio $3.00 audio/video in, $12.00 audio out, $0.50/$2.00 text; free tier on both
findings.relevance: Cost lever for always-on listening; ~$2.4/day for 8 h of streamed audio vs ~$9/day on OpenAI.

findings.claim: Independent packet-level measurement of OpenAI's WebRTC Realtime API (Jan 2025, gpt-4o-realtime era) found ~1.7 s from end of user speech to start of model speech, with STUN round-trip of 60–70 ms — i.e. network was <5% of the turn latency.
findings.source_title: webrtcHacks — Measuring the response latency of OpenAI's WebRTC-based Realtime API
findings.numbers: 1.68 / 1.78 / 1.66 s manual; 1.764 / 1.86 / 1.796 s via silero-vad; RTT 60–70 ms; n=3 turns; measured 2025-01-04
findings.relevance: Baseline showing hosted turn latency is model/endpointing-bound, not link-bound; a 10 Hz local Model A cannot wait on it.

findings.claim: Full-Duplex-Bench-v3 (Apr 2026) with zero-latency mock tools measured gpt-realtime-1.5 at pass@1 0.600, tool-selection F1 0.876, argument accuracy 0.680 and 6.89 s average latency; gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview at 0.540 / 0.817 / 0.588 / 4.25 s but silent (no speech) in 22% of scenarios; a Whisper->GPT-4o->TTS cascade at 0.450 / 10.12 s; self-correction pass@1 was 0.588 (GPT-Realtime) down to 0.176 (cascade).
findings.source_title: Full-Duplex-Bench-v3: naturalistic speech and multi-step tool use (arXiv 2604.04847)
findings.numbers: GPT-Realtime take-turn 96.0%, interrupts user 13.5%, filler 16.9%; Gemini 3.1 take-turn 78.0%, interrupt 19.2%, filler 31.7%; Ultravox interrupts 47.9%; 100 real recordings, 4 domains, 21 self-correction cases; latency = t_agent_start − t_user_end, decomposed into first-response / tool-call / task-completion
findings.relevance: Quantifies why every hosted proposal must pass Parcel's deterministic broker and why Model B must be able to force narration after a tool result.

findings.claim: DuplexSLA-Bench (May 2026) measured turn-taking without context prefill at 96.50% accuracy / 1.57 s delay for GPT-Realtime-1.5 with semantic VAD high, 85.50% / 0.83 s with a 40 ms server VAD (pause accuracy 79.70%), 93.17% / 1.17 s for Gemini-3.1-flash-live, and 22.34% / 0.47 s for PersonaPlex; an ASR+LLM cascade reached 91.33% tool-call accuracy at 2.77 s delay vs a 7B duplex speech-LM at 85.56% / 0.64 s.
findings.source_title: DuplexSLA-Bench (arXiv 2605.20755)
findings.numbers: 2,100 cases (1,200 turn-taking + 900 tool-call); legal tool trigger window −1.0 s / +3.0 s of ground truth; multi-action cascade delay 4.71 s; Freeze-Omni 10.67%/0.36 s; MiniCPM-o 82.00%/0.61 s
findings.relevance: Gives the endpointing-vs-accuracy trade-off Model B must tune (fast VAD mis-fires on pauses) and a ready-made tool-trigger legality metric for the sim-to-real rig.

findings.claim: Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5 measured GPT-4o Realtime stopping its speech 0.23 s after a user interruption (response 1.50 s) but resuming after backchannels only 70% of the time and after side-talk 2% of the time, while Gemini 2.0 Flash Live stopped in 2.20 s (response 2.62 s) yet resumed after backchannels 93% and side-talk 99%; Moshi stopped in 1.16 s, Freeze-Omni 1.42 s.
findings.source_title: Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5: overlap behaviour of full-duplex models (arXiv 2507.23159)
findings.numbers: interruption respond rate 0.78 (GPT-4o) / 0.33 (Gemini) / 0.50 (Moshi); backchannel stop latency 0.21 s (GPT-4o), 0.66 s (Gemini); background-speech resume 0.04 (GPT-4o), 0.98 (Nova Sonic)
findings.relevance: Barge-in must be split: a fast reflex (slow/hold Model A on speech_started) and a slow validated decision, because the hosted model cannot distinguish backchannel from amendment.

findings.claim: OpenAI's reference 'chat-supervisor' pattern has the realtime model say a filler ('give me a moment to check on that') and hand tool work to a text model; the measured gap from end of filler to start of the real answer is ~2 s, and 'more assistant responses will start with Let me think'.
findings.source_title: openai/openai-realtime-agents — Chat-Supervisor and Sequential Handoff patterns
findings.numbers: ~2 s filler-to-answer gap; handoff = session.update with new instructions/tools; realtime-mini + gpt-4.1 cheaper than full realtime
findings.relevance: Direct template for Model B: hosted voice narrates immediately, the local system decides; also shows session.update is the sanctioned way to swap instruction sets (e.g. following vs navigating persona).

findings.claim: WSO2 built a Unitree Go2 EDU voice agent on the OpenAI Realtime API running on the robot's Jetson Orin NX (100 TOPS) in three weeks; motion tools (dance, go forward, turn right, stretch, sit, take photo) were served by a Flask lock-wrapper because the Unitree Python SDK 'wasn't concurrency-safe', and the onboard mic/speaker were 'incredibly noisy' so a Jabra Speak 710 was mounted.
findings.source_title: WSO2 — How we gave life to an AI agent with the Unitree Go2 robot (code: https://github.com/wso2-incubator/unitree-go2-realtime-agent, Apache 2.0)
findings.numbers: Jetson Orin NX 100 TOPS; 5 tool groups; 3 weeks; Python 3.11.9, unitree_sdk2 + cyclonedds; no latency numbers published
findings.relevance: Confirms the Realtime client runs on Orin-class hardware and that a single lock-holding motion server plus external audio is the working pattern — matching Parcel's gateway and XVF3800.

findings.claim: The ROS 2 package by_your_command (OpenAI Realtime + Gemini Live) measures Silero VAD at <50 ms, 1–2 s voice response, and <100 ms API-to-speaker playback; interruption is implemented as response.cancel + conversation.item.truncate + a ROS /interruption_signal that aborts PyAudio, with session cycling and a ConversationContext carried across sessions.
findings.source_title: pondersome/by_your_command — ROS 2 voice command processor using LLMs (Apache 2.0)
findings.numbers: VAD <50 ms; response 1–2 s; playback <100 ms; OpenAI 24 kHz resampled to 16 kHz; Gemini 16 kHz in / 24 kHz out; compound commands 'tenhut@rightish'
findings.relevance: Provides the ROS-side pipeline (audio_capturer -> echo_suppressor -> silero_vad -> agent) and a measured local-VAD budget for Parcel's sim-to-real instrumentation.

findings.claim: Pollen Robotics' Reachy Mini conversation app (Gemini 3.1 Flash Live default, OpenAI Realtime alternative) runs tool calls in background tasks 'so the audio stream isn't blocked', queues moves into a 60 Hz MovementManager while blending speech-reactive wobble, sends camera frames at 1 FPS as JPEG, and returns tool results so the model 'can narrate what happened'.
findings.source_title: Google AI — Build a talking robot with Gemini Live and Reachy Mini (repo: https://github.com/pollen-robotics/reachy_mini_conversation_app)
findings.numbers: 60 Hz control loop; 1 FPS video; tools dance/play_emotion/camera/move_head/head_tracking/go_to_sleep/sweep_look/remember/forget + MCP; Apache 2.0
findings.relevance: Closest published analogue of tight speech-motion coupling: motion owns its own clock, tool calls only enqueue, narration follows completion.

findings.claim: Kyutai Moshi is a 7B full-duplex speech model (Mimi codec 12.5 Hz, 1.1 kbps, 80 ms frames) with 160 ms theoretical / 200 ms practical latency on an L4, needs a 24 GB GPU in bf16, ships weights under CC-BY 4.0, and has no tool/function calling; NVIDIA PersonaPlex-7B (Moshi weights fine-tuned 6 h on 8xA100 with 1,840 h + 410 h dialog) reports 0.070–0.240 s user-interruption latency and 0.170 s smooth turn-taking on Full-Duplex-Bench but also lacks tools.
findings.source_title: Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue (arXiv 2410.00037); PersonaPlex at https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06053 and https://huggingface.co/nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1
findings.numbers: 7B temporal + 6-layer depth transformer; 7M h audio, Fisher 2,000 h, >20k h synthetic; 24 GB bf16; PersonaPlex pause TOR 0.584/0.662, backchannel TOR 0.327, Service-Duplex-Bench 4.48 vs Moshi 1.75; tested on A100 80 GB; NVIDIA Open Model License
findings.relevance: Shows the open duplex route is fast but tool-less and turn-taking-weak (22% on DuplexSLA no-prefill); a local fallback voice on the Orin must be a cascade, not a duplex model.

findings.claim: Kyutai Unmute (STT -> vLLM LLM -> TTS over an OpenAI-Realtime-compatible WebSocket protocol) reaches under 1 s end-to-end with TTS latency ~750 ms on one L40S or ~450 ms on three GPUs, needs a minimum 16 GB VRAM, and states tool calling is 'not fully integrated yet'; Kyutai STT-1B has a 0.5 s delay with semantic VAD (2.6B: 2.5 s) and an H100 serves 400 real-time streams.
findings.source_title: kyutai-labs/unmute — Make text LLMs listen and speak (STT numbers at https://github.com/kyutai-labs/delayed-streams-modeling)
findings.numbers: TTS ~750 ms (1 GPU) / ~450 ms (3 GPUs); total <1 s; 16 GB VRAM min; STT 1B 0.5 s delay; L40S 64 connections at 3x real-time; MIT code, CC-BY 4.0 weights
findings.relevance: Candidate offline voice for Starlink dropouts that can speak the same Model B narration stream, with tools handled in the LLM wrapper.

findings.claim: tau-voice (Mar 2026) shows voice agents complete only 31–51% of 278 grounded multi-turn tasks in clean audio and 26–38% with noise and diverse accents, versus 85% for text GPT-5 with reasoning — retaining 30–45% of text capability — and 79–90% of failures are agent behaviour rather than ASR.
findings.source_title: tau-voice: evaluating voice agents on grounded tasks (arXiv 2603.13686)
findings.numbers: 278 tasks; 85% vs 31–51% vs 26–38%; 79–90% failures agent-side
findings.relevance: Argues for adding acoustic-condition tiers to Parcel's instruction-following matrix and for keeping task state in Model A/B rather than in the hosted model.

findings.claim: A misconfigured Gemini Live VAD (low end_of_speech_sensitivity with 8 kHz audio) produced 7–15 s time-to-first-token spikes and 30 s transcript delays because noise kept the turn open until the ~30 s server timeout; Google's fix was end_of_speech_sensitivity HIGH and silence_duration_ms 1000.
findings.source_title: Google AI Developers Forum — Live API latency spikes
findings.numbers: 7–15 s spikes; 30 s timeout; silence_duration_ms 1000 recommended; model gemini-live-2.5-flash-preview
findings.relevance: Concrete evidence that the robot, not the vendor VAD, must own endpointing (Parcel should set create_response/interrupt_response false and commit turns from local VAD).

findings.claim: [secondary] A June 2026 head-to-head over 20 wired conversations measured median end-of-user-speech to first audio byte of ~410 ms (OpenAI Realtime), ~380 ms (Gemini Live) and ~440 ms (Pipecat-JS); OpenAI barge-in came 'free' via WebRTC while Gemini required a manual PCM buffer flush on the interrupted signal (~40 lines).
findings.source_title: vadimall.com — OpenAI Realtime API vs Gemini Live vs Pipecat for voice AI in TypeScript
findings.numbers: 410 / 380 / 440 ms medians; n=20; Tel Aviv wired
findings.relevance: Best-case first-audio latency for 2026 hosted models under ideal network; still 4+ frames of Parcel's 10 Hz clock and far above local VAD reflex times.

design_implications: Model A (local, duplex, 10 Hz) must never block on the hosted voice: measured hosted numbers are 0.4 s best-case first audio, 0.8-1.6 s turn-taking delay, 1.5-2.6 s response under overlap, and 4-7 s task completion for a tool chain even with zero-latency tools — i.e. 4-70 frames. The hosted model is narrator + intent source; only Model A's act tokens and plan queue move the dog.

Implement Model B's owner-command path as: hosted model emits an advisory tool call (navigate/amend/queue) -> Parcel's deterministic broker validates -> Model B decides revise/keep/queue against the historical plan queue. Treat proposals as ~0.6 pass@1 / ~0.68 argument accuracy (Full-Duplex-Bench-v3) and require confirmation for destructive amendments.

Use asynchronous tool semantics on both vendors so the voice says 'Sure, I'll check the sofa' in the same turn Model A starts moving: OpenAI GA async function calling with function_call_output delivered later (or an out-of-band response.create with conversation:'none', input:[state item], metadata:{event}); Gemini NON_BLOCKING with scheduling INTERRUPT (arrival/blocked), WHEN_IDLE (progress), SILENT (routine StateDigest).

Split barge-in into a fast reflex and a slow decision: on input_audio_buffer.speech_started / Gemini interrupted (~0.2 s), Model B sends a soft signal to Model A (slow, hold heading, keep plan); the hard revise/keep/queue decision waits for the validated tool call ~1 s later, because 30-98% of overlaps are backchannels or side-talk the hosted model misclassifies. Keep vendor VAD but set create_response/interrupt_response false and commit turns from the XVF3800 + local Silero/Kyutai VAD (<50 ms, 0.5 s semantic).

Send the whisperer StateDigest and Model A's representation as small, event-driven TEXT items (role system/user on OpenAI; send_realtime_input text on Gemini 3.1), never audio (~10x tokens) and never by editing earlier items (prefix-cache bust at $32/M vs $0.40/M). Budget ~1,800 audio tokens/min of conversation inside the 128k window and keep instructions+tools well under 16k tokens.

Model B must be able to force narration: Gemini 3.1 produced no speech in 22% of tool scenarios ('silent worker'); use an out-of-band response with explicit instructions ('say one sentence confirming X') rather than assuming the model speaks after a tool result.

Plan for finite sessions and always-on cost: OpenAI 60-min sessions, Gemini 15-min audio / ~10-min connections with resumption handles; cycle sessions with a text summary carried over (OpenAI cookbook pattern). Input audio is billed whether or not the model answers ($0.0192/min OpenAI, $0.005/min Gemini 3.1), so gate streaming with local wake/VAD; 8 h/day streamed is ~$9/day (OpenAI) or ~$2.4/day (Gemini) for listening alone.

Robot-side architecture from published integrations: one lock-holding motion server in front of the non-thread-safe Unitree SDK (WSO2), a watchdog that neutralises motion if the voice link stalls (RDK X5/ES02), motion on its own 60 Hz loop that only enqueues moves from tool calls (Reachy Mini), external mic/speaker because the Go2's onboard audio is unusable (WSO2, HackMD); use the OpenAI sideband (call_id) so audio I/O and Model B control are separate processes on the Orin.

Local fallback for Starlink loss: Moshi/PersonaPlex (7B, ~24 GB bf16) are fast but tool-less and score 22% turn-taking without prefill; the realistic offline voice on the Orin is a Kyutai-style cascade (STT-1B 0.5 s + small text LLM + TTS, <1 s, 16 GB) speaking the same Model B narration contract with tools in the LLM wrapper.

Instrument the sim-to-real rig with the benchmark vocabulary that already exists: per turn log first-response latency, tool-call latency, task-completion latency, take-turn / interrupt / filler rates and self-correction pass@1 (Full-Duplex-Bench-v3), tool-trigger legality within (-1.0 s, +3.0 s) of ground truth (DuplexSLA-Bench), and add noise/accent tiers (tau-voice: voice agents keep only 30-45% of text capability) to the instruction-navigation matrix.
open_questions: No public measurement of hosted tool round-trip latency from a Jetson over a satellite (Starlink) link; all measured numbers are wired urban clients or zero-latency mocks — Parcel must measure this itself in the sim-to-real rig.

OpenAI's own 'delivering low-latency voice AI at scale' post and the gpt-realtime / gpt-realtime-2 launch pages returned HTTP 403; official p50/p95 turn latencies for gpt-realtime-2.x remain uncited and only the 'p95 -25%' relative claim is documented.

Can gpt-realtime-2.x async function calling deliver multiple deferred outputs for one call_id (progress -> done), or must each progress event be a separate out-of-band response? Do Gemini SILENT tool results count toward the 15-minute audio session budget?
No source measures barge-in-to-motion latency on a real robot; every integration stops audio, none reports when legs/wheels reacted.
No source quantifies hosted-model behaviour when the robot's own speaker leaks into the mic array while moving (echo + gait noise); by_your_command has an echo_suppressor node but no numbers.

Current Realtime API concurrency/session limits beyond RPM/TPM are undocumented in the fetched pages (the 2024 '100 requests per day' cap seen in the Mamezou ROS 2 report is obsolete but no replacement figure was found).

Full-Duplex-Bench-v3 and DuplexSLA-Bench tested gpt-realtime-1.5 and gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview; whether gpt-realtime-2.1's 'improved interruption behavior' changes the overlap/backchannel resume rates has not been independently measured.

results.claim: OpenAI bills Realtime audio at 1 token per 100 ms of input and 1 token per 50 ms of output; gpt-realtime-2/2.1 cost $32 per 1M audio-input tokens ($0.40 cached) and $64 per 1M audio-output tokens, so listening costs $0.0192/min and speaking $0.0768/min before context re-reads; the mini tier is $10/$0.30/$20.
results.evidence_quote: Costs guide: "Audio tokens in user messages are 1 token per 100 ms of audio, while audio tokens in assistant messages are 1 token per 50ms of audio." ... "A 32k context model with 4,096 max output tokens can only include 28,224 tokens in the context before truncation occurs." ... "The server defaults to a value of 1.0, meaning truncation will remove only the items necessary. A value of 0.8 means a truncation would retain 80% of the maximum" ... "we recommend reducing limiting the number of tokens and setting a retention_ratio less than 1" ... "Removing or changing content in the conversation will 'bust' the cache up to the point of the change". Pricing page (Realtime and audio generation models, per 1M tokens): "gpt-realtime-2.1 Audio $32.00 $0.40 $64.00 Text $4.00 $0.40 $24.00 Image $5.00 $0.50"; "gpt-realtime-2.1-mini Audio $10.00 $0.30 $20.00 Text $0.60 $0.06 $2.40"; hidden-model rows in the page data: gpt-realtime-2 Audio 32/0.4/64, Text 4/0.4/24, Image 5/0.5; gpt-realtime-mini Audio 10/0.3/20, Text 0.6/0.06/2.4.
results.correction: None needed. Arithmetic checks: 600 tok/min x $32/1M = $0.0192/min; 1,200 tok/min x $64/1M = $0.0768/min. Note the per-token prices live on the pricing page, not the costs guide (the costs guide says pricing is 'listed on the model pages'); and the older gpt-realtime / gpt-realtime-1.5 rows have text output at $16 (not $24) - irrelevant to the claim as written, which names 2/2.1 only.

results.claim: The Realtime API exposes every mechanism Model B needs: server VAD with interrupt_response/create_response switches (keep VAD, decide locally), conversation.item.truncate for barge-in on WebSocket (automatic on WebRTC/SIP), out-of-band responses (response.create with conversation:'none', custom input array, metadata), per-response instruction/tool overrides, function_call_output items, session.update at any time, and a hard 60-minute session cap.
results.evidence_quote: "you can set turn_detection.interrupt_response and turn_detection.create_response to false with the session.update client event. This will retain all the behavior of VAD but not automatically create new Responses." ... "In WebRTC and SIP connections the server manages a buffer of output audio... The server will automatically truncate unplayed audio when there's a user interruption. With a WebSocket connection the client manages audio playback, and thus must stop playback and handle truncation." (client sends conversation.item.truncate with item_id / content_index / audio_end_ms) ... response.create example: "conversation": "none" ("indicates the response is out of band, and will not be added to the default conversation"), "metadata": {"topic": "classification"}, "instructions": prompt, and a custom "input": [...] array; "An empty input array removes all prior context" ... conversation.item.create with "type": "function_call_output", "call_id" ... "Most session properties can be updated at any time, except for the voice the model uses for audio output, after the model has responded with audio once during the session. The maximum duration of a Realtime session is 60 minutes." ... "Each chunk cannot exceed 15 MB in size."
results.correction: None needed. Only nuance: session.update is 'at any time' except the voice once audio has been produced, which the claim's numbers field already records.

results.claim: gpt-realtime (GA 2025-08-28) added asynchronous function calling in which the model keeps talking while a tool runs and emits placeholder utterances instead of hallucinating results; the GA model had a 32,768-token window (4,096 max response, 28,672 input, 16,384 for instructions+tools), idle_timeout_ms on server VAD, and a sideband server connection for tools/instructions.
results.evidence_quote: (Blog dated Sep 12, 2025, Peter Bakkum) "The Realtime API and speech-to-speech (s2s) model graduated to general availability (GA)" ... "EU data residency is now supported specifically for the gpt-realtime-2025-08-28" ... "the Realtime API allows clients to continue a session while a function call is pending. This continuation is good for UX... but the model sometimes hallucinates the content of a nonexistent function response. To mitigate this issue, the GA Responses API adds placeholder responses with content we've evaluated and tuned in experiments to ensure the model performs gracefully, even while awaiting a function response. If you ask the model for the results of a function call, it'll say something like, 'I'm still waiting on that.'" ... Feature table: "Async function calling ✅ [GA model] ❌ [Beta model]" ... "Realtime sessions can now last up to 60 minutes, up from 30 minutes. The gpt-realtime model has a token window of 32,768 tokens. Responses can consume a maximum of 4,096 tokens. This means the model has a maximum input of 28,672 tokens. The session instructions plus tools can have a maximum length of 16,384 tokens." ... "Enable this feature by setting idle_timeout_ms on the server_vad settings for turn detection." ... "A sideband connection means there are two active connections to the same realtime session: one from the user's client and one from your application server. The server connection can be used to monitor the session, update instructions, and respond to tool calls".
results.correction: Substantively correct. Two soft points: (a) the page never states the GA date; '2025-08-28' is inferred from the snapshot ID gpt-realtime-2025-08-28 (the post itself is dated Sep 12, 2025 and says 'We recently announced'); (b) the page says the *session* continues while the call is pending and the model uses tuned placeholder responses - 'the model keeps talking' is a fair paraphrase but slightly stronger than the text.

results.claim: Gemini Live supports NON_BLOCKING function declarations whose results are delivered with scheduling INTERRUPT (speak now), WHEN_IDLE (wait until current speech ends) or SILENT (absorb without speaking); by default function calling is sequential and 'execution pauses until the results of each function call are available'.
results.evidence_quote: "Function calling executes sequentially by default, meaning execution pauses until the results of each function call are available. This ensures sequential processing, which means you won't be able to continue interacting with the model while the functions are being run. Note: Asynchronous function calling is not yet supported in Gemini 3.1 Flash Live. The model will not start responding until you've sent the tool response." ... "behavior": "NON_BLOCKING" ... "It can either: Interrupt what it's doing and tell you about the response it got right away (scheduling="INTERRUPT"), Wait until it's finished with what it's currently doing (scheduling="WHEN_IDLE"), Or do nothing and use that knowledge later on in the discussion (scheduling="SILENT")" ... Tool table: "Function calling | Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Preview: Supported (synchronous only) | Gemini 2.5 Flash Live Preview: Supported (synchronous and asynchronous)"; "Google Maps Not supported Not supported; Code execution Not supported Not supported; URL context Not supported Not supported". Changelog (ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/changelog): "May 20, 2025 ... Launched support for asynchronous function calls in the Live API."
results.correction: The mechanism and all three scheduling semantics are quoted accurately, but the blanket 'Gemini Live supports' hides a load-bearing restriction: NON_BLOCKING/scheduling is available only on Gemini 2.5 Flash Live Preview; the current Gemini 3.1 Flash Live model supports synchronous function calling only ('Asynchronous function calling is not yet supported in Gemini 3.1 Flash Live'). Any design that pairs the INTERRUPT/WHEN_IDLE/SILENT policy with the 3.1 model benchmarked in claims 5-6 is not currently possible.
