findings.relevance: Only Go2 paper with a per-condition real-world table; hardware matches Parcel's MID360 + camera; gives the 'people' axis of the transfer gap.

findings.claim: On the Go2 EDU's onboard Orin NX 16 GB, a quantised Qwen2-VL-2B draft model takes 288 ms per draft round while cloud verification with Qwen2-VL-7B on an A100 takes 620 ms plus 120 ms network.
findings.source_title: Fast and Cost-effective Speculative Edge-Cloud Decoding with Early Exits
findings.numbers: Go2 EDU Jetson Orin: 8-core Cortex-A78AE, 16 GB LPDDR5; draft 288 ms (gamma=4), verify 620 ms, comm 120 ms, latency ratio 0.11; 21% speedup over cloud autoregressive; no success rate
findings.relevance: Measured edge/cloud split on the exact robot family; sets expectations for a hosted Model B feeding an on-robot Model A.

findings.claim: QUART-Online raises a Fuyu-8B quadruped multimodal model from 2 Hz to 50 Hz by discretising action chunks, improving QUARD success from 0.37-0.52 to 0.68-0.79.
findings.source_title: QUART-Online: Latency-Free Large Multimodal Language Model for Quadruped Robot Learning
findings.numbers: base Fuyu-8b; action chunks 1/5/10; 2 Hz -> 50 Hz; avg SR 0.37-0.52 -> 0.68-0.79 (+65%); Isaac Gym; real-robot hardware unspecified
findings.relevance: Supports Parcel's discrete act-token codec as the way to get a large model to control-rate output.

findings.claim: Habitat 3.0 provides humanoid avatars, social navigation/rearrangement tasks and a recordable, replayable human-in-the-loop tool (keyboard/VR/browser); its 30-participant study found automated humanoid evaluation preserves the relative ordering of policies seen with real humans, but the simulator has no audio or speech.
findings.source_title: Habitat 3.0: A Co-Habitat for Humans, Avatars and Robots
findings.numbers: 188+/-2 FPS one humanoid, 245+/-19 robot, 136+/-8 both, 1191+/-3 FPS over 16 envs on one GPU; 12 avatar base models; HSSD 37/12/10 scenes; social nav heuristic S 1.00/SPS 0.97/F 0.51/CR 0.52 vs RL S 0.97/SPS 0.65/F 0.44/CR 0.51; social rearrangement Plan-Pop3 71.79+/-7.38; HITL 30 participants x 10 episodes/condition, relative efficiency solo 100, Learn-Single 133.80, Plan-Pop3 123.46; HITL apps run at 30 SPS; habitat-lab MIT
findings.relevance: Reference design for Parcel's HITL evaluation and episode recording/replay; confirms no off-the-shelf sim covers speech.

findings.claim: PARTNR scaled Habitat 3.0 HITL to a browser/AWS server with 129 participants on 2,000 tasks and showed LLM partners score 0.30 with a simulated LLM human but 0.91-0.92 with real humans (who adapt to robot mistakes); a fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B matched a 70B ReAct planner at 8.6x lower latency.
findings.source_title: PARTNR: A Benchmark for Planning and Reasoning in Embodied Multi-agent Tasks
findings.numbers: 100,000 tasks, 60 houses, 5,819 objects; 100k train episodes/37 scenes, 1,000 val/13, 1,000 test/10 (HSSD); 129 non-expert participants, 1000 val + 1000 test tasks, 3-5 min per task, up to 3 tries, matchmaking lobby; SR single 0.93, multi 0.93, human-ReAct 0.91, human-Finetuned 0.92; sim steps 3046.99 / 2369.55 / 4267.71 / 3443.33; offloading 0.59 / 0.16 / 0.26; LLM alone 0.30 non-privileged, 0.73 with oracle; finetuned 8B 0.70 vs 70B 0.73, 8.6x faster; 1.5x steps vs two humans, 1.1x vs one; partnr-planner MIT (385 stars)
findings.relevance: Shows simulated-user evals underestimate and that small fine-tuned planners are better teammates; directly informs Model B sizing and the eval plan.

findings.claim: An LLM user simulator over TEACh/AI2-THOR predicts when the human should speak at only ~43% F1 (GPT-4) and the dialogue act at 51-62% F1, and degrades sharply when robot motion actions are in context; it is text-only.
findings.source_title: Simulating User Agents for Embodied Conversational-AI
findings.numbers: TEACh ~3,000 sessions; val-seen 181 sessions / 7,923 steps; Speak-F1 GPT-4 zero-shot 42.0%, few-shot 43.4%; DA-F1 35.15% / 51.13% / RoBERTa fine-tuned 62.48%; with move actions Speak-F1 43.39% -> 26.79%; robot turns 13.2% conversational, 69.2% nav/manipulation
findings.relevance: Calibrates how trustworthy an LLM 'owner simulator' is for interruption/amendment evals.

findings.claim: tau-Voice is a full-duplex voice-agent benchmark with a wall-clock-decoupled LLM user simulator, 200 ms discrete ticks, LLM-driven barge-in, per-tick event logging and pass@1 + responsiveness/latency/interrupt/selectivity scoring; hosted voice agents reach only 31-51% vs 85% for text GPT-5.
findings.source_title: tau-Voice: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Voice Agents on Real-World Domains
findings.numbers: 278 tasks (Retail 114, Airline 50, Telecom 114); 200 ms simulation ticks; clean SR voice agents 31-51% vs GPT-5 text 85%; realistic 26-38% (30-45% of text capability); OpenAI fastest latency 0.90 s, selectivity 6%; Google loses 17% vs 24-28%; 79-90% of failures from agent behaviour; CC BY 4.0; code in tau2-bench
findings.relevance: The harness shape (discrete time, simulated interrupting user, event logs, multi-axis scoring) is the model for Parcel's well-instrumented voice+navigation sim rig.

findings.claim: Isaac Lab ships 11 quadruped morphologies including Go1/Go2 with ray-cast LiDAR sensors, million-FPS state-based throughput, and reports robust sim-to-real for ANYmal and Spot; it is BSD-3 while Isaac Sim itself is proprietary.
findings.source_title: Isaac Lab: A GPU-Accelerated Simulation Framework for Multi-Modal Robot Learning
findings.numbers: quadrupeds A1, G1, H1, Go1/2, Anymal-B/C/D, Cassie, Digit, Spot; >900K FPS (DextrAH) and >1.6M FPS (Franka cabinet) on 8 GPUs; RayCaster height scanner / solid-state / rotating LiDAR; tiled camera rendering; repo BSD-3, Isaac Lab 3.0 beta 2 on Isaac Sim 6.0.0/6.0.1, >30 envs, >16 robots
findings.relevance: The de-facto Go2 locomotion training stack that NaVILA/NavDP/community repos build on.

findings.claim: Isaac Sim's ROS 2 Nav2 tutorial supports adding people assets that the simulated LiDAR sees, and its actor simulation is a YAML routine-driven, NavMesh-based offline data tool; neither simulates audio or LLM interaction.
findings.source_title: ROS 2 Navigation - Isaac Sim Documentation (6.0.0)
findings.numbers: Nova Carter / iw.hub; RTX LiDAR; occupancy map Z bound 0.62 m for Carter; people assets detected by LiDAR into Nav2; Replicator Agent actors via omni.behavior.tree with NavMesh; no audio, no LLM
findings.relevance: Defines what an Isaac-based Parcel city could and could not cover (people yes, speech no).

findings.claim: Community Go2-in-Isaac platforms already expose a Go2 with LiDAR/RGB-D/YOLO topics in 70+ environments and accept natural-language commands via an MCP server, but publish no FPS or success numbers.
findings.source_title: Go2_Isaac_ros2 - Unitree Go2 simulation in NVIDIA IsaacLab/Isaac Sim with ROS2
findings.numbers: Isaac Sim 4.5.0 + IsaacLab 2.1.1 (6.0 / 3.0 beta in progress); ROS 2 Humble; topics cmd_vel, RGB/depth/semantic, detection_image, lidar/point_cloud, odom, pose; 70+ environments; MCP natural-language control + web portal; PPO/distillation; 36 stars; sibling Zhefan-Xu/isaac-go2-ros2 on Isaac Sim 4.5 / Lab 2.1.0 with warehouse and sparse/medium/dense obstacle fields
findings.relevance: Cheapest starting point if Parcel adds an Isaac Go2 twin next to the MuJoCo city.

findings.claim: The most-used community Go2 ROS 2 stack (go2_ros2_sdk) reaches Nav2 + slam_toolbox over WebRTC/CycloneDDS, but the robot only streams LiDAR at 7 Hz and joint states at 1 Hz, and the popular Go2 MCP server and HackMD voice guide report no measured latencies (the guide targets ~3 s end-to-end).
findings.source_title: go2_ros2_sdk - Unofficial ROS2 SDK for Unitree Go2
findings.numbers: BSD-2, 1,000+ stars, 213 forks; Go2 AIR/PRO/EDU; LiDAR 7 Hz (was 2 Hz); joint states 1 Hz (firmware-limited); Nav2 + slam_toolbox; COCO detection. Go2 MCP server (lpigeon): Apache 2.0, 86 stars, ROS 2 sport commands, no latency. HackMD guide: Whisper -> gpt-3.5-turbo -> TTS, keyword matching, 'respond within ~3 seconds' target, no official audio API on Go2
findings.relevance: Baseline of what the Go2 exposes over ROS 2 and the absence of measured voice-to-motion latency in community work.

findings.claim: OpenMind OM1 is an MIT-licensed inputs->fusers->LLM->actions runtime with Go2/G1 autonomy (LiDAR, SLAM, Nav2), pluggable ASR/TTS/LLM providers, Gazebo and Isaac Sim twins for the Go2, and Prometheus/Grafana dashboards for LLM and ASR latency, but publishes no latency figures.
findings.source_title: OpenMind OM1 - Modular AI runtime for robots
findings.numbers: MIT; 2.9k stars, 993 forks; Go2 & G1 with BrainPack (SLAM, LiDAR, Nav2); ASR/TTS in config/conversation.json5; LLMs OpenAI, xAI, DeepSeek, Anthropic, Meta, Gemini, NearAI, Ollama; Gazebo (Go2) + Isaac Sim (Go2, G1); Robot Report 2025-09-18: Google ASR, Riva/ElevenLabs TTS, $20M raised
findings.relevance: Closest existing 'LLM voice agent on a Go2 with a sim twin' stack; shows the field instruments latency but has not published it.

findings.claim: TartanGround is a ~15 TB photorealistic ground-robot dataset (UE4/AirSim, ANYmal-D legged trajectories via Gazebo) that shows large cross-domain generalisation gaps for occupancy prediction and SLAM, contains no people or audio, and is non-commercial.
findings.source_title: TartanGround: A Large-Scale Dataset for Ground Robot Perception and Navigation
findings.numbers: body: 878 trajectories (440 omni, 198 diff-drive, 240 legged), 63 envs, 1.44M samples, 17.3M RGB, ~15 TB; abstract: 910 / 70 / 1.5M; 6 stereo RGB cams at 90 deg FOV, depth, flow, disparity, simulated LiDAR, semantic occupancy; SurroundOcc IoU 12.91-22.15 urban vs 6.39-13.89 natural; ORB-SLAM3 loses tracking; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
findings.relevance: Useful only for perception pre-training experiments; licence and missing people/audio make it a poor fit for Model A training.

findings.claim: A published Isaac Sim -> Gazebo -> real ROS 2 pipeline transferred an end-to-end LiDAR local planner zero-shot to a TurtleBot 4 with 7-10/10 success per scenario and Nav2-comparable behaviour, plus dynamic-obstacle avoidance that Nav2's cost map failed on.
findings.source_title: Sim-to-Real Transfer for Mobile Robots with Reinforcement Learning: from NVIDIA Isaac Sim to Gazebo and Real ROS 2 Robots
findings.numbers: TurtleBot 4 Lite, RPLIDAR A1M8 (2 m range, 3 deg), RPi 4B, ROS 2 Galactic, 0.31 m/s; 10 trials x 4 experiments: 10/10, 10/10, 8/10, 7/10; min LiDAR range 0.25-0.43 m; avg vel 0.13-0.15 m/s; dynamic box 0.1-0.3 m/s; code github.com/sahars93/RL-Navigation
findings.relevance: Clean recipe for the sim-to-sim-to-real ladder Parcel's harness should copy (Isaac/MuJoCo -> ROS 2 twin -> hardware).

findings.claim: Genesis (Apache-2.0) claims 10-80x speedups over Isaac Gym/Sim/Lab and MuJoCo MJX and ships a 50 Hz Go2 locomotion tutorial with simulated ~20 ms action latency, and is the physics base of the LLM-agent 'Virtual Community' city simulator (GPT-4o agents, 35 scenes, 5 robot types); neither simulates audio.
findings.source_title: What is Genesis - Genesis documentation
findings.numbers: '10-80x faster than prior GPU-accelerated simulators'; Go2 tutorial 50 Hz, ~20 ms (one dt) action latency; repo Apache 2.0, 29.8k stars; Virtual Community (arXiv 2508.14893, ICLR 2026): Genesis, 35 scenes, GPT-4o planners 47.2 vs heuristic 42.1, robot challenge heuristic 19.9 / RL 14.3, 196 stars
findings.relevance: Fast alternative physics base for the MuJoCo city if throughput becomes the bottleneck for training Model A.

findings.claim: In a 15-participant HRI study, an LLM-driven robot (GPT-4o-mini) had 2.5 s API response latency that constrained real-time interaction, yet participants spent twice as much time on task with the LLM condition as with scripted dialogue.
findings.source_title: Evaluating Efficiency and Engagement in Scripted and LLM-Enhanced Human-Robot Interactions
findings.numbers: NAO on forklift; GPT-4o-mini; 15 participants (20-65 y, M=30.1); API latency 2.5 s; time on task 31.65% (LLM) vs 15.74% (scripted); trust median 44 vs 42 (n.s.); Tobii Glasses 3 + YOLOv8 gaze
findings.relevance: Independent measurement of hosted-LLM latency in a live HRI loop; a 2.5 s reply is the regime Model B narration must bridge.

design_implications: Split Model A into a fast on-robot loop (10 Hz act tokens, as TIC-VLA 10 Hz / QUART-Online 50 Hz chunked tokens) and a slow language loop (~0.5-1 Hz, as NaVILA/TIC-VLA), and train Model A with injected slow-loop latency sampled from 0-10 s so late plan amendments from Model B or the hosted voice do not destabilise motion.

Keep the Model A -> locomotion interface a small discrete vocabulary (NaVILA's 4 words at 0.5 m/s and +/-pi/6 rad/s reached 88% real SR; HA-VLN used 0.25 m / 15 deg steps); this is exactly what Parcel's act-token codec is, and it gives Model B a verifiable vocabulary to narrate.

Size Model A for the Orin and Model B for the hosted side: measured on-Go2 numbers are 1B VLM at 120 ms/policy step and 4.8 s/reasoning step on Orin NX, 2B quantised at 288 ms/draft, 8B not run on-robot at all; TIC-VLA lost 10 SR points moving to the Orin. Evaluate Model A at its true on-device latency, and let Model B be an 8B-class fine-tune (PARTNR: 8B matches 70B at 8.6x lower latency and coordinates better with real humans).

Report the sim-to-real gap on three axes the literature shows are each large: moving people (HA-VLN Go2 NSR 0.44 -> 0.18), embodiment (NavDP 9/10 wheeled vs 7/10 Go2), and latency (TIC-VLA 0.85 -> 0.75); Parcel's headless-city/MuJoCo evals should run with and without moving people and at real vs idealised Model A latency, using a frozen instruction set that is later replayed on hardware (NaVILA 25 x 3, HA-VLN 30 trials per instance).

Use an LLM owner-simulator for ranking Model B variants but not for the acceptance bar: PARTNR shows an LLM-simulated partner yields 0.30 SR where real humans yield 0.91-0.92 because humans adapt to robot mistakes, while Habitat 3.0 shows automated evaluation preserves policy ordering; plan a small real-owner HITL run on the frozen matrix.

Build the voice side of the sim-to-real rig in tau-Voice's shape: discrete simulation time (200 ms ticks), a user simulator decoupled from wall-clock, LLM-driven barge-in and backchannel decisions, per-tick logs of turn-taking events, audio effects, act tokens and whisperer digests, and scoring by final state plus responsiveness / latency / interrupt / selectivity; pair it with Habitat-HITL-style multi-level episode recording and replay.

Compose audio yourself: no robotics simulator fetched emits speech (SoundSpaces gives spatial environmental sound only); synthesise owner speech (TTS + room IR + XVF3800 model) into the sim, or run the hosted voice lane on real audio against a simulated body, mirroring NaVILA's off-board VLM split.

Bootstrap Model B's command -> revise/keep/queue head from procedurally generated data (LOVON: 1M synthetic language-motion samples trained in ~1 h; NavDP: 2,500 sim trajectories/GPU/day) over Parcel's task-executive logs before collecting human data.

Licence hygiene: NavDP and TartanGround are CC BY-NC-SA (no product training); Matterport3D-based benchmarks need their own licence; Isaac Sim is proprietary (Isaac Lab BSD-3); Habitat, HA-VLN, OM1, partnr-planner MIT; NaVILA code Apache-2.0 with YouTube data as IDs only; Genesis Apache-2.0.
open_questions: No fetched Go2 paper reports an 8B-class VLA on an AGX Orin 64 GB; NaVILA's quantisation figures (half memory, +40% speed) are workstation-side, so Model A's true on-AGX budget at INT8/INT4 is unmeasured.
HA-VLN 2.0's real Go2 run used a Jetson NX + Raspberry Pi 4B with 0.25 m steps and a panoramic rotation per step; how the policy was shrunk and its per-step latency are not stated.

No published pipeline runs a hosted voice LLM (audio in/out with barge-in) against a simulated Go2 with logged, replayable, scored episodes; tau-Voice (no robot) and Habitat/PARTNR HITL (no audio) are the closest halves.

The WebSearch budget ran out before checking NVIDIA's own Go2 + LLM demos beyond two community Isaac repos, LLM-driven pedestrian simulators (HuNavSim / Arena-Rosnav style), and the status of omni.anim.people under Isaac Sim 6.0 (URL 404s; the Replicator Agent page is the replacement found).
OM1 exposes Prometheus/Grafana LLM/ASR latency metrics and OpenGo measured instruction-to-execution response time on a real Go2, but neither publishes the numbers.
TartanGround's abstract (910 trajectories / 70 envs / 1.5M samples) and body (878 / 63 / 1.44M) disagree; cite the specific version used.

results.claim: NaVILA (8B VLM + Isaac-Lab locomotion policy) runs its language loop off-robot at ~1 s per action and reached 88% real-world success on 25 Go2 instructions; on-robot deployment of the VLM is explicitly left as future work.
results.evidence_quote: "the VLA inference time is approximately 0.6 seconds per sample" ... "NaVILA's current wait time between each action is about 1 second, which is practical for real-world deployment" (latency budget includes "image transmission time from Go2 to the server, and the VLA inference time") ... "25 instructions, each repeated three times" ... "88% success rate on 25 instructions, including a 75% success rate on complex instructions across diverse scenes" ... "These optimizations make NaVILA deployable directly on the robot, which will eliminate image transmission time significantly. We leave this as future work." Model is "NaVILA-8B"; locomotion policy "trained in the Isaac Sim simulator using Isaac Lab"; "over 60K FPS on an RTX 4090 GPU"; LiDAR "at a frequency of 15Hz"; quantisation: "memory requirements dropped by half, and processing speed improved by about 40%".
results.correction: None needed. Note the ~1 s figure is total wait between actions (image transmission Go2 -> server + ~0.6 s VLA inference), and the 88% is over 25 instructions x 3 repeats.

results.claim: TIC-VLA decouples a 10 Hz action policy from 0.5 Hz VLM reasoning, trains with random 0-10 s reasoning delays, and loses ~10 SR points on a real Go2 when moved from a laptop GPU to a Jetson Orin NX purely from latency.
results.evidence_quote: "the action policy running at 10 Hz and asynchronous VLM reasoning running at 0.5 Hz" ... "we sample reasoning delays Δt uniformly from [0, 10] seconds and condition the policy on: (1) the current image input and robot state, (2) KV cache features from the delayed VLM reasoning output, (3) explicit latency metadata" ... Table 3 (Real-world testing results): "TIC-VLA 4060 0.85 85.73 / 3430.73; TIC-VLA Orin NX 0.75 120.27 / 4831.73; TIC-VLA A6000 0.80 32.70 / 1681.66" ... "The navigation policy is executed on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot" ... "For each task, we conduct five trials and report the average success rate." ... "Across compute platforms, TIC-VLA maintains a 0.75 success rate on the Jetson Orin NX despite multi-second VLM reasoning latency, demonstrating its suitability for edge deployment. Although the A6000 reduces VLM latency, its success rate does not exceed local RTX 4060 deployment, likely due to remote communication overhead. These results show that real-world performance depends not only on inference speed, but also on communication latency and closed-loop control frequency."
results.correction: The 10 Hz / 0.5 Hz split, U[0,10] s training delays, Go2 platform, and 0.85 (RTX 4060, 50 W) vs 0.75 (Orin NX, 25 W) results are all verbatim. But the paper does not attribute the 10-point drop 'purely to latency': it presents 0.75 as robustness 'despite multi-second VLM reasoning latency', and its own remote-A6000 row (lower latency, 0.80) undercuts a latency-only reading. Also note the small sample (five trials per task). Restate as: 'the same model scored 0.75 on an Orin NX vs 0.85 on a laptop RTX 4060 (policy/reasoning latency 120/4832 ms vs 86/3431 ms); the paper reports these side by side but does not isolate latency as the sole cause.'

results.claim: HA-VLN 2.0 validated a sim-trained human-aware VLN policy on a Go2-EDU (Jetson NX + RPi 4B) and measured that 2-4 free-moving people cut real-world navigation success from 0.44 to 0.18; human-aware sim training gave 0.18 vs 0.12 for plain VLN-CE training.
results.evidence_quote: arXiv:2503.14229v2 (27 May 2025, then titled 'HA-VLN: A Benchmark for Human-Aware Navigation in Discrete-Continuous Environments with Dynamic Multi-Human Interactions, Real-World Validation, and an Open Leaderboard'): "Table 8. Navigation success rate across different region layouts with (w/) and without (w/o) human presence. Each result is averaged over 30 episodes across 3 instances of each region type." ALL column: "HA-VLN-VL (trained on HA-VLN) ... 0.44 0.18"; "HA-VLN-VL (trained on VLN-CE) ... 0.40 0.12"; "HA-VLN-CMA-Base (trained on HA-VLN) ... 0.25 0.15"; "HA-VLN-CMA-Base (trained on VLN-CE) ... 0.26 0.09" ... "agents trained on HA-VLN achieve higher NSR (0.18 vs. 0.12) than VLN-CE" ... Appendix D.5: "the robot is equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson NX for AI inference and a Raspberry Pi 4B for motion control ... We set a minimum step size of 0.25 m and a rotation increment of 15 degrees." (but Figure A10 in the same version says "The platform integrates an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX for onboard computation"). "each populated by 2-4 free-moving volunteers". CONTRADICTION at the cited URL: the unversioned URL resolves to v5 (18 Aug 2026, 'HA-VLN 2.0'); v3/v4/v5 fetches all report: "No mentions of 'Jetson,' 'Raspberry Pi,' or 'RPi 4B'" and "The document contains no table comparing real-world results with columns labeled 'w/o humans' vs 'w/ humans' ... Section 7.2 mentions real-world validation but provides only qualitative description"; v1 instead has "Table 9: Navigation Success Rate (NSR, %) ... averaged over 10 trials" with different values.
results.correction: The numbers are exactly right but only in arXiv v2 (May 2025), which is titled 'HA-VLN', not 'HA-VLN 2.0'. The current 'HA-VLN 2.0' version at the source URL (v5, Aug 2026; also v3, v4) removed the quantitative real-world table, the 30-episode x 3-instance protocol, and the Jetson NX / RPi 4B compute details, keeping only qualitative real-world validation ('2-4 free-moving volunteers'). Cite arXiv:2503.14229v2 explicitly, and note v2 is internally inconsistent about the compute (Jetson NX in App. D.5 vs Jetson Orin NX in Fig. A10). Real-world success is reported as NSR (navigation success rate).

results.claim: Habitat 3.0 provides humanoid avatars, social navigation/rearrangement tasks and a recordable, replayable human-in-the-loop tool (keyboard/VR/browser); its 30-participant study found automated humanoid evaluation preserves the relative ordering of policies seen with real humans, but the simulator has no audio or speech.
results.evidence_quote: "a library of avatars made from 12 base models with multiple gender representations, body shapes, and appearances" ... Social Navigation: "a robot must locate and follow the humanoid while maintaining a safety distance ranging from 1m to 2m"; Social Rearrangement: "a humanoid and a robot collaborate to move objects from their initial to target locations in a scene" ... "porting the client to other platforms, e.g., resource-constrained web browsers and VR devices. Hence, users can use this tool for a range of tasks: small-scale local evaluations using mouse and keyboard, large-scale data-collection on a browser, or high-fidelity human-robot interaction in VR." ... "Replayability. To support data collection and reproducibility, our platform provides functionalities for recording and replaying of HITL episodes." ... "(HITL) infrastructure across 30 participants ... Each participant performs the task for 10 episodes per condition" ... "our automated evaluation with humanoids can provide an indication of the relative ordering of different policies when evaluated with real human collaborators" ... "the relative order of average RE and RC between our automated and HITL evaluations holds" (RE: Solo 100.0, Learn-Single 133.80, Plan-Pop3 123.46). Audio: the only occurrence of 'audio/sound/speech' in the full PDF is the bibliography entry "SoundSpaces: Audio-visual navigation in 3d environments"; no simulator feature mentions audio or speech.
results.correction: None needed. Two nuances: 'no audio or speech' holds by omission (the paper never claims or discusses audio; it is not stated as a limitation), and the paper hedges the ordering result ('can give an indication') while adding 'Our ZSC agents do not accurately capture the dynamics of human-robot interaction'.

results.claim: PARTNR scaled Habitat 3.0 HITL to a browser/AWS server with 129 participants on 2,000 tasks and showed LLM partners score 0.30 with a simulated LLM human but 0.91-0.92 with real humans (who adapt to robot mistakes); a fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B matched a 70B ReAct planner at 8.6x lower latency.
results.evidence_quote: "We build on the human-in-the-loop infrastructure from Habitat 3.0 (Puig et al., 2024) and adapt it to a server-client architecture, with the server hosted on AWS ... with 129 non-expert human participants" ... "Figure 13 HITL on Web-browser. Our HITL system can be deployed on web browsers enabling large-scale collection." ... "the system includes a matchmaking service ... redirected to a 'lobby screen'" ... "we conduct comprehensive evaluations of 1000 tasks from the validation set, and 1000 tasks from the test set" ... "Each task took on average 3-5 minutes to complete." ... "Each task was completed up to 3 times" ... Table 3: "Human-ReAct 0.91 ± 0.01 ... Human-Finetuned 0.92 ± 0.01" ... "the ReAct model without any privileged information, achieves a significantly lower success rate of 0.30 (row (i) of Table 2) ... Note that the LLM baselines like ReAct and Finetuned achieve a success rate of 0.92 and 0.91 when evaluated with real humans (Table 3), because humans are able to adapt to LLM mistakes. On the other hand, the simulated human in Table 2 is an LLM, which is unable to recover from partner mistakes." ... Table 2 row (i): "ReAct Decentralized Learned ConceptGraph 12490.80 ± 208.90 0.30 ± 0.01"; row (e): "ReAct Decentralized Oracle Partial ... 0.73"; row (g): "Finetuned Decentralized Oracle Partial ... 0.70" ... "a smaller fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B achieves a similar performance to a Llama3.1-70B without finetuning, while being 8.6x faster" ... abstract: "1.5x as many steps as two humans collaborating and 1.1x more steps than a single human".
results.correction: Everything checks except the framing of 0.30: that number is ReAct with the simulated LLM human AND learned skills plus ConceptGraph (non-privileged) perception (Table 2 row i), so it conflates the simulated-partner effect with the perception/skill downgrade. The apples-to-apples simulated-LLM-human numbers with oracle skills/privileged perception are 0.73 (ReAct, Llama3.1-70B) and 0.70 (finetuned Llama3.1-8B) vs 0.91 / 0.92 with real humans. Restate as: 'with a simulated LLM human, planners score 0.70-0.73 (and only 0.30 once perception/skills are also non-privileged), versus 0.91-0.92 with real humans, who adapt to robot mistakes.' Minor: the paper says '8.6x faster at inference', i.e. throughput, not 'lower latency' per se.

results.claim: tau-Voice is a full-duplex voice-agent benchmark with a wall-clock-decoupled LLM user simulator, 200 ms discrete ticks, LLM-driven barge-in, per-tick event logging and pass@1 + responsiveness/latency/interrupt/selectivity scoring; hosted voice agents reach only 31-51% vs 85% for text GPT-5.
results.evidence_quote: "By decoupling simulation time from wall-clock time, we allow the user simulator to use the most capable LLM without real-time constraints." ... "We discretize the continuous audio stream into fixed-duration ticks (τ=200ms by default). Each tick, both parties exchange exactly τ ms of audio." ... "An LLM periodically evaluates whether to interrupt based on conversation context. A separate LLM decides whether to backchannel." ... "We instrument each simulation to log turn-taking events, audio effects, and agent responses, then derive metrics." ... "We report pass@1—the proportion of tasks completed successfully on a single attempt." plus Responsiveness, Latency, Interrupt rate, Selectivity ... "Under Clean conditions, voice agents achieve only 31–51% vs 85% GPT-5 (reasoning)—a 34–54pp gap." ... "Under Realistic conditions (noise, accents, turn-taking), performance falls further to 26–38%—retaining only 30–45% of text SOTA capability." ... 278 tasks: "Retail (114 tasks) ... Airline (50 tasks) ... Telecom (114 tasks)"; "CC BY 4.0"; "Code ... available at https://github.com/sierra-research/tau2-bench".
results.correction: None needed. Note the 85% text baseline is 'GPT-5 (reasoning)' under Clean conditions; the paper describes tick-based simulation and event logging but does not literally use the phrase 'per-tick event logging'.

sweeps.topic: Making a navigating robot look alive and attentive while it moves: sound-driven orienting, saliency/attention-driven gaze, idle/secondary motion, learned gaze during locomotion, expressive quadruped locomotion, and the liveliness-vs-task trade-off

findings.claim: Disney's animatronic gaze system is a three-engine stack: an attention engine computing a per-person curiosity score from movement and distance with habituation and a 'guestbase', a behaviour-selection state machine (Read / Glance / Engage / Acknowledge), and a subsumption-layered motor layer whose always-on base show (breathing, blinking, saccades) is overridden by higher layers; eyes lead the head and each actuator group has its own motion bandwidth.
findings.source_title: Realistic and Interactive Robot Gaze (Pan, Choi, Kennedy, McIntosh, Campos Zamora, Niemeyer, Kim, Wieland; IROS 2020)
findings.numbers: Saccades generated at 20 Hz with 0.1–0.5 s dwell between a guest's eyes and nose; behaviours Read/Glance/Engage/Acknowledge; base 'alive' layer = breathing + blinking + saccades; no controlled user-study numbers (show-floor evaluation).
findings.relevance: Reference pattern for Parcel's liveness layer: a fixed alive base, an attention layer with habituation, and task behaviours on top — the same decomposition Model A/Model B needs.

findings.claim: The iCub multimodal attention framework fuses visual and acoustic saliency by max into a head-centred ego-sphere with short-term memory, habituation and inhibition-of-return; the interplay yields emergent exploratory gaze (scan salient points in decreasing order, then revisit), and a voice injects auditory saliency that shifts gaze.
findings.source_title: Multimodal Saliency-Based Bottom-Up Attention: A Framework for the Humanoid Robot iCub (Ruesch et al., ICRA 2008)
findings.numbers: Ego-sphere 320x240 (1.125° lat / 0.75° long per cell) updated 5–10 times/s; motor loop >20 Hz; d_mem=0.95, d_a=0.03, d_h=0.2, t_h=0.85, sigma_ior=6° (12° in multimodal run); auditory blob sigma≈25°; 6-DOF head; all three salient marks visited equally often.
findings.relevance: Gives concrete decay/habituation constants at a ~10 Hz tick — directly reusable for a saliency state inside Parcel's 10 Hz duplex frame clock and its act-token gaze output.

findings.claim: Pepper/NAO's ALBasicAwareness reacts to Sound, Movement, People and Touch stimuli by looking at the stimulus origin, checking for a human, and otherwise looking back; the SemiEngaged mode glances at any new stimulus but always returns to the engaged person, and tracking can be Head-only, BodyRotation, WholeBody or MoveContextually.
findings.source_title: ALBasicAwareness — Aldebaran NAOqi documentation
findings.numbers: 4 stimulus types; 3 engagement modes (Unengaged, FullyEngaged, SemiEngaged); 4 tracking modes; LookStimulusSpeed/LookBackSpeed exposed as (0,1] floats (defaults not shown on fetched page).
findings.relevance: Shipped product policy for 'glance at a sound, verify, return' — the primitive Parcel needs while navigating so a sound never silently hijacks the goal.

findings.claim: Small robot microphone arrays give coarse but usable direction-of-arrival for head turns: NAO's 4-mic TDOA has ~10° theoretical accuracy, Pepper ~7–10°, single-source only, needs SNR >= ~3 dB, and is unreliable for sources more than 120° behind the front.
findings.source_title: ALSoundLocalization — Aldebaran NAOqi documentation
findings.numbers: NAO: 4 mics, 'maximum theoretical accuracy is about 10 degrees', CPU 3–5% (10% spikes); Pepper: average 10°, theoretical ~7°; SNR 'generally good at 3dB+'; tested at 80 dB / 2 m; unreliable >120° from front; output azimuth, elevation (rad), confidence.
findings.relevance: Sets expectations for the owner's 4-mic-class array: enough for a glance/body-yaw token, not for precise goal placement — confirm visually before amending the plan.

findings.claim: ODAS performs sound-source localisation (SRP-PHAT hierarchical search), Kalman tracking of up to four sources and separation on Raspberry-Pi-class hardware, and has been deployed on several mobile robots.
findings.source_title: ODAS: Open embeddeD Audition System (Grondin et al., Frontiers in Robotics and AI 2022)
findings.numbers: Typical arrays 4–8 mics (also 16); up to 4 DOAs per frame; RPi3 single-core: localisation 8-mic 38%→14%, tracking 1 source 24%→0.8%, 4 sources 98%→7%; deployed on Azimut-3, SecurBot, Beam, T-Top; open source on GitHub.
findings.relevance: Off-the-shelf DoA/tracking that fits on the Orin with negligible load; multi-source tracking feeds the saliency map rather than a single 'loudest' direction.

findings.claim: A 16-channel array on a UGV with a close-talk operator mic and AEC+MVDR+SRP-PHAT localises the operator's voice outdoors to a few degrees even at 1 dB SNR, enabling 'follow me' orienting.
findings.source_title: Sound Source Localization for Human-Robot Interaction in Outdoor Environments (Liu, Du, Sehn, Collier, Grondin; arXiv 2507.21431)
findings.numbers: 16 omnidirectional mics at 51.6 cm radius on Argo J8; average error 4°, 95% within 5° at 1 dB SNR; 0.95° at 3 m static; 98.75% within 5° at 10 m; ~2 s per mask computation on a 16-core workstation.
findings.relevance: Upper bound on what array size buys; a wearable/close-talk mic for the owner is a cheap way to make 'orient to owner' robust outdoors.

findings.claim: Event-driven attention on iCub locates the focus of attention orders of magnitude faster than frame-based saliency, which matters for reacting to unexpected dynamic events with gaze.
findings.source_title: Event-driven visual attention for the humanoid robot iCub (Rea, Metta, Bartolozzi; Frontiers in Neuroscience 2013)
findings.numbers: EVA latency 23 µs (15 µs sensor + 8 µs algorithm) vs frame-based iNVT ≈56 ms (33 + 23 ms); 158.2 vs 1.89 attentional shifts/s; CPU per shift 0.2% vs 6.79%; ~7 kAE/s event rate.
findings.relevance: A 10 Hz frame clock is fine for deliberate gaze, but startle/orienting to sudden motion or sound wants a faster reflex path beside Model A.

findings.claim: A single RL locomotion policy conditioned on a small human-readable behaviour vector (gait phase offsets, step frequency, body height, pitch, stance width, footswing height) executes trotting, pronking, pacing, bounding, dance and posture changes on a Unitree Go1 at 50 Hz, with a stated cost to in-distribution sprint performance.
findings.source_title: Walk These Ways: Tuning Robot Control for Generalization with Multiplicity of Behavior (Margolis & Agrawal, CoRL 2022)
findings.numbers: Go1 Edu, Jetson TX2 NX, 50 Hz; command c=[vx,vy,wz] + 8-dim b=[θ1,θ2,θ3,f,h_z,φ,s_y,h_z^f]; gait switches 2↔4 Hz; dance at 90 bpm; 60 cm leap; crawl under 22 cm bar; power at 3 m/s trot 98±9 W vs bound 127±35 W vs gait-free 102 W; platform-terrain survival trot 0.88 vs gait-free 0.83; ~20 ms modelled latency; 'MoB can come at a cost to in-distribution task performance'.
findings.relevance: The action interface Model A should emit on the Go2: a style vector plus velocity command, tracked by a fixed RL policy, rather than raw joints — and a measured example of the liveliness-vs-performance cost.

findings.claim: Disney's bipedal character layers animator-authored motion (perpetual balance/idle, periodic walk cycles, episodic clips) through an animation engine whose blended output is tracked by an RL policy; the head counter-rotates to hold gaze while torso yaw/pitch are modulated, and the system ran ~10 h in public without a fall.
findings.source_title: Design and Control of a Bipedal Robotic Character (Grandia et al., RSS 2024; arXiv 2501.05204)
findings.numbers: 5 DoF/leg + 4-DoF neck/head, 15.4 kg, 0.66 m; policy 50 Hz, actuator bus 600 Hz; Isaac Gym, 100,000 iterations ≈ 22 days on RTX 4090; 0.7 m/s fwd, 0.4 m/s lateral, 1.8 rad/s; standing tracking error 0.035 rad; ~10 h runtime without a fall.
findings.relevance: Proven recipe for keeping liveness (idle, look-at, clips) as an animation layer on top of a robust locomotion tracker — the BD-X pattern maps onto Go2 + WTW-style policy.

findings.claim: Expression-driven movement (functional utility + γ·expressive utility) roughly doubles ratings of engagement, character and connection versus function-only movement, but the gain vanishes on function-oriented tasks and older participants prefer less expressiveness.
findings.source_title: ELEGNT: Expressive and Functional Movement Design for Non-anthropomorphic Robot (Hu, Huang, Sivapurapu, Zhang; Apple, DIS 2025)
findings.numbers: N=21, within-subject F(γ=0) vs E(γ>0), 6 tasks, six 0–100 scales; E M=56.16 vs F M=28.77, t=19.85, p<0.0001; per-metric t: character 10.58, human-likeness 9.32, engagement 8.80, connection 8.50, willingness 7.37, intelligence 5.22; no significant difference on photograph-light / project-assistance / failure-indication tasks; older participants less receptive p<0.001; non-roboticists higher p=0.006.
findings.relevance: Quantifies the liveliness-vs-function trade-off and argues for a context-set expressiveness gain γ that Model B controls per segment (social vs functional) and per owner profile.

findings.claim: Canine-inspired body language added to Spot's locomotion by software alone raised pedestrians' ratings of animacy and cynomorphism in an in-the-wild between-subjects study, with no cost to perceived intelligence.
findings.source_title: Influencing Incidental Human-Robot Encounters: Expressive movement improves pedestrians' impressions of a quadruped service robot (Hauser et al., HICSS 2024)
findings.numbers: N=222 (112 body-language, 110 control), UT Austin intersection, March 2022; tail wag roll/yaw ±π/16 and ±π/8 rad, play bow 3π/14, sit π/7, circling 1.5 rad/s at 2 m/s, spin 1 rad/s; animacy F(1,220)=6.18 p=0.01; cynomorphism F=4.10 p=0.04; likeability F=3.21 p=0.07; intelligence F=0.18 p=0.67.
findings.relevance: Cheap hand-coded episodic clips already move animacy on a quadruped; a starting library for Parcel's Go2 and a template for in-the-wild evaluation.

findings.claim: Body language alone is a weak channel for a quadruped's navigation intent compared with audio or text, while coordinated multimodal cues are best and conflicting cues worst.
findings.source_title: Do Robots Need Body Language? Comparing Communication Modalities for Legible Motion Intent in Human-Shared Spaces (Cohen, Shimizu, Song, Bharath, Larson, Maes; arXiv 2604.03451)
findings.numbers: Online video study with Spot, ≈210 participants, 4 scenarios; intent-prediction accuracy ≈14% no signal, ≈44% body language, ≈58% lights, ≈82% audio, ≈88% text; coordinated multimodal best; body language raised perceived safety/trust.
findings.relevance: Direct support for tight speech–movement coupling: Model B's narration ('Sure, I'll check the sofa') must be time-locked to the anticipatory glance/turn rather than replaced by it.

findings.claim: Slow idle head motion makes a social robot read as more anthropomorphic and intelligent and elicits more spontaneous postural mirroring, whereas fast idle motion produces rigid, defensive listener posture; idle frequency did not change likeability or animacy.
findings.source_title: The Effect of Robot Posture and Idle Motion on Spontaneous Emotional Contagion during Robot-Human Interactions (Casso, Li, Nazir, Delevoye-Turrell; SCRITA @ RO-MAN 2022)
findings.numbers: Buddy robot, N=15, three sad stories, head up/down at low/medium/high frequency, Qualisys mocap; Godspeed main effect of idle frequency on Anthropomorphism p<0.001 and Perceived Intelligence p<0.001 (slow = higher); no effect on Likeability or Animacy.
findings.relevance: Sets the tempo rule for the alive base layer: slow, low-amplitude idle motion; fast fidgeting reads as threat.

findings.claim: Smooth (naturalistic) motion raises likeability regardless of form and raises animacy only when the robot looks humanlike, but a humanlike form moving naturalistically is rated more disturbing.
findings.source_title: Effects of form and motion on judgments of social robots' animacy, likability, trustworthiness and unpleasantness (Castro-González, Admoni, Scassellati; IJHCS 2016)
findings.numbers: Baxter, Tic-Tac-Toe 10 rounds; 2x2 naturalistic vs mechanical motion × one-arm vs full-body form + control; 56 recruited, 13 excluded (~42 analysed).
findings.relevance: For a dog-shaped Go2 (non-human form) smooth motion is a safe win for likeability; the uncanny penalty applies to humanlike forms, not Parcel.

findings.claim: Across 27 HRI user studies, secondary action (idle/breathing-type motion layered on the main action) is the most used animation principle, and animation techniques consistently improve perceived robot qualities and legibility of intent and emotion.
findings.source_title: Animation Techniques in Human-Robot Interaction User Studies: A Systematic Literature Review (Schulz, Torresen, Herstad; ACM THRI 2019)
findings.numbers: 27 articles (≈1,180 participants total); secondary action used in 8 studies, then anticipation, slow-in/slow-out, follow-through, timing, arcs; gaps: few long-term studies, few non-humanoid platforms.
findings.relevance: Justifies putting secondary action (always-on micro-motion) at the base of the stack and anticipation (glance before turn) in the attention layer.

findings.claim: Humans walking near a mobile robot fixate at 2–3 Hz with ~300–400 ms fixations, the head contributes about half of small gaze shifts, only ~25% of 40–50° shifts and >90% of shifts beyond 70°, and attention toward the robot stays constant regardless of activity.
findings.source_title: Human Gaze and Head Rotation during Navigation, Exploration and Object Manipulation in Shared Environments with Robots (Schreiter, Rudenko, Magnusson, Lilienthal; RO-MAN 2024)
findings.numbers: THÖR-MAGNI: 40 participants, 468 min eye tracking from 16; fixation duration ≈310–435 ms, rate 2.1–2.8 Hz; 80% of fixations within 28% of image; head contribution ≈50% (<10°), ≈25% (40–50°), >90% (>70°); walking speed 0.65–1.16 m/s; head-eye alignment vs speed ρ=-0.04, p<0.01.
findings.relevance: Target statistics for a neck-less Go2's 'gaze' (body yaw/pitch + camera crop + eye display): how often to shift, how long to dwell, when the body must turn.

findings.claim: A sideways gaze cue from an approaching human, Pepper, or eyed delivery robot makes pedestrians skirt to the cued side more often, independent of robot morphology, so eyes/gaze can signal a moving robot's intended direction.
findings.source_title: Gaze-Cues of Humans and Robots on Pedestrian Ways (Jakobowsky, Abrams, Rosenthal-von der Pütten; Int J Social Robotics 2023)
findings.numbers: Study 1 n=92 recruited/79 analysed, 645 trials; robots approach at ≈1.3 km/h in ~5 s videos; gaze-left → skirt left 59% vs 45% for straight eyes (b=-0.94, p<0.001); Study 2 n=176 left-hand-driving countries; counterpart type no effect; RoSAS discomfort Pepper 3.57 vs delivery robot 2.66 (p=0.04).
findings.relevance: Anticipatory gaze/heading cues are legible even on non-humanoid bodies; Parcel's pre-turn glance doubles as a navigation-intent signal in shared spaces.

findings.claim: Human gaze precedes head orientation, and both precede trajectory changes, so gaze predicts a walker's path earlier than head orientation; the authors propose the same cue for signalling a robot's path.
findings.source_title: Watch Where You're Going! Gaze and Head Orientation as Predictors for Social Robot Navigation (Holman, Anwar, Singh, Tec, Hart, Stone; ICRA 2021)
findings.numbers: Eye-tracked hallway walking with obstacles; direction predictable from gaze ≈95% vs head ≈89% at one-third of the path (reported figures); gaze leads head leads body.
findings.relevance: Orders the timing of Model A's outputs: gaze token first, body yaw next, path update last — matching Model B's 'Sure, I'll check…' utterance to the first step.

findings.claim: Active gaze for humanoid locomotion emerges from RL reward alone, runs onboard a Jetson Orin, and sharply raises success on terrain that requires looking at footholds.
findings.source_title: TAGA: Terrain-aware Active Gaze Learning for Generalizable Agile Humanoid Locomotion (Li et al.; arXiv 2606.05880)
findings.numbers: Unitree G1 + Jetson Orin; stepping stones 97.90% vs 52.30% vision-only; gap crossing 98.30% learned gaze vs 57.10% inactive gaze; 120 cm gap (+50% over prior best); beam 98.5%; stairs 100%.
findings.relevance: Shows Model A can learn a where-to-look action from navigation reward in sim, making attentive looking a by-product of competence rather than a scripted flourish.

findings.claim: A gimbal 'eyeball' trained by a BC-RL loop learns search, fixation, target switching and tracking purely from task reward, with a categorical 8-direction+stay gaze action, and outperforms fixed external cameras in large workspaces.
findings.source_title: Eye, Robot: Learning Hand-Eye Coordination with Reinforcement Learning (CoRL 2025 submission, Berkeley AUTOLab)
findings.numbers: 2-DOF gimbal + fisheye global-shutter camera on UR5e; EyeGym from 5.7K/30 fps 360° video; scene search exact-match 66.5% vs 28.1% random; object search 87% success, 1.8 s average; Eraser 60% vs exo 0%; E-Stop error 4.0 cm vs 7.8 cm; Towel 72.2% vs 62.1% without pretraining; eye action = 8 azimuth-elevation directions + stay.
findings.relevance: Template for a discrete look-at token in Parcel's act-token codec and for training gaze from downstream-task reward; authors flag mounting on a mobile robot as next step.

findings.claim: Language-guided preference learning finds user-preferred expressive quadruped gaits in a 5-dim behaviour space with only a handful of human queries.
findings.source_title: Efficiently Generating Expressive Quadruped Behaviors via Language-Guided Preference Learning (Clark, Hejna, Sadigh; arXiv 2502.03717)
findings.numbers: Pupper v3, Isaac Gym+PPO; ω∈R^5 (velocity, pitch, trot/pace/bound primitives); 'as few as four queries'; 53% lower L2 than preference learning, 62% lower than LLM-only; preferred 75.83±5.14% (11 people offline) and 76.67±10.59% (5 people active).
findings.relevance: A cheap way to personalise Parcel's expressive gait per owner (age/comfort) — ELEGNT's demographic effect handled by a few preference queries.

findings.claim: Video-diffusion priors can mass-produce language-annotated expressive Go2 motions that RL tracking policies execute on the real robot with high success, without animal motion capture.
findings.source_title: Unleashing Infinite Motion: Scaling Expressive Quadrupedal Motion via Generative Video Priors (Uni-Mo; Liu et al.; arXiv 2606.28237)
findings.numbers: Unitree Go2, 19-dim state; Quad-Imaginarium 7,488 motions / 18.5 h; retention 68.1% (97.0% semantic × 70.2% geometric gate); sim 97.6%; real 96.7% over 392 motions × 5 trials; body-link error 40.6 mm; human ratings identity 7.30/10, naturalness 6.24/10, text-action 4.75/10; FID 66.65→26.98.
findings.relevance: Supplies an episodic-clip library for the Go2 that Model B can trigger by language; text-action alignment (4.75/10) is the weak spot to watch.

findings.claim: Robot SSL array size trades accuracy against cost and latency, ego-noise from a moving robot significantly degrades localisation, and CNN methods beat spatial-spectrum methods on real robot data.
findings.source_title: A Review on Sound Source Localization in Robotics: Focusing on Deep Learning Methods (Jalayer, Jalayer, Baniasadi; Applied Sciences 2025)
findings.numbers: Binaural 2 mics; linear 3–8; circular 8–32; spherical 12–16; up to 64; ego-noise (robot vacuum) degrades SSL; platforms Pepper, NAO, iCub, quadrotors; CC BY 4.0.
findings.relevance: Flags Go2 locomotion ego-noise as a sim-to-real risk for sound-driven head turns; motivates gating DoA on stance phases or using a close-talk mic.

findings.claim: Active camera control for object navigation can be cast as an MDP and learned with RL, coordinated with the navigation action, improving multi-object navigation over fixed-camera baselines.
findings.source_title: Learning Active Camera for Multi-Object Navigation (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2022)
findings.numbers: Camera policy conditions on navigation action; exploration reward + rule-based guidance; 'consistently improves the performance of multi-object navigation over four baselines on two datasets' (exact SR/SPL not on the fetched pages).
findings.relevance: Precedent for a camera/heading action co-trained with navigation — the curiosity head-turn as a learned exploration action in Parcel's sim.

findings.claim: Idle motions versus meaningful motions modulate people's social responses to a robot in line with a threshold model of social influence: more social verification in the motion yields more social response.
findings.source_title: Motions of Robots Matter! The Social Effects of Idle and Meaningful Motions (Cuijpers & Knops, ICSR 2015)
findings.numbers: Two conditions (idle = low social verification, meaningful = high); N and effect sizes not on the fetched abstract page.
findings.relevance: Canonical statement that 'robots typically remain immobile' is itself a social signal; idle motion is the floor, goal-directed glances the ceiling.

findings.claim: Human gaze in crowds is tied to the presence and motion of other people, and a gaze-informed planner predicts socially salient pedestrians and lowers trajectory error.
findings.source_title: Learning from Human Gaze: Human-like Robot Social Navigation in Dense Crowds (Yu et al., AAAI-26)
findings.numbers: GazeNav egocentric video+gaze+trajectory dataset; 87.6% salient-pedestrian prediction accuracy; 15.4% lower trajectory error than SOTA.
findings.relevance: Human gaze data is a supervision source for where a navigating dog should look in crowds — the same data can drive a human-like attention prior in sim.

design_implications: Make liveness a fixed layered controller beneath Model A, not a Model A output: an always-on 'alive' base (slow breathing/sway, blink/LED, micro-saccades — slow tempo per Casso 2022), an attention layer (glance / engage / acknowledge with habituation + inhibition-of-return, Disney 2020 + Ruesch 2008 constants d_mem 0.95, d_h 0.2, t_h 0.85, d_a 0.03, sigma 6°), and the task layer; Model A only modulates amplitude/tempo and gain (BD-X animation-engine pattern).

Define Model A's local-movement action on the Go2 as a Walk-These-Ways-style behaviour vector (phase offsets, step frequency, body height, pitch, stance width, footswing) plus velocity command plus a discrete look-at token (EyeRobot: 8 azimuth-elevation directions + stay), all tracked by a fixed 50 Hz RL policy; this keeps expressiveness human-readable for Model B and evaluable for cost (WTW power/sprint numbers).

Adopt Pepper's SemiEngaged rule for sound: on a DoA event, emit a glance/body-yaw token and a StateDigest field (orienting_to_sound, azimuth, confidence), verify with the camera, then return; only after visual confirmation may the executive amend the goal. Expect ~7–10° azimuth from a 4-mic array, ~1–4° from 16 mics, and measure Go2 locomotion ego-noise in sim-to-real (gate DoA on stance phases or add a close-talk owner mic).

Expose an expressiveness gain γ (ELEGNT) that Model B sets from context: high during social segments and narration, low during functional/efficiency-critical segments and for owners who dislike it (older users, p<0.001); log γ in the StateDigest so narration and motion agree.

Time-lock Model B's narration to the body's anticipatory cue in the human order gaze → head/body yaw → path change (Holman 2021), so 'Sure, I'll check the sofa' lands on the first glance; body language alone conveys intent at ≈44% vs audio ≈82% (Cohen 2026), so speech + glance together is the legible channel.

Train where-to-look inside the simulator as a gaze/heading action rewarded by navigation/terrain and goal-finding (TAGA, EyeRobot, Learning Active Camera); curiosity head-turns then come from IOR/habituation on the saliency map rather than a script, and the visible looking is the liveness.

Imitate human locomotion gaze statistics for a neck-less Go2: fixations 300–400 ms at 2.3–2.8 Hz, small shifts by camera crop/eye display, body yaw once a shift exceeds ~40–50° and always beyond ~70° (Schreiter 2024); a sideways glance before turning is a legible path cue for bystanders (59% vs 45% skirting, Jakobowsky 2023).

Build a small episodic clip library for the Go2 (play-bow, sit, wiggle, look-around) — hand-coded canine behaviours already raised animacy on Spot in the wild (N=222, p=0.01) — and grow it with language-guided preference learning (4 queries) or video-prior datasets (Uni-Mo, 96.7% real success); Model B triggers clips, the animation layer blends them.

Evaluate liveliness and task performance jointly, which no fetched paper does on a quadruped: navigation SR/SPL and instruction-following on the frozen matrix alongside Godspeed/RoSAS (animacy, anthropomorphism, likeability, discomfort), an intent-legibility test for the pre-turn glance, and the liveness layer's cost in power and SR (Walk-These-Ways-style tables).
open_questions: XMOS XVF3800 (the owner's reSpeaker array) DoA resolution, update rate and latency are unverified: xmos.com returned 406 to the fetcher; only a search snippet says DoA is read via AEC_AZIMUTH_VALUES (four beam azimuths). Needs a manual datasheet read before sizing the sound→glance loop.

Matthis, Yates & Hayhoe 2018 (human look-ahead during walking on rough vs flat terrain) and Ribeiro & Paiva 2012 (animation principles for robots) could not be fetched from any host; their canonical numbers are not in these notes.
No fetched study measures perceived liveliness and navigation success concurrently on a quadruped; the size of the trade-off on a Go2 (SR/SPL vs animacy) is unknown and would be a new result.
How much ego-noise Go2 locomotion (gait frequency 2–4 Hz, Orin fans) injects into a 4-mic DoA estimate, and whether DoA must be gated to stance phases or supplemented by a wearable owner mic.

The Go2 has no neck: how much 'gaze' can body yaw/pitch plus camera crop and an eye/LED display convey, and what latency budget (event-based orienting at ms scale vs the 10 Hz frame clock) is needed for believable startle/orienting.

Whether animation-layer commands (glances, play-bow, body-height changes) can be made provably safe against the LiDAR occupancy planner and e-stop paths, i.e. how the liveness layer is subsumed by safety in the task executive.
Cuijpers & Knops 2015 effect sizes and N were not on the fetched page; the idle-vs-meaningful motion result is qualitative here.

results.claim: Disney's animatronic gaze system is a three-engine stack: an attention engine computing a per-person curiosity score from movement and distance with habituation and a 'guestbase', a behaviour-selection state machine (Read / Glance / Engage / Acknowledge), and a subsumption-layered motor layer whose always-on base show (breathing, blinking, saccades) is overridden by higher layers; eyes lead the head and each actuator group has its own motion bandwidth.
results.evidence_quote: "The architecture of our robot gaze interaction consists of three components: the attention engine, behavior selection engine, and behavior library (Fig. 2)." ... "Φ = Θ(t) ∗ w_distance ∗ f(d_nose) ∗ w_raised_hand(h_r_hand + h_l_hand) + w_hand(v̂_r_hand + v̂_l_hand) + w_nose v̂_nose + w_distance f(d_nose) ... where Θ(t) ∈ [0, 1] is a habituation factor" ... "2) Guestbase: In addition to a state machine, the behavior selection engine also contains a database of people in the scene, called the guestbase, which functions as a form of short-term memory." ... "higher levels are able to 'subsume' lower levels – i.e., they are able to integrate, modify, suppress or even completely override lower levels." ... "L1 Alive Show: This level provides the minimum requirements for the robot to be perceived as animate. This includes behaviors such as breathing, eye blinking, saccades, etc." ... "Our Audio-Animatronics® figure is able to saccade with a frequency of 20 Hz. For our mutual gaze actions (glance and engage), the eyes saccade randomly between three points forming a triangle on a person-of-interest: the eyes and nose. Timing of saccadic movements is random with a range of 0.1 to 0.5s." ... "eyelid motion had a frequency of 10 Hz, whereas head/neck motion was limited to 5 Hz or less. ... with any turn-to-glance or turn-to-engage movement, the head turning is always led with the eyes, i.e., the eyes reach the gaze position first at a high rate of speed, followed by the head at a lower rate of speed" ... Discussion: "The architecture and implementation for human-like robot gaze appears to produce life-like gaze on our robot character." (no participants, questionnaire, or user study anywhere in the paper)
results.correction: Gist and all numbers hold (20 Hz saccades, 0.1–0.5 s random timing between eyes/nose points, Read/Glance/Engage/Acknowledge states, L1 Alive Show = breathing/blinking/saccades, eyes lead head, eyelid 10 Hz vs head/neck ≤5 Hz, no user study — evaluation is qualitative, not explicitly 'show-floor'). One detail is misplaced: the guestbase (short-term memory of persons) belongs to the behaviour-selection engine alongside the state machine, not to the attention engine; the attention engine computes the curiosity score from hand/nose velocity, raised hands, distance and a habituation factor Θ(t). The paper names the third component the 'behavior library' (show objects layered by subsumption L0 Zero → L1 Alive → L2 Read → L3 Glance → L4 Engage → L5 Acknowledge); a separate perception engine (wrnch skeleton fitting) feeds it.

results.claim: The iCub multimodal attention framework fuses visual and acoustic saliency by max into a head-centred ego-sphere with short-term memory, habituation and inhibition-of-return; the interplay yields emergent exploratory gaze (scan salient points in decreasing order, then revisit), and a voice injects auditory saliency that shifts gaze.
results.evidence_quote: "it is required to combine the different sensory modalities into a single final map. This is done by taking the maximum value across all saliency channels at each location." ... "The ego-sphere is head-centered and fixed with respect to the robot's torso." ... "The egocentric saliency map corresponds to a short-term memory for salient regions." ... "This exploratory behavior results from the interplay between the attention selection and inhibition mechanisms." ... "After having focused on the first most salient location, the system continues, driven by inhibition of return, to explore next most salient locations in an emergent sequence. ... We can see from the results that all points are visited the same number of times." ... "talking to the robot causes auditory saliency being added to the egocentric map and results in a shift in gaze direction. ... For this setup σior = 12◦ was used." ... "The saliency ego-sphere uses a resolution R_ego of 320 by 240 pixels. This corresponds to a spatial discretization of 1.125◦ in latitudinal and 0.75◦ in longitudinal direction. ... While the motor control module operates at a frequency higher than 20 Hz, the ego-sphere is updated between five to ten times per second." Table I: "dmem 0.95 short-term memory decay; da 0.03 inhibition decay; dh 0.2 visual habituation gain; th 0.85 threshold for triggering inhibition; σior 6◦". Fig. 3: "sound source ... with an extension σϑ and σϕ of 25◦ corresponding to the calculated uncertainty". Fig. 2: "The iCub head: six degrees of freedom".
results.correction: None needed. Note only that the 25° auditory blob width is the calculated uncertainty in the Fig. 3 example, not a fixed constant, and that all experiments used the head only with the torso fixed.

results.claim: Pepper/NAO's ALBasicAwareness reacts to Sound, Movement, People and Touch stimuli by looking at the stimulus origin, checking for a human, and otherwise looking back; the SemiEngaged mode glances at any new stimulus but always returns to the engaged person, and tracking can be Head-only, BodyRotation, WholeBody or MoveContextually.
results.evidence_quote: Stimulus types: "Sound", "Movement", "People", "Touch". "looks at the origin of the stimulus and checks if there is a human there" ... otherwise it "goes back to its previous occupation". "SemiEngaged: it keeps listening to the stimuli, and if it gets a stimulus, it will look in its direction, but it will always go back to the person it is engaged with." Tracking modes: "Head: the tracking only uses the head"; "BodyRotation: the tracking uses the head and the rotation of the body"; "WholeBody: the tracking uses the whole body, but doesn't make it rotate"; "MoveContextually: performs small moves such as approaching the tracked person, stepping backward, rotating". Page is NAOqi "Aldebaran Software 2.1.0.18". Companion API page (albasicawareness-api.html): "LookStimulusSpeed: speed of head moves when looking at a stimulus (float in ]0;1])", "LookBackSpeed: speed of head moves when looking back to previous position after false alarm (float in ]0;1])" — no defaults given.
results.correction: None needed. LookStimulusSpeed/LookBackSpeed are on the separate API page, not the overview page cited; their range ]0;1] is confirmed, defaults are not documented.

results.claim: A single RL locomotion policy conditioned on a small human-readable behaviour vector (gait phase offsets, step frequency, body height, pitch, stance width, footswing height) executes trotting, pronking, pacing, bounding, dance and posture changes on a Unitree Go1 at 50 Hz, with a stated cost to in-distribution sprint performance.
results.evidence_quote: "We deploy our controller in the real world on the Unitree Go1 Edu robot [27]. An onboard Jetson TX2 NX computer runs our trained policy. ... training and deployment, the control frequency is 50Hz." ... "a 3-dimensional command vector ct = [vx_cmd, vy_cmd, ωz_cmd]" ... "We parameterize the style of task completion by an 8-dimensional vector of behavior parameters, bt = [θ1_cmd, θ2_cmd, θ3_cmd, f_cmd, hz_cmd, φ_cmd, sy_cmd, hz_f,cmd]" ... "A learned controller transitions between classical structured gaits: trotting, pronking, pacing, and bounding in place at alternating frequencies 2Hz and 4Hz." ... "we identify a latency of around 20 ms in our system and model this as a constant action delay" ... Table 3 (3.0 m/s column): Trotting 98±9, Bounding 127±35, Gait-free Baseline 102±14. Table 4 Survival: Trotting 0.88±0.01, Gait-free 0.83±0.01. "the distance from the location of the robot's front feet at takeoff to the location of the hind feet upon landing is 60 cm" ... "22 cm bar; the robot body thickness is 13 cm" ... "90 bpm" ... "Our experiments show that the benefits of adding MoB can come at a cost to in-distribution task performance, specifically limiting the robot's flat-ground sprinting performance (Table 5, appendix)."
results.correction: None needed. Caveat for the relevance note: the Table 3 power figures and Table 4 survival rates are simulation results (fraction of maximum episodic reward), not on-robot measurements; the hardware demos (gait switching, 60 cm leap, 22 cm crawl, 90 bpm dance, payload pitch) are real-world.

results.claim: Expression-driven movement (functional utility + γ·expressive utility) roughly doubles ratings of engagement, character and connection versus function-only movement, but the gain vanishes on function-oriented tasks and older participants prefer less expressiveness.
results.evidence_quote: "max F(τ)+γE(τ)" ... "a within-subject study design in which each participant viewed videos of the robot completing six different tasks" ... "recruited 30 participants...resulted in 21 valid participants (N=21)" ... "robots with expression-driven movements are rated much higher (M=56.16, std=27.15) than robots incorporating only function-driven movements (M=28.77, std=27.15) ... Welch's t-test revealed a statistical significance in the difference, t=19.85, p<0.0001" ... "Perceived character (t=10.58), followed by Human-likeliness (t=9.32), Engagement (t=8.80), Sense of Connection (t=8.50), then Willingness to Interact (t=7.37), and Perceived Intelligence (t=5.22)" ... "for function-oriented tasks (photograph light, project assistance, failure indication), the two robots show no significant differences in metrics such as Perceived intelligence, Willingness to interact, and Engagement." ... "for social-oriented tasks (play music, conversation, remind water), expression-driven robots significantly outperform function-driven robots across all metrics." ... results.correction: All numbers check out, but 'the gain vanishes on function-oriented tasks' overstates the finding: on the three function-oriented tasks the E–F difference is non-significant for perceived intelligence, willingness to interact and engagement; the paper does not say character, connection or human-likeness differences vanish there (on social-oriented tasks E beats F on all metrics). Also the ~2x figure (56.16 vs 28.77) is the pooled mean over all six 0–100 scales and all tasks; the paper reports per-metric t-values, not per-metric means, so 'roughly doubles engagement, character and connection' individually is an inference rather than a stated result.

strongest_designs: Model A = TIC-VLA-shaped dual-rate controller on-Orin (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.02459v2, verified): a <=1B VLM (InternVL3-1B: InternViT-300M + Qwen2.5-0.5B) at 0.5-2 Hz writes KV-cache features + waypoint/pixel goals that a 10 Hz act-token policy consumes asynchronously, trained under randomized reasoning delay U(0,10 s); 0.75 SR on a real Go2 from a Jetson Orin NX (0.85 on a laptop GPU). Add LiveVLN's guard-buffer + revisable-tail handoff (https://arxiv.org/html/2604.19536, verified: 30.5% waiting ratio, 94.9% stop-and-go on a G1; -72.8/-77.7% waiting with SR preserved 59.9 vs 61.4 / 57.2 vs 56.4) so motion never stalls while the slow lane thinks. Use RGB-D/stereo input (VLN-PE: RGB-only loses ~12 pts in low light vs 2-3 for RGB-D; StereoNav 81.1% vs StreamVLN 24.3% real). The narratable representation is the slow lane's language 'motion/subtask' line (RT-H / pi0.5 style), emitted at <=1 Hz, never at 10 Hz.

Model B = Hi Robot over Model A (https://arxiv.org/html/2502.19417): a high-level VLM re-invoked every ~1 s AND immediately on an owner utterance, emitting (a) an atomic language command / goal amendment for Model A and (b) an utterance for the voice lane, grounded in the current image and StateDigest; trained on VLM-synthesised situated interjections labelled with InterruptBench's Addition / Revision / Retraction -> queue / revise / retract. Injection follows YAY Robot: the spoken correction temporarily overrides the high-level language command while the low-level policy keeps running; corrections logged with prior context and used to fine-tune (4-11% extra data gave +15-45 pts). Gate the whole path with owner speaker-verification + addressee detection (gap above).

Plan queue = explicit, not implicit: a stored, snapshot-able historical queue (CoMuRoS INTERRUPTED marking + Robots-Can-Multitask per-task snapshot + JARVIS-1 plan memory) with ITP's replanning rule (completed steps + guidelines + new request + chat history) and an explicit map/plan store because implicit transformer memory does not carry across instructions (IVLN t-nDTW 61 -> 45). Success is externally verified (frontier LLM controllers believe they succeeded in every trial), and EchoChain's three failure modes (contextual inertia, interruption amnesia, objective displacement) become named eval rows.

Narration lane = push-not-pull into the hosted voice: StateDigest + a rolling natural-language ledger (past-tense completed skills / future-tense next milestone; +4-22 pts long-horizon) pushed as out-of-band items, because realtime backends under-invoke perception tools (recall ~0.6). Use OpenAI Realtime's sideband connection + async function calling with filler utterances, or Gemini Live NON_BLOCKING tools with WHEN_IDLE/SILENT scheduling; Gemini resumes after side-talk 0.99 vs GPT-4o Realtime 0.02 (https://arxiv.org/html/2507.23159, verified), which matters more in a household than GPT's 0.23 s stop latency. Content follows Kox (what + why on every deviation), the verbalization space (abstraction/locality/specificity), and a proactivity gate (users prefer moderate over non-stop).

Eval harness = tau-Voice's 200 ms tick orchestrator with an environment-tied LLM user simulator (tau2: 16% error tied vs 40-47% prompt-only; report pass^k not pass^1) wrapped around a Habitat-3.0/Isaac Go2 twin with an added audio channel; score SR/SPL/nDTW (R2R-CE/RxR-CE/HM3D-OVON/GOAT), LiveVLN idle ratio, Full-Duplex-Bench stop/resume rates, IHBench-style typed interruptions (Normal/Impatient/Correction/Topic switch/Filler/Pushback) injected at InterruptBench's 60% point, personal-space compliance from Social-HM3D, and chance-corrected kappa for every LLM judge (raw agreement overstates kappa by 34-41 pp).
risks: A 10 Hz language stream is infeasible on published evidence: ELLSA (LLaMA-3.1-8B) needs 786-854 ms per 1 s block on an A100 (verified https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16756); DuplexSLA fits <=10 action-channel tokens per 160 ms chunk (verified); every narrating navigator ran on a remote 4090/A100. Model A's representation must be a <=1 Hz slow-tick output or the 10 Hz loop will stall (LiveVLN's 30.5% idle is the measured symptom).

Speaking while acting costs control quality: ELLSA drops 84.4% -> 73.2% (11.2 pts) on LIBERO-Long when it speaks, and it is simulation-only with no real-robot validation (verified). Whether the penalty is weight-sharing or token-budget sharing is unablated, so a unified Model A may pay it on navigation too.

Speech-conditioned behaviour has never crossed sim-to-real: ELLSA is sim-only, RoboEgo releases nothing, VITA-E is tabletop; the Go2 gap is already dominated by camera height / lighting / locomotion mismatch (NaVid 22.4% -> 4.7% on a 0.5 m quadruped) and motion blur/oscillation (StreamVLN-class 57% -> 35%/20%), and 2-4 moving people cut a real Go2 from 0.44 to 0.18 SR.

Hosted voice in a household: GPT-4o Realtime resumes after side-talk 0.02 and background speech 0.04 (verified) so the dog's narration will be silenced by any ambient conversation; IHBench (verified https://arxiv.org/html/2606.19595) finds GPT-family continue correctly after a filler only 7-31% and Gemini 3.x regresses to 13-32% (the digest's 'Gemini 62-68%' is the 2.5 family, not the recommended 3.1 Flash Live); task fulfilment decays -0.030 per turn; voice agents retain only 30-45% of text capability; tool-bearing turns take 4-7 s.

Session lifetime: OpenAI Realtime hard 60-minute cap; Gemini Live 15-minute audio cap without compression, ~10-minute connections; no researcher designed the reconnect/carry-over for an all-day companion; a mis-tuned VAD produced 7-15 s spikes.

Benchmark numbers are not comparable across hardware: TIC-VLA's Table 3 runs each method on a different GPU (Orin NX / RTX 4060 / A6000) and says so; NaVILA's own 88% (25 instructions, remote GPU) vs 0.35 in TIC-VLA's reproduction shows real-Go2 SR swings by 50 pts with task set and platform.

Licensing blocks a commercial training corpus: Matterport3D ToU (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0) covers R2R-CE/RxR-CE scenes, TartanGround and Alexa Arena are non-commercial, NaVILA weights carry no license, Isaac Sim is proprietary, Robostral Navigate release terms unstated; only Uni-NaVid (MIT), LOVON (MIT), GR00T N1 (CC BY 4.0), Moshi (CC-BY 4.0), RxR annotations (CC-BY), OM1 (MIT), Genesis (Apache-2.0) are clean.

Judge reliability is weaker than the digest implies: IHBench's actual judge-human Cohen's kappa is 0.45-0.51 (task) and 0.41-0.44 (recovery) — not 0.75/0.70 — and LLM-judge raw agreement overstates kappa by 33.8-41.3 pp; Parcel's conversation-quality scorer (2/10, 3/13) is small-N and un-chance-corrected.

Narration can manufacture over-trust: users could not detect fabricated museum answers, transparency utterances inflate inferred capabilities, reasoning text is misread as causal, and explanations help only unreliable robots (Wang 2016); a companion that narrates plans it then fails will convert every deviation into a trust violation unless it says what and why.

Interruption handling itself is the failure source: EchoChain's half-duplex control shows handling the interruption causes most failures; InterruptBench success ~20-55%; tau2 dual-control costs 18-25 pp; SIF collapses 81% -> 29% when the referent moves. Expect the interruption tier of the headless-city matrix to start far below the SR 0.20 of the frozen matrix.

Microphone reality: no ASR/DoA numbers exist for a walking Go2; WSO2 called the onboard audio 'incredibly noisy' and mounted a Jabra; XVF3800 DoA update rate unverified; PersonaPlex/Moshi numbers (0.07-0.24 s interruption) assume clean audio.
Compute on the AGX Orin 64 GB is unmeasured for any 7-8B navigator; the digest's only Jetson result is a 0.5B LLM, so 'fully duplex over all sensors' with a 7B backbone is an assumption.

Survey coverage is thin for mid-2026: five of ten researcher sessions and this critic's session exhausted the 200-search budget before reaching quadruped self-narration, SoundSpaces/AVLEN, NVIDIA Go2+LLM demos, Model Interruption Bench, and Show-Your-Work HRI-2026; the strongest-design list may be missing a direct precedent.

Data-hungry fine-tuning vs weak scaling: Qwen-RobotNav needed 15.6M samples / 2,816 H100-h for OVON SR 53.1, yet 'What Limits VLN' finds scale correlates weakly with success; trainability in Parcel's desktop sim may hinge on physics/visual realism (VLN-PE 7.1% -> 28.6% after physics-sim fine-tuning) rather than sample count.
contradictions: NaVILA real-Go2 success: 88% on 25 instructions in its own paper vs 0.35 in TIC-VLA's Table 3 (verified); the digest's 'same real tasks' holds only within TIC-VLA's task set, and TIC-VLA explicitly notes each method ran on a different platform (Orin NX / RTX 4060 / A6000), so neither the 0.75-vs-0.50-vs-0.35 ranking nor the 88% is a clean cross-paper comparison.

IHBench judge agreement: the benchmarks digest cites kappa 0.75 / 0.70; the paper's HTML reports Cohen's kappa 0.45-0.51 (task fulfilment) and 0.41-0.44 (recovery), and names Gemini 2.5 Flash (thinking, .704) not GPT Realtime 2 as the recovery-quality leader (verified https://arxiv.org/html/2606.19595).

DuplexSLA backbone size: the dual-system digest flags README '~7B' vs HTML '77B-scale'; the HTML still literally says '77B-scale backbone, initialized from Step-Audio 2 mini' (verified) — a 'mini' initialization makes 77B implausible but the PDF must settle it before DuplexSLA is cited as an on-robot-feasible shape. Also DuplexSLA's tool-call accuracy (85.56%) is BELOW the ASR+LLM cascade (91.33%); it wins only on delay (0.64 s vs 2.77 s).

Hosted-voice turn latency is quoted at 1.7 s (Jan 2025 packet study), 1.57 s / 0.83 s (DuplexSLA-Bench, semantic vs 40 ms server VAD), ~410 ms median (June 2026 blog), 6.89 s (Full-Duplex-Bench v3 with tools) and 'p95 -25%' (OpenAI, unverified) — these are different metrics, VAD settings and model versions, and the hosted-voice digest presents them as one quantity.

Backchannel/filler handling for GPT realtime: Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5 says GPT-4o Realtime resumes after a backchannel 70% (verified) while IHBench says GPT-family continue correctly after a filler only 7-31%; for Gemini, FDB v1.5 gives 93% (2.0 Flash Live) and IHBench gives 62-68% (2.5) but 13-32% (3.x). Model generations and protocols differ; the digest's 'Gemini handles fillers well' is not established for the 3.1 Flash Live the hosted-voice digest recommends.

What dominates the Go2 sim-to-real gap: VLN-PE says camera height / lighting / locomotion controller; 'What Limits VLN' says motion blur and viewpoint oscillation (fix: stereo); LiveVLN says stop-and-go timing; NavDP says missing real-to-sim data (+30%); OVMM winners say error detection/recovery. The streaming-VLN and go2-sim2real digests each assert a different dominant cause.

Data scale: 'What Limits VLN' finds training-data scale correlates weakly with success, while the benchmarks digest's SOTA (Qwen-RobotNav, 15.6M samples), RAINbow (238K synthetic dialog episodes doubling unseen success) and NavDP (+30% with more data) argue the opposite.

History length: NaVILA says 8 frames saturate R2R-CE; Uni-NaVid says instruction following collapses without long-term memory; IVLN says implicit memory does not carry across instructions; MemoryVLA says 64 entries is worse than 16; StreamVLN says bounded pruned memory beats unbounded. The world-state digest presents these as one 'less is more' lesson, but they measure different tasks and none under interruption.

Asking for help: HANNA/VNLA/Just Ask/DialFRED report 2-6x success from agent-initiated questions, while the plan-queue digest's HRI evidence says interleaving or extra interaction lowers perceived competence and DialFRED says asking every step buys little; the dialogue digest recommends asking, the HRI evidence recommends restraint — the two are reconciled only by a cost-weighted ask policy nobody in the digest benchmarked for navigation.

Interface choice for Model A: the dual-system digest argues for a language interface (Hi Robot / pi0.5 / RT-H) because it is narratable, while the fastest deployed navigators use latent interfaces (DualVLN latent queries, TIC-VLA KV features, Helix latent vector, GR00T cross-attention); the digest itself admits no paper compares the two on control quality or narratability.

Native duplex vs cascade: the dual-system digest holds up Moshi ('no explicit turn model needed') and PersonaPlex (0.07-0.24 s interruption latency), but Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5 measures Moshi stopping in 1.16 s and resuming after a backchannel 6% of the time (verified), SID-Bench reports ~14% false interruptions, and VoiceBench/DuplexSLA-Bench show cascades match or beat end-to-end models on accuracy.

Trust effect of narration: Wang 2016 finds explanations help only an unreliable robot; Dobby finds every participant preferred the narrating robot; Inner Thoughts finds users dislike non-stop chatter; Kox finds four updates per mission keep trust with no workload cost. The self-narration digest treats narration as uniformly positive; the evidence says it is rate- and reliability-dependent.

Minor extraction inconsistencies to resolve before any number is load-bearing: Falcon Social-HM3D SR = SPL = 55.15 (identical values suggest a mis-read); GOAT-Bench radius rendered '11m' vs 1 m; VLN-CE turn angle 15 vs 30 degrees; TartanGround abstract vs body counts; ELLSA's penalty is 84.4 -> 73.2 = 11.2 pts (the digest's '11' is right; a 13.3 figure from one extraction is arithmetic error).
